input to D flip-flop.
When L = 1 and L ' = 0 then input data is passed to flip-flop input and this logic is illustrated in 
Fig. 8.55.
When L = 0 and L ' = 1 then flip-flop output is rewritten as input and this logic is illustrated in 
Fig. 8.56.
Buffer and Controlled Buffer Register
In a digital system, during data transmission, when an n-bit register is used in between two digital 
devices in order to provide signal current level matching then the register is called buffer register. When 
control signals are provided to load and clear the content of buffer register then the buffer register is called 
controlled buffer register. 
8.6  Shift Register
A register capable of shifting the binary information from one flip-flop to another (or one cell to 
another) is called shift register.
There are four types of shift registers.
1. Serial-in Serial-out shift register
2. Serial-in Parallel-out shift register
3. Parallel-in Serial-out shift register
4. Parallel-in Parallel-out shift register.
8.6.1  Serial-In Serial-Out Shift Register
Right Shift Register
A 4-bit serial-in serial-out shift register for right shift operation is shown in Fig. 8.57. The input 
data is given to left most flip-flop and output data is obtained from right most flip-flop. The output of flip-
flops are cascaded, i.e, output of one becomes input for next and so on. For every clock pulse the data bit 
is shifted by one position from left to right as shown in Table 8.23

Reset facility and shift control are also provided in 
the shift register.
When reset is 0 all the flip-flop outputs will be 
cleared. Usually, the output of flip-flops are cleared in the 
beginning by making reset low and then reset is tied to high.
The shift control is provided to allow or disallow the 
clock. When shift control is 1, clock is allowed. When shift 
control is 0, clock is not allowed. The data will shift only 
when clock is allowed and so shift operation is performed 
as long as shift control is 1.
Left Shift Register
For left shift operation the shifting is performed from right to left and the connections in Fig. 8.57

Shift Register for Right and Left Shift Operation
The left to right and right to left shift operation can be performed in a single serial-in serial-out shift 
register with additional logic circuits and two shift control signals as shown in Fig. 8.59.
The input of flip-flops are applied through AND-OR combinational circuit. The flip-flop input for 
left to right shift is logically ANDed with RS control signal. The flip-flop input for right to left shift is 
logically ANDed with LS control signal. The output of both AND gates are logically ORed and applied as 
flip-flop inputs. The arrangement will allow only one shift data to flip-flop inputs.
When RS = 1 and LS = 0, the left to right shift data is allowed to flip-flop inputs to perform right 
shift operation. When RS = 0 and LS = 1, the right to left shift data is allowed to flip-flop inputs to perform 
left shift operation. 
The RS and LS control signals are also used to control the input and output data and also clock 
signal. When both RS and LS are either 0 or 1 then clock is not allowed and no shift operation is performed.

When shift control is 0, the data can be loaded in parallel and clock also not allowed. When shift

not loaded in output.
8.6.5  Universal Shift Register
A shift register that can accept serial or parallel input data and output data in parallel along with 
right or left shift operation is called universal shift register. 
Therefore, an universal shift register can be used to implement any type of shift register with right/
left shift selection.
The universal shift register will have the following features.
●   A reset/clear control in order to clear the output to 0.
●   A clock input to synchronize the operations.
●   A shift right control.
●   A shift left control.
●   A parallel load control.
●   Parallel output lines.
●   No-change state.
A 4-bit universal shift register using D flip-flops is shown in Fig. 8.63. The input to D flip-flops 
are applied through 4:1 MUX which has two selection lines which are used as operation mode control.

8.6.6  Applications of Shift Register
● Serial-to-Parallel Conversion: Shift registers can convert serial data into parallel data. This is 
useful for interfacing serial devices with parallel devices in microcontrollers, display devices or memory.
● Parallel-to-Serial Conversion: Shift registers can convert parallel data into serial data. This is 
useful for interfacing parallel devices with serial devices in microcontrollers, display devices or memory.
●  Data Storage and Memory Expansion: Shift registers can be used as temporary storage elements 
to store data temporarily. 
● Data Serializing and de-serializing:  In communication systems, shift registers are often used 
to serialize parallel data for transmission over a serial link and de-serialize serial data back into parallel 
form at the receiving end.
● Shift and Rotate Operations: Shift registers can perform shift and rotate operations on data. This 
is useful in applications such as cryptography and error detection/correction algorithms and to implement 
arithmetic and logical operations in digital systems. 
● Frequency Division and Counting: Shift registers can be configured as frequency dividers or 
counters. 
● LED and Display Drivers: Shift registers can be used to implement multiplexed display drivers 
in LED based display devices to reduce power requirements. 
● Pattern Generation and Pattern Detection: Shift registers can generate complex patterns by 
loading specific bit sequences into the register. They can also be used for pattern detection in applications 
such as data compression, image processing, or sequence recognition.
Serial Adder
              A serial adder is a digital circuit that performs addition operation on binary numbers serially. The 
serial adder adds one bit at a time, starting from the least significant bit (LSB) to the most significant bit 
(MSB). Serial adders are commonly used in applications where resources are limited or when sequential 
processing is required. A 4-bit serial adder is shown in Fig. 8.69. The two data to be added are stored in 
shift registers and shifted to a full adder.
           The binary digits (bits) are added one pair at a time using a full-adder circuit. The carry generated 
from the full adder is transferred to a D-flip flop. Thus, the output of this D-flip flop is then used as the 
carry input for the next pair of addition. The sum bit S is transferred to a third shift register. The input data 
are loaded parallely in shift registers and addition is performed serially and after all bits addition the sum 
can be read parallely.

8.7.1  Designing of Rolling Display
The rolling display is rolling a message with alpha-numeric symbols from left to right or vice-versa. 
In digital system, the alpha-numeric symbols are expressed as ASCII codes. In rolling display the message 
to be displayed is input as ASCII codes. Each character of message consists of 7-bit ASCII code and 1 
parity bit. The 7-segment LED displays are selected to display the message. 
Rolling display system to roll a 5 character word or message is developed using universal shift 
registers and ASCII-to-7-segment decoder as shown in Fig. 8.70. Here, the serial output of a lower order 
shift register is connected to serial input of next higher order shift register in order to left shift the characters 
serially from one register to another register.
The universal shift register has the facility to input and output the data both in parallel and serial. 
The message to be displayed is initially loaded in parallel to shift registers and then output in parallel to 
ASCII-to-7-segment decoder for display. After a delay called shift time the 8-bit characters loaded in shift 
registers are serially shifted bit-by-bit left 8 times so that the character data in one shift register move to 
next register. 
During this shift time the 7-segment display has to be blanked using a blanking control signal 
to prevent ghosting of information. After shifting the ASCII characters the data is output in parallel for 
display. This process is repeated again and again, so that the message will roll from left to right as shown in  
Fig. 8.70. A control circuit has to be designed to take care of parallel loading, shifting and blanking control.     
8.7.2  Designing of Real Time Clock  
The real time clock is a digital clock that maintains the time in hours, minutes and seconds. The 12 
hours real time clock is developed using ripple carry MOD counters and 7-segment LED displays as shown 
in Fig. 8.71. The clock is designed to show seconds using two 7-segment displays in order to display 0 to 
59 seconds. Similarly, two 7-segment displays are used to display minutes from 0 to 59 and two 7-segment 
displays are used to display hours from 0 to 12. MOD-10 and MOD-6 counters are used to count seconds 
and minutes. MOD-10 and MOD-2 counters are used to count hours. The basic timing signal is selected 
as 1 Hz clock signal. The inverse of frequency is time period and so the time period or duration of every 
clock pulse is one second. 
The 1 Hz clock is directly applied to clock of MOD-10 seconds counter, so that it is increment by 1 
in every one second. The MOD-10 seconds counter will generate a reset signal in every 10th clock pulse to 
reset the counter and this reset is also divide-by-10 clock of 1 Hz clock signal. The frequency of this clock 
is 1/10 = 0.1 Hz and time period is 1/0.1 = 10 seconds. The 0.1 Hz clock out of MOD-10 seconds counter 
is used as input clock of the MOD-6 seconds counter, so that it increment by 1 in every 10 seconds.     
The MOD-6 seconds counter will generate a reset signal in every 6th clock pulse to reset the counter 
and this reset is also divide-by-6 clock of 0.1 Hz clock signal. The frequency of this clock is 0.1/6 Hz and 
the time period is 6/0.1 = 60 seconds or 1 minute. The 0.1/6 Hz clock out of MOD-6 seconds counter is 
used as input clock of the MOD-10 minutes counter, so that it increment by 1 in every 60 seconds. 
The divide-by-10 clock out of MOD-10 minutes counte r will have a frequency of  
(0.1/6)/10 = 0.1/60 Hz and the time period is 60/0.1 = 600 seconds or 600/60 = 10 minutes and this clock 
is used as input clock of the MOD-6 minutes counter, so that it increment by 1 in every 10 minutes.

The divide-by-6 clock out of MOD-6 minutes counter will have a frequency of  
(0.1/60)/6 = 0.1/360 Hz and the time period is 360/0.1 = 3600 seconds or 3600/60 = 60 minutes = 1 hour 
and this clock is used as input clock of the MOD-8 hours counter, so that it increment by 1 in every 60 
minutes.
The divide-by-10 clock out of MOD-10 hour’s counter  will have a frequency of  
(0.1/360)/10 = 0.1/3600 Hz and the time period is 3600/0.1 = 36000 seconds or 36000/60 = 600 minutes or 
600/60 = 10 hours and this clock is used as input clock of the MOD-2 hour’s counter, so that it increment 
by 1 in every 10 hours. The MOD-2 counter generates a divide-by-2 output clock signal with a frequency 
of (0.1/3600)/2 = 0.1/7200 Hz and with a time period 7200/0.1 = 72000 seconds or 72000/6000 = 12 hours, 
which is used as master reset to reset all counters when the time reaches 12 hours.
The real time clock needs a facility to load or preset initial timing in the beginning or during switch 
ON, so that the clock will maintain the time from this initial value.           
8.8  Summary of Important Concepts
1. In sequential circuits with unused states, when clock pulses are applied, if the sequential circuit cycle  
 through only unused states and never arrives at in a used state then this condition is called lock-out.
2. A register that goes through prescribed (or predefined) sequence of states upon the application of clock  
 pulses is called a counter.
3. A counter that follows a binary count sequence is called binary counter. 
4. An n-bit binary counter consists of n flip-flops and can count binary from 0 to 2 n - 1.
5. The modulus of the counter refers to number states a counter will pass through before coming back to  
 initial state. 
6. An n-bit counter will have 2 n possible states and if the n-bit counter passes through all possible states 
 before coming to initial state then it is called MOD-2 n counter.
7. An n-bit binary counter divides the clock frequency by 2 n and so n-bit counter is also called divide-by-2n 
 counter
8. The n-bit MOD-N counter uses only N states in the 2 n possible states of n-bit counter and the remaining 
 states are unused states. 
9. MOD-N counters can be designed using n-bit binary counter by using only N states of n-bit counter  
 provided N < 2 n
10. The MOD-N counter divides the clock frequency by N and so it is also called divide-by-N counter.
11. The counters can be broadly classified into two categories: Ripple counters and synchronous counters.
12. In a ripple counter, a flip-flop output will act as clock for another flip-flop.
13. In synchronous counters all the flip-flops are triggered simultaneously by a common clock.
14. A binary ripple counter is constructed using a series of complementing flip-flops.
15. In up counter, the output will increment for every  clock pulse and the count sequence will be from 0 to 2n-1.
16. In down counter, the output will decrement for every clock pulse and counter the count sequence will be  
 from 2 n - 1 to 0.
17. A BCD counter has to count only from 0 to 9, and when the count reaches 1010, the output has to be  
 reset to all zero, so that next count sequence will start. 
18. The BCD counter is also called MOD-10 counter.

--- Page 741 ---
8.126                                              Digital Logic Circuits
19. The synchronous counters are designed using complementing flip-flops similar to ripple counters, but 
 the clock is applied simultaneously to all the flip-flops.
20. In synchronous counters, the flip-flop inputs are applied through some combinational logic circuits.
21. A ring counter is a circular shift register with only one flip-flop output being set at a time and all other  
 flip-flop outputs are cleared. 
22. A ring counter produces a sequence of timing signals that are shifted by one clock time period. 
23. Johnson counter is basically a ring counter with complement of last flip-flop connected to input of first  
 flip-flop. This arrangement is called switch tail ring counter.
24. In general, k bit Johnson counter will generate 2k distinguishable states and they decoded to generate 2k  
 unique output signals that resembles the output of a decoder.
25. A register is a group of flip-flops that can store binary information. 
26. Each flip-flop in a register can store one bit binary and so, in order to store n-bit binary the register should  
 have n flip-flops.
27. A register capable of shifting the binary information from one flip-flop to another (or one cell to another)  
 is called shift register. 
28. The four types of shift registers are serial-in serial-out, serial-in parallel-out, parallel-in serial out and  
 parallel-in parallel out shift register.
29. A shift register that can accept serial or parallel input data and output data in parallel along with right or  
 left shift is called universal shift register.
8.9  Short-Answer Questions
Q8.1 Define lock-out condition?
 In sequential circuits with some don’t-care or unused states, the sequential circuit may find itself in some 
 unused state during starting or switch ON. If next state of the unused state is again some unused one and if  
 the sequential circuit cycle through only unused states and never arrives at in a used state then this condition  
 is called lock-out.
Q8.2 Define counter and its classifications.
 A register that goes through prescribed (or predefined) sequence of states upon the application of  clock 
 pulses is called a counter. The counters are used to generate or go through a sequence binary code known  
 as count sequence.
 The counters can be broadly classified into two categories: Ripple counters and synchronous counters.
 In a ripple counter, a flip-flop output will act as clock for another flip-flop.
 In synchronous counters all the flip-flops are triggered simultaneously by a common clock.
Q8.3 Define binary counter.
 A counter that follows a binary count sequence is called binary counter. An n-bit binary counter consists  
 of n flip-flops and can count binary from 0 to 2 n - 1.
Q8.4 What is switch tail ring counter?
 Johnson counter is basically a ring counter with complement of last flip-flop connected to input of first  
 flip-flop. This arrangement is called switch tail ring counter.

--- Page 742 ---
Chapter 8 - Sequential Logic-Counters and Registers 8.127
Q8.5 Explain ring counter.
 A ring counter is a circular shift register with only one flip-flop output being set at a time and all other  
 flip-flop outputs are cleared. Using preset facility, a 1 is loaded in one flip-flop output and all other outputs  
 are loaded 0. When clock pulses are applied the 1 will shift by one position. This produces a sequence of  
 timing signals that are shifted by one clock time period. 
Q8.6 How to make the counter self starting?
 In order to make the counter self starting the unused states can be connected to enter used states.Once the 
 counter enter an used state it will circle through used states and counter becomes self starting.
Q8.7     How many fiip-flops will be complemented in a 10-bit ripple counter to reach the next count after the  
 count value of  1001100111?
 Add 1 to the binary value 1001100111 in order to get next count value.
               1001100111
              +  1
 1001101000
 In the result of above addition we observe that 4 bits are complemented. In a counter, each bit is stored in a 
 flip-flop. Therefore, 4 flip-flops will be complemented in a 10-bit ripple counter to reach the next count after  
 the count of 1001100111.
Q8.8 Define BCD or MOD-10 counter.
 A BCD counter has to count only from 0 to 9, and when the count reaches 10 10, the output has to be reset to 
 all zero, so that next count sequence will start. The BCD counter is also called MOD-10 counter. 
Q8.9 Comment about a presettable counter and ripple counter.
 A presettable counter will have a preload facility to load a count value before the start of the count and count  
 sequence starts from this preloaded value. But in a ripple counter without a preload facility the count sequence  
 will be all possible combinations of binary.

Chapter 9 - Asynchronous Sequential Circuits 9.1
ASYNCHRONOUS SEQUENTIAL 
CIRCUITS
9.1  Introduction to Asynchronous Sequential Logic Circuits
The combinational logic circuits with feedback and without clock are called asynchronous sequential 
circuits. Since there is no clock, the changes in internal states occur immediately when there is a change in 
input and so the response in an asynchronous sequential circuit will be fast. In the design of asynchronous 
sequential circuit sufficient care must be taken to ensure that every change in state leads to a stable condition. 
Table 9.1: Differences between Synchronous and Asynchronous Sequential Circuits
 
 
 
 
  Basically, an asynchronous sequential circuit can be expressed as a combinational circuit with 
feedback paths having delay elements. The asynchronous sequential circuits will have input, output and state 
variables. The present and next state variables of asynchronous sequential circuit are called secondary and 
excitation variables respectively. The block diagram of asynchronous sequential circuit is shown in Fig. 9.1.  
Here,    x1, x2, ….., xn = n input variables
              Z1, Z2, ….., Zm = m output variables
              Y1, Y2, ….., Yk = k excitation variables (next state variables)
              y1, y2, ….., yk = k secondary variables (present state variables)
In asynchronous circuits the state transitions occur when there is a change in input. The circuit will 
attain a stable condition when excitation (or next state) variables are same as secondary (or present) state 
variables. Therefore, a change in input is allowed only after the circuit attains a stable state due to previous 
change in input. Also, when there are multiple inputs, only one input is allowed to change at any one time 
in order to ensure proper operation of circuit and this is called fundamental mode of operation. Therefore, 
the fundamental mode of operation is defined as the operating mode in which only one input is allowed 
to change when the circuit is in stable state. 
CHAPTER 9
          Synchronous Sequential Circuit                        Asynchronous Sequential Circuit
1.  Provided with clock                                1.  Do not have a clock
2.  Changes in internal states occur in                    2.  Changes in internal states occur when there is a
     response to clock.                                     change in input variables. 
3.  Memory elements are clocked flip-flops.          3.  Memory elements are either latches (unclocked

9.2                                              Digital Logic Circuits
9.1.1  Fundamental and Pulse Mode Sequential Circuits
In fundamental mode asynchronous sequential circuits the inputs are level triggered inputs, whereas 
in pulse mode asynchronous sequential circuits the inputs are pulses of sufficient duration for the output 
to change for a given input.  
Design of Fundamental Mode Asynchronous Sequential Circuits
The design of fundamental asynchronous sequential logic circuit is designing a race-free and hazard 
free logic circuit from the given system specifications. The following procedural steps can be followed 
for the design. 
●  Develop a primitive flow table from the word description of asynchronous circuit
●  Minimize the number of states in the flow table.
●  Assign race-free binary codes to states.
●  Construct the transition table.
●  Construct excitation maps and find Boolean equations for a hazard free realization.
●  Check for essential hazards.
●  Draw the logic circuit by implementing methods to eliminate essential hazards.
The examples presented in sections 9.1 to 9.6 in this chapter are related to design of fundamental 
mode asynchronous circuits.    
9.1.2  Transition Table
In asynchronous sequential circuit, the state table is called transition table. Practically, the state 
table itself is listing of all possible transitions between the states of a circuit. In asynchronous circuit state 
table, there should be at least one next state that is equal to present state in each row.
The procedure to form transition table is as follows,
1. Identify all feedback paths in the circuit. Let the circuit has k number of feedback paths.
2.  Assign secondary (or present state) and excitation (or next state) variables to each feedback  
 path. Let, y 1, y2, …, yk be secondary variables and Y1, Y2, ……., Yk be excitation variables.

3. Now, the excitation variables are functions of secondary variables and circuit external inputs.  
 Determine the Boolean equations for excitation variables in terms of secondary variables and  
 inputs. Note that, the secondary variables are inputs to a combinational circuit and excitation  
 variables are output from the combinational circuit. The excitation variables are given as inputs  
 to feedback paths.
4. Draw maps similar to K-maps for every excitation variable, Y 1, Y2, ……., Yk. In these maps, 
 the rows are formed by secondary variables and columns by inputs.
5. Now, there will be k number of maps. Combine all the k number of maps into a single map, by  
 combining the corresponding entries in each square of individual map. Now each square will  
 have k-bit binary representing next state.
6. In each row mark the next states (Y 1 Y2 …Yk) that are same as present state (y 1 y2….yk) by 
 circles. The circled entries represent stable stat es and uncircled entries represent unstable states.        
The transition table lists the possible state transitions for all possible changes in inputs and so it 
can be used to analyze the circuit behavior.

9.1.3  Stable and Unstable States
A state is a circuit condition represented by a set of variables called state variables.
The states are represented either by letter symbols a, b, c, d, .... or by binary codes. The circuit 
of Fig. 9.2 has two state variables and so states are represented by 2-bit binary codes 00, 01, 11 and 10.
The circuit will change from one state to another state when there is a change in input. During a 
state transition when the next state is same as present state then the circuit attains a stable condition and 
the corresponding state is called stable state. On the other hand in a state transition, if the next state is not 
equal to present state then the corresponding state is called unstable state.
 In the transition table shown in Fig. 9.3(c), the entries in each square represents next state. Therefore, 
in each row, the squares that have identical values with present state are marked with circles. The circled 
entries represent stable states and uncircled entries represent unstable states.
Normally, an asynchronous sequential circuit will remain in a stable state for a given input. The 
transition from one stable state to another stable state occurs due to changes in input. 
Consider the circuit shown in Fig. 9.2 and its transition table shown in Fig. 9.3. In this circuit, the 
following four state transitions due to changes in input are possible as shown in Fig. 9.4.
When in state 00, if the input changes from 1 to 0, then state transitions occur as shown in Fig. 9.4(a).
When in state 01, if the input changes from 0 to 1, then state transitions occur as shown in Fig. 9.4(b).
When in state 11, if the input changes from 1 to 0, then state transitions occur as shown in Fig. 9.4(c).
When in state10, if the input changes from 0 to 1, then state transitions occur as shown in Fig. 9.4(d).
In an asynchronous circuit, the state changes occurs immediately when there is a change in input, 
and so the input value can be combined with state to declare a condition called total state of the circuit. 
All possible combinations of state variables and inputs are called total states. The total state in the circuit 
of Fig. 9.2 is given by the possible binary values of y1y2x1. With three variables 8 different total states can 
be formed, in which the four states that are circled in transition table are stable states and the other four 
states are unstable
Stable total states: 001, 010, 111, 100
Unstable total states: 000, 011, 110, 101
Using the transition table, the state table for 
asynchronous circuit similar to that of a state table 
of synchronous circuit can be constructed as shown 
in Table 9.3. In state table of asynchronous circuit, at 
least one entry of each row should have same present 
state and next state. 
Unstable Condition in Asynchronous Circuit
Consider the transition table of an asynchronous circuit shown in Fig. 9.5(a). In this transition table, 
there, is no stable state when input is 11. Hence, when input changes from 01 to 11 or 10 to 11 the circuit 
will enter an unstable condition with next state keeps on changing from 1 to 0 and 0 to 1 continuously as 
shown in Figs. 9.5(b) and (c).

9.6                                              Digital Logic Circuits
While designing asynchronous sequential circuits such unstable conditions should be avoided and 
this can be achieved by ensuring one stable state for every input.
The continuous change between two unstable states is also called metastability which refers to an 
equilibrium condition in an unstable circuit.
9.1.4  Flow Table
The flow table lists all state transitions from present state to next state along with output for all 
possible changes in input. It is similar to transition table, but has two differences. One is the states are 
represented by letter symbols and not by binary values. Another difference is that the output is also listed 
in each square along with next state. 
A flow table may have one or more stable states in a row. When 
there is only one stable state in each row of a flow table then it is called 
a primitive flow table. The flow table for the circuit of Fig. 9.2 is shown 
in Fig. 9.6. Here, the following letter symbols are  assigned to binary 
values of states.
y1 y2  →  y 00  →  a
  01  →  b
  11  →  c
  10  →  d    
9.1.5  Cycles and Races
In an asynchronous sequential circuit, when there are changes in two or more state variables due to 
change in input, a race condition may exist, in which changes in variables may occur at different timings 
due to difference in delay in the feedback paths. This leads to unpredictable transition paths during a 
change in state. 
For example, consider the state change from 011 to 100. Some of the possible transition paths are 
shown below:
011 → 111 → 101 → 100                              
011 → 010 → 000 → 100
011 → 001 → 101 → 100

The race condition may be classified into critical and noncritical race. In a state transition, if the 
final stable state depends on the order of change in state variables, then the race is called critical race. On 
the other hand, in a state transition, if the final stable state does not depends on the order of change in state 
variables, then the race is called noncritical race.
Examples of noncritical race are shown in Fig. 9.7 and examples of critical race are shown in Fig. 9.8.
Races are identified by tracing possible state transitions through unstable states with one bit change 
while going from one stable state to another stable state for a change in input. The actual race is through 
internal states or secondary variables.
In the transition table shown in Fig. 9.7(a), while in stable state 00, if the input changes from 0 to 1, 
there are two possible transition paths and in both the transition paths the circuit go to same stable next 
state 11 as shown in Fig. 9.7(b). Hence they are noncritical race. Similarly, two more state transitions from 
stable state 01 to 11 and 10 to 11 for change in input from 0 to 1 are shown in Figs. 9.7(c) and (d). In these 
transitions also races are noncritical. 
                                        00 → 01 → 11                                          01 → 11                                                10 → 11
                                                  00 → 10 → 11                                01 → 00 → 10 → 11                             10 → 00 → 01 → 11
In the transition table shown in Fig. 9.8(a), while in stable state 00, if the input changes from 0 to 1, 
there are three possible state transition paths and in each transition path the circuit go to different stable 
next state as shown in Fig. 9.8(b). Hence they are critical race.
Also, it can be observed that when a column has only one stable state the critical race do not occur.
                                                                                 00 → 01  ;  00 → 11  ;  00 → 10       

--- Page 757 ---
9.8                                              Digital Logic Circuits
Races can be avoided by proper choice of binary values to states. While assigning binary values 
to states, if the values are assigned such that only one variable change at a time during a state transition 
in a flow table then the races can be avoided. The race free state assignment is discussed in this chapter 
in Section 9.1.6. 
When the state transitions in a circuit go through a unique sequence of unstable states then that 
condition is called a cycle. Races can also be avoided by using cycles, which terminate on a stable state. 
When a cycle does not terminate on a stable state then the entire circuit will be unstable.
The following state transitions shown in Fig. 9.7 is also examples of cycles because while going 
from one stable state to another stable state, the transitions go through unstable states. 
00 → 01 → 11              01 → 00 → 10 → 11             10 → 00 → 01 → 11
00 → 10 → 11              01 → 10 → 11                       10 → 01 → 11
00 → 01 → 10 → 11

input x on columns as shown in Figs. 3(a) and (b) and the squares in the maps are filled with values of Y1 and Y2 listed

Fig. 3(c). The output map is constructed as shown in Fig. 3(d) and the squares are filled with values of Z. 
 In each row of the transition table, the squares that have identical values with secondary values are marked 
with circles. The circled entries represent stable states and uncircled entries represent unstable states.
In the transition table it can be observed that each column has two stable states for every input. But, for a 
given input the circuit will remain in one of the stable state.
The transition from one stable state to another stable state occurs due to changes in input.
Since there are two stable states for each input the circuit can go to any one of the stable state for a change 
in input as shown in Fig. 4 and hence every change in input leads to a critical race.
When in state 00, if the input changes from 0 to 1, then state transitions occur as shown in Fig. 4(a).
When in state 11, if the input changes from 0 to 1, then state transitions occur as shown in Fig. 4(b).
When in state 01, if the input changes from 1 to 0, then state transitions occur as shown in Fig. 4(c).
When in state 10, if the input changes from 1 to 0, then state transitions occur as shown in Fig. 4(d).

Solution
State Transitions Due to Change in Input
Here, each input has one stable state. State transitions occur only when there is a change in input. Normally, when 
the input is stable or when no change in input the circuit remain in the stable state corresponding to the present input.
Here, there are four possible combinations of inputs. When the circuit remain in a stable state at any one input 
then state transitions will occur when the input changes to other possible inputs with one bit change. 
When input is 00, the circuit remain in state 1. Th e input can change from 00 to 01 or 00 to 10 and th e 
corresponding state transitions will occur as shown in Fig. 2. 
When input is 01, the circuit remain in state 0. The input can change from 01 to 11 or 01 to 00 and the corresponding 
state transitions will occur as shown in Fig. 3. 
When input is 11, the circuit remain in state 1. The input can change from 11 to 10 or 11 to 01 and the corresponding 
state transitions will occur as shown in Fig. 4. 
When input is 10, the circuit remain in state 0. The input can change from 10 to 00 or 10 to 11 and the corresponding 
state transitions will occur as shown in Fig. 5. 
The state transitions shown in Figs. 2 to 5 are listed in Table 1. It can be observed that there are no races and 
cycles in the state transitions.

Example 9.8
Investigate the transition table of Fig. 1, and determine all race conditions 
and whether they are critical or noncritical. Determine also whether there are 
any cycles.
Solution
State Transitions Due to Change in Input
State transitions occur only when there is a change in input. Normally, 
when the input is stable or when no change in input the circuit remain in one 
of the stable state corresponding to the input.
Here, there are four possible combinations of inputs. When the circuit 
remain in a stable state at any one input then state transitions will occur when 
the input changes to other possible inputs with one bit change.
Here, two inputs has one stable state each and the other two inputs has two stable states each. Hence at any 
one input the circuit can remain in one of the stable state. 
When input is 00, the circuit remain in state 01. The input can change from 00 to 01 or 00 to 10 and the 
corresponding state transitions will occur as shown in Fig. 2. 
When input is 01, the circuit remain in state 00. The input can change from 01 to 11 or 01 to 00 and the 
corresponding state transitions will occur as shown in Fig. 3. 
When input is 11, the circuit remain in either state 11 or 10. The input can change from 11 to 10 or 11 to 01 and 
the corresponding state transitions will occur as shown in Fig. 4.

9.1.6  Race-Free Assignment
In order to avoid critical races, the state assignment or binary code assignment should be such that 
only one variable change at a time when a state transition occurs in a flow table. Two binary codes are said 
to be adjacent if they differ by only one variable. For example the 3-bit code 011 and 001 are adjacent, 
because they differ by only one variable. In order to avoid critical races, the two states between which a 
transition occurs should be assigned adjacent codes. Assigning adjacent codes to states to avoid critical 
races is called race-free assignment. Sometimes, race free assignment needs addition of extra rows in flow 
table which can be achieved by the following two methods.

9.26                                              Digital Logic Circuits
Method 1: Additional Rows with Extra States 
Using the flow table, a transition diagram can be co nstructed that 
represents all possible state transitions. Binary code assignment for states can 
be made in the transition diagram such that states that are involved in every 
transition are assigned adjacent codes. 
When adjacent code assignment is not possible for a  pair of states 
involved in a state transition insert an additional state such that the state transition 
between the pair of states go via the additional states. The concept of inserting 
additional state can be extended to all state pair involved in state transitions 
that do not have adjacent state assignment. 
The insertion of additional states leads to extra rows in flow table. For 
every extra state one row is added in flow table. 
Consider a state transition between two rows a and d as shown in  
Fig. 9.9(a).
Let a and d are not adjacent. Now an additional state f is added such that 
the transition from a to d go via state f as shown below:
a → d     ⇒     a → f → d
In order to assure this transition an additional state named state f is selected which leads to an 
additional row for state f in flow table table as shown in Fig. 9.9(b). Now, the state d in row a is replaced 
by f and the corresponding column in row f is filled by d and all other columns in row f are don't-cares.
Method 2: Multiple Row with Complement States 
In multiple row method each row in a flow table is represented by two or more equivalent rows. 
In two rows representation, each row is represented by two rows and they are known as original row and 
equivalent row. 
The rows corresponding to original flow table are assigned binary codes such that they are adjacent. 
The complement of binary codes are assigned to equivalent rows. The stable states are filled with subscript 
1 in original rows and subscript 2 in the equivalent rows. The unstable states are filled such that they are 
adjacent to stable states. (Refer Example 9.9(b) for multiple row method).  
9.1.7  Transition Diagram
The transition table lists all possible state transitions from present to next state. The state transitions 
between unstable states in each row of transition table can be converted to transition diagram which will 
be more useful for race free state assignment. The diagrammetic way of representing all possible state 
transitions between unstable states in every row of transition table is called transition diagram.
An example of drawing the transition diagram from a transition table is shown in Fig. 9.10. 
From the transition table shown in Fig. 9.10(a) we can observe the following state transition.

9.2  State Reduction
In asynchronous sequential circuits, the state reduction is performed via an implication table. In 
the original state table, the equivalent states are identified and each pair of equivalent states is merged as 
a single state.
The rows of state tables can be classified in to following three groups.
Equivalent States: State pairs that have same next state and output for the same input are equivalent 
states.
Not equivalent states:  State pairs having different next state and output for same input are not 
equivalent states.
Implied state pairs: A pair of states can be equivalent only if one pair implies the other pair. If a 
pair of state having same outputs for the same inputs and go to same equivalent next state then the pair is 
said to be implied pair.
A pair of states (or two states) are said to be equivalent if they go to same next states with same 
output for all possible changes in inputs. Alternatively, they can go to same equivalent next states with 
same output.
Consider the state table shown in Table 9.4. In this table, state a and b has same output for same 
inputs. Similarly, state c and d has same output for same inputs. In this example, it can be shown that if 
state c and d are equivalent then state a and b will also be equivalent. Let us replace state b by a as shown 
in Table 9.5. Now, in Table 9.5, if state d is equal to c then state a and b will be equivalent as well as state 
c and d are also equivalent. Hence we can say that (a, b) implies (c, d).
 The state table with state d replaced by state c is shown in Table 9.6 and from this table we can say 
that state a and b are equivalent and also, state c and d are equivalent. Hence, one of the equivalent states 
can be removed and reduced state table can be formed as shown in Table 9.7.

in Input     State        Transitions

9.2.1  Implication Table
When the state table has large number of rows it is difficult to find equivalent and implied states and 
in this situation implication table is used to find equivalent and implied states and then form the reduced 
state table.   
The implication table is constructed by listing the states on rows and columns in order to form 
squares at the intersection of every row and column. Each square represent a pair of state. While forming 
rows, the first state is not considered and while forming column the last state is not considered so that only 
state pairs are represented by squares. The implication table is also known as merger table.
Consider the state table of asynchronous sequential circuit with 7 states a, b, c, d, e, f and g shown 
in Table 9.8. Now, the implication table is formed by listing states b, c, d, e, f and g on rows and states a, 
b, c, d, e, and f on columns in order to form squares at the intersection of each row and column as shown 
in Fig. 9.11(a). The state pair represented by each square is shown in Fig. 9.11(b).

     d            a         d           0      1

First mark × in the squares in which the pair of states do not have same output for same inputs 
as shown in Fig. 9.12(a). The state pairs marked by × are not equivalent pairs. Next mark a tick ( :) in 
the squares in which the state pairs are equivalent as shown in Fig. 9.12(b). Here, the state pair (d, e) is 
equivalent because they go to same next state and output for same input. 
The next step is to identify the implied pairs among the state pairs that are not marked by × and tick 
(:) in Figs. 9.12(a) and (b). Mark the next state pairs corresponding to the state pair represented by the 
squares that are blank in Figs. 9.12(a) and (b), as shown in Fig. 9.12(c). 
When next state pair and present state pair are same then those state pairs can be ignored in Fig.

9.2.2  Merger Diagram to /f_ind Equivalent State Groups
Merger diagrams are used to find equivalent state groups. A merger diagram is a circle with dots 
where the dots represent the states and the equivalent pair of states is connected by straight lines. The 
merger diagram is also known as merger graph.
The geometrical patterns obtained in the merger diagram are used to determine the equivalent state 
groups. The different types of geometrical patterns in the merger diagram are,
• A single dot without a connection represents a state not equivalent with any other state.
• A line between two states represents a equivalent pair of states.
• A triangle between three dots represents an equivalent group with three states.
• An n-sided polygon with all the diagonals connected represents a group of n-equivalent states  
 connected by polygon.

9.2.3  Merging of Rows of Flow Tables with Incompletely Speci/f_ied States
In asynchronous circuits with incompletely specified states, the states can be reduced by identifying 
compatible pairs. Two states are said to be a compatible pair if the specified outputs and next states are 
same. Here, dashes are used to represent unspecified states or outputs. While identifying compatible pairs 
the dashes can be used to match any desired state or output.
The two rows representing compatible pair of states can be merged to a single row in a flow table.
Maximum compatible states:  It is a group of compatible states that includes a ll possible 
combinations of compatible states.
Refer Examples 9.13 and 9.14 for merging of rows of flow tables with incompletely specified states. 
9.2.4  Merger Diagram to /f_ind Maximum Compatible States
Merger diagrams are used to find maximum compatible states. A merger diagram is a circle with dots 
where the dots represent the compatible states and the compatible pair of states is connected by straight lines. 
The geometrical patterns obtained in the merger diagram are used to determine the compatible state 
groups. The different types of geometrical patterns in the merger diagram are,
• A single dot without a connection represents a state not compatible with any other state.

9.2.5  Maximum Compatible
The maximum compatible is a group of compatible states that includes all the possible combinations 
of compatible states. The maximum compatible states can be determined from merger diagram. The states 
forming various geometrical patterns in the merger diagram are the maximum compatibles.
The reduced flow table can be formed by taking one member of each maximum compatible set as 
a row in reduced flow table. 
In many cases, the maximum compatibles will not be a minimal set of compatibles. A minimum set 
of compatibles can be determined from closed-covering condition.      
9.2.6  Closed-Covering Condition
In implication table, the compatible pairs may or may not have implied pairs. Hence the closed 
condition can be defined for two different types of implication table.
1. In implication table, if the compatible pairs does not have implied pairs then the closed-condition 
refers to a set of compatibles that does not include implied states. 
2. In implication table, when the compatible pairs has implied states then the implied pairs should 
be included in selected compatible pairs.
The covering-condition refers to inclusion of all states of original state table in the compatible 
sets. The closed-covering condition refers to set o f compatibles that covers all the states and satisf y 
covering condition. The set of compatibles that satisfy the closed-covering condition form the minimal 
set of compatibles. The reduced flow table can be formed by taking one element of each of the minimal 
compatible set to form the rows of reduced flow table.  
9.2.7  Assigning Outputs in Flow Table with Incompletely Speci/f_ied States
In flow tables with incompletely specified states, every stable state will be associated with an output. 
Normally, output will not specified for unstable states. But in order to find compatible pairs and reduce the 
states, output is necessary for unstable states too. Hence, output has to be assigned to all unstable states 
such that no transient outputs are generated during a transition from one stable state to another stable state. 
Therefore, the following rules are followed to assign output to unstable states in a flow table.
Rule 1 : Assign 0 to an output of an unstable state which is transient state during a transition between 
two stable states that have a 0 as output.
Rule 2 : Assign 1 to an output of an unstable state which is transient state during a transition between 
two stable states that have a 1 as output.
Rule 3 : Assign a don't-care condition to an output of an unstable state which is transient state 
during a transition between two stable states that have a different values (0 and 1 or 1 and 0) as output.

--- Page 793 ---
9.44                                              Digital Logic Circuits
Examples of output assignment using the above rules are shown in Fig. 9.14. 
Refer Examples 9.16, 9.18 in Chapter 9 and 10.5 in Chapter 10 for output assignment.

e, f, g and h.
(e, f, g, h), (a, b, h), (c, d, h)

the compatible pairs (a, b) and (c, d).

(a, b) (c, d) (e, f, g, h)

(e, f) has an implied pair (e, h) which is included in (e, f, g, h). 
Therefore, the closure condition is also satisfied by the selected compatible pairs.
Conclusion: The compatible pairs that satisfy closed-covering condition are,
(a, b), (c, d), (e, f, g, h)

Merge the primitive flow table shown in Fig. 1. Find all compatible pairs by means 
of an implication table. Find the maximal compatibles by means of a merger diagram. 
Find a minimal set of compatibles that covers all the states and is closed.
Solution
The given flow table (Table 1) has 10 states a, b, c, d, e, f, g, h, j and k. The 
states b, c, d, e, f, g, h, j and k are listed to form rows and the states a, b, c, d, e, f, g, 
h and j are listed to form columns in implication table. 
Here, three implication tables (Figs. 2(a), (b) and (c)) are drawn to separately 
show the not compatible, compatible and implied pairs.
The given flow table has 4 combinations of inputs. Hence compatibility of states 
for all the four inputs should be marked in each square of implication table.
The dashes in the given flow table represents unspecified states or outputs. While 
identifying compatible pairs the dashes can be used to match any desired state or output.
First mark × in squares in Fig. 2(a) in which the state pairs do not have same 
outputs for same inputs.
●  When input is 00, present state pair (a, c), go to next state (a, c) with different 
output.
●  When input is 00, present state pair (a, h), go to next state (a, h) with different output.
●  When input is 01, present state pair (d, f), go to next state (d, f) with different output.
●  When input is 11, present state pair (g, j), go to next state (g, j) with different output.
●  When input is 10, present state pair (b, e), go to next state (b, e) with different output.
●  When input is 10, present state pair (e, k), go to next state (e, k) with different output.
Hence squares representing (a, c), (a, h), (b, e), (d, f), (e, k) and (g, j) are marked × in Fig. 2(a). The not compatible 
state pairs that has transitions to stable states with different output are listed in Table 1.
Next mark tick ( :) in squares in Fig. 2(b) in which state pairs are compatible. Here, dashes are matched with 
states and outputs to form compatible pairs. The state pair (a, e) goes to same next state with same output when dashes 
are considered as same state and output and so (a, e) is compatible pair. 
Similarly, (a, f), (b, c), (b, j), (c, d), (d, g), (e, f) and (g, h) are compatible state pairs. The compatible state pairs 
are listed in Table 2.

9.3  Asynchronous Circuits with SR Latches
The latches are used as memory elements in asynchronous circuits. Therefore, in an n-variable 
asynchronous circuit, n number of SR latches are employed to store the n variables. There are two types 
of SR latches: one type is constructed using two cross coupled NOR gate and another type is constructed 
using two cross coupled NAND gates. Both these two latches has two inputs S and R. The working of SR 
latch is discussed in detail in Chapter-6, Section 6.1.  
9.3.1  NOR Based SR Latch
The NOR based SR latch is constructed using two cross coupled NOR gates as shown in Fig. 9.15(a) 
and the feedback path circuit is shown in Fig. 9.15(b).
Let, y = Present state
       Y = Next state
From the feedback circuit of Fig. 9.15(b), we get the following equation for next state or output of 
NOR based SR latch.

     Y = (R + (S + y)' )' = R' (S + y) = R' S + R' y
∴ Y = SR' + R' y 
From the truth table of NOR based SR latch we can say that both S 
and R should not be equal to 1 simultaneously and this can be transferred to a 
condition that logical AND of S and R should not be 1 or should be always 0. 
Therefore, in NOR based SR latch, S . R = 0. 
Consider the Boolean expression, SR' + SR.
Now, SR' + SR = S(R' + R )
Since R' + R = 1, we can write, SR' + SR = S
From the above equation we can say that if SR = 0, then SR' = S.
On substituting, SR ' = S in the next state equation of SR latch we get the following simplified 
equation for NOR based SR latch.
 Y = SR' + R' y       ⇒        Y = S + R' y   
                                           (Simplified equation of SR latch)
The simplified equation of SR latch can be used to analyze and design the asynchronous circuit 
using NOR based SR latch when SR = 0. 
9.3.2  NAND Based SR Latch
The NAND based SR latch is constructed using two cr oss coupled NAND gates as shown in  
Fig. 9.16(a) and the feedback path circuit is shown in Fig. 9.16(b).
Let, y = Present state
       Y = Next state
From the truth table of NAND based SR latch we can say that both S 
and R should not be equal to 0 simultaneously. This can be transferred to a 
condition that logical AND of S' and R' should not be 1 or should be always 0. 
Therefore, in NAND based SR latch, S' . R' = 0. From the feedback circuit of 
Fig. 9.16(b), we get the following equation for next state or output of NAND 
based SR latch.
     Y = S' + Ry
On comparing the above equation with NOR based SR latch we can 
observe that S is replaced by S ' and R ' is replaced by R and so the above 
equation will be valid only when S' R' = 0. Therefore, the above equation can be used to analyze and design 
the asynchronous circuit using NAND based SR latch when S' R' = 0.

9.3.3  Design using SR Latches
The design of asynchronous circuits can start with either Boolean equations of asynchronous circuit 
or with transition table.
Method-1: Design from Specified Boolean Equations of Asynchronous Circuit
The following procedure can be used to analyze and design asynchronous sequential circuits using 
SR latches from the specified Boolean equations of the circuit.
Let, Y1, Y2, …. Yn = n variables of the asynchronous circuit.  
Now, y1, y2, …. yn are present state variables and Y1, Y2, …. Yn are next state variables.
In order to store n variables, choose n number of NOR or NAND based SR latches.   
Determine the Boolean functions for the R and S input of each latch by comparing the given equations 
with following next state equation of SR latch.
For NOR based SR latch:     Yj =  Sj + Rj yj   ; for j = 1, 2, … n.
For NAND based SR latch:  Yj =  Sj + Rj yj   ; for j = 1, 2, … n.
When NOR based SR latch is selected, check for Sj Rj = 0 for j = 1, 2, … n.
When NAND based SR latch is selected, check for Sj Rj = 0 for for j = 1, 2, … n.
When the above condition is not satisfied, the circuit designed using given equation may not work 
properly and so design is not possible. When the above condition is satisfied, draw the logic circuit using 
equations of Yj for j = 1, 2, … n.
The asynchronous circuit can be analyzed for cycles and races by constructing transition table using 
the equations of Yj for j = 1, 2, … n.
Method-2: Design from Specified Transition Table of Asynchronous Circuit
The following procedure can be used to analyze and design asynchronous sequential circuits using 
SR latches from the specified transition table of the circuit.
Let, Y1, Y2, …. Yn = n variables of the asynchronous circuit.  
Now, y1, y2, …. yn are present state variables and Y1, Y2, …. Yn are next state variables.
In order to store n variables, choose n number of NOR or NAND based SR latches.  
When the states are denoted by letter symbols, assign race-free binary codes for states.
The design starts from the transition table with binary codes for states. The entries in the squares of 
transition tables are binary values for next states Y 1, Y2, ..., Yn. From the knowledge of present state and 
next state values, the excitation table of SR latch is used to determine the binary values of S and R inputs 
of all SR latches and list in a table.
Then construct K-map for every S and R inputs and determine the simplified Boolean equations 
for latch inputs.   
'
'
' '

--- Page 804 ---
Chapter 9 - Asynchronous Sequential Circuits 9.55
It can be observed that the S and R inputs in the excitation table of NOR and NAND latches are 
complements. The equations obtained from K-map for NOR implemented can be complemented and used 
for NAND implementation.
When NOR based SR latch is selected, check for Sj Rj = 0 for j = 1, 2, … n.
When NAND based SR latch is selected, check for Sj Rj = 0 for for j = 1, 2, … n.
When the above condition is not satisfied, the circuit designed using given equation may not work 
properly and so design is not possible. When the above condition is satisfied, draw the combinational logic 
circuit to generate latch inputs, using equations of  Sj and Rj for j = 1, 2, … n. The complete logic circuit 
is given by this combinational logic circuit connected to SR latches. 
Short-cut Method for Deriving SR Latch Input Equations
The following theorem is stated without proof.
In realization of a flow table with race-free state assignment using SR latches there exists equations 
for inputs Si and Ri of latch-i independent of yi.
The above theorem can be used to find equations for latch inputs from the maps of next state 
variables. For example, consider a flow table with two state varaibles Y 1 and Y2. The maps of Y1 and Y2 
are shown in Figs. 9.17 and 9.18.
From the map of Y1 we can get equations for S1 and R1 independent of y1. Hence divide the map of 
Y1 into two maps: One map when y1 = 0 and another map when y1 = 1. 
In the map of Fig. 9.17(b), the prime implicants are formed by considering adjacent 1's. The sum of 
prime implicants gives the equation for S1. In the map of Fig. 9.17(c), the prime implicants are formed by 
considering adjacent 0's. The complement of sum of prime implicants gives the equation for R1.
Similarly, from the map of Y2 we get the equations for S2 and R2 independent of y2. Here, the map 
of Y2 is divided into two: One map when y2 = 0 and another map when y2 = 1. The formation of equations 
for S2 and R2 is similar to that of formation of equations for S1 amd R1.

Example 9.15
An asynchronous sequential circuit is described by the following excitation and output functions 
Y = x1x2 +(x1 + x2) y   ;  Z = Y
Implement the above equations in a logic circuit
a) using NOR latch        
b) using NAND latch
Solution
a) Implementation using NOR Latch
The excitation function of the asynchronous sequential circuit is,
        Y = x1x2 + (x1 + x2) y                                                                                                                            .....(1)
The excitation function of SR latch using NOR gate is, 
       Y = S + R' y                                                                                                                                           .....(2)  
On comparing equations (1) and (2) we get,
S = x1x2
R'  = x1 + x2     ⇒      R = (x1 + x2)' = x1x2    
Let us check for SR = 0.
SR = x1x2 . x1 x2 = (x1 x1) . (x2 x2) 
                         = 0.0 = 0 
Since, SR = 0, the given equation can be implemented using NOR based SR latch as shown in Fig. 1. 
b) Implementation using NAND Latch       
The excitation function of the asynchronous sequential circuit is,
       Y = x1x2 + (x1 + x2) y                                                                                                                            .....(3)
The excitation function of SR latch using NAND gate is, 
       Y = S'  + Ry                                                                                                                                           .....(4)
On comparing equations (3) and (4) we get, 
       S'  = x1x2       ⇒      S = (x1x2)'  = x1 + x2 
       R = x1 + x2 
Let us check for S' R'  = 0.
       S' R' = x1x2 (x1+ x2)'  = x1x2 . x1x2= (x1x1) . (x2x2) = 0.0 = 0 
Since, S' R'  = 0, the given equation can be implemented using NAND based SR latch as shown in Fig. 2.

Example 9.16   
a) Obtain a binary state assignment for the reduced flow table shown in 
Fig. 1 to avoid critical race condition.
b) Assign output to unstable states and obtain the output equation.
c) Implement the logic circuit using NOR based SR latch.
d) Implement the logic circuit using NAND based SR latch.
Solution
a) Race-Free State Assignment
The given flow table has only two states a and b. Therefore, state transitions can occur either from a to b or b to a. 
For two states, 1-bit state assignment is sufficient and in 1-bit state assignment there will not be any race condition.
Let us assign binary code 0 to state a and binary code 1 to state b. The transition and flow table with binary 
code assignment is shown in Fig. 2.
  
b) To Assign Output and Determine the Output Equation 
In	flow	table,	the	dashes	in	the	output	are	assigned	values	according	to	the	following	rules	to	prevent	transient	
output during a transition.
Rule 1 :  Assign 0 to an output of an unstable state which is transient state during a transition between two 
stable states that have a 0 as output.
Rule 2 : Assign 1 to an output of an unstable state which is  transient state during a transition between two 
stable states that have a 1 as output.
Rule 3 : Assign a don't-care condition  to an output of an unstable state which is transient state during a transition  
between two stable states that have a different values (0 and 1 or 1 and 0) as output. 
The	state	transitions	that	are	used	to	assign	output	using	the	above	rules	are	shown	in	Fig.	3	and	the	flow	table	
with output assigned to unstable states is shown in Fig. 4. The output map of Z is shown in Fig. 5.

Example 9.17
 The Boolean functions for the S and R inputs of SR latch based asynchronous logic circuit are, 
  S1 = x1y2         S2 = x1x2 
  R1 = x1 x2              R2 = x2 y1
Analyze the circuit and find the stability and race condition.
Solution
The given Boolean equations are, 
S1 = x1y2         S2 = x1x2 
R1 = x1 x2              R2 = x2 y1
Let us check for S1R1 = 0 and S2R2 = 0
S1R1 = x1y2 . x1x2 = (x1x1) . y2x2 = 0 . y2x2 = 0
S2R2 = x1x2 . x2y1 = x1 . (x2x2) . y1 = x1.0.y = 0
Since the given equations satisfy the condition SR = 0, the equations can be implemented by a logic circuit 
using NOR based SR latch as shown in Fig. 1.

Stability Condition
In the transition table of Fig. 4, it can be observed that every column has at least one stable state, so that the 
circuit remain in a stable state for every possible input and so the circuit is stable.
State Transitions due to Change in Input
State transitions occurs only when there is a change in input. Normally, when the input is stable or when no 
change in input the circuit remain in one of the stable state corresponding to the input.
Here, there are four possible combinations of inputs. When the circuit remain in a stable state at any one input 
then state transitions will occur when the input changes to other possible inputs with one bit change.
When input is 00, the circuit remain in either state 00 or 01. The input can change from 00 to 01 or 00 to 10 and 
the corresponding state transitions will occur as shown in Fig. 5.
When input is 01, the circuit remain in either state 00 or 01. The input can change from 01 to 11 or 01 to 00 and 
the corresponding state transitions will occur as shown in Fig. 6. 
                                  00 → 00  ;   00 → 00                                                  01 → 01  ;  01 → 11 → 10  ;  01 → 00
When input is 11, the circuit remain in state 11. The input can change from 11 to 10 or 11 to 01 and the 
corresponding	state	transitions	will	occur	as	shown	in	Fig.	7.	
When input is 10, the circuit remain in state 00. The input can change from 10 to 00 or 10 to 11 and the 
corresponding state transitions will occur as shown in Fig. 8.

Example 9.18
a)  Obtain a binary state assignment for the reduced flow table shown in 
Fig. 1 to avoid critical race condition.
b)  Assign outputs to unstable states.
c)  Implement the logic diagram using NOR based SR latch.
d)  Implement the logic diagram using NAND based SR latch.

b) To Assign Output for Unstable States
The dashes in the output are assigned values according to the following rules.
Rule 1 :  Assign 0 to an output of an unstable state which is transient state during a transition between two 
stable states that have a 0 as output.
Rule 2 :  Assign 1 to an output of an unstable state which is transient state during a transition between two 
stable states that have a 1 as output.
Rule 3 : Assign a don't-care condition  to an output of an unstable state which is transient state during a transition 
between two stable states that have a different values (0 and 1 or 1 and 0) as output.
The	state	transitions	that	are	used	to	assign	output	using	the	above	rules	are	shown	in	Fig.	6	and	the	flow	table	
with	output	assigned	to	unstable	states	is	shown	in	Fig.	7.

equation for output. 
Output, Z = y2' x2 + y2' x1

d) Logic Implementation using NAND based SR Latch
The Boolean equations to generate inputs for NAND based SR latches are given by complement of the equations 
for NOR based SR latch.
Therefore, the Boolean equations to generate inputs for NAND based SR latches are, 
S1 = (x1 x2 )'        S2 = (y1 x1 x2)'          R1 = (x1)'        R2 = (y1 x1 x2 + y1x2)'              Z = y2 x2 + y2 x1
     = x1 + x2            = y1 + x1+ x2              = x1                          = (y1 x1 x2)' . (y1x2)'
                                                                                                    = (y1+x1+x2) . (y1+x2)
The output equation is obtained from output map. Using the above equations the combinational logic circuit to 
generate latch inputs are drawn as shown in Fig. 18. The complete logic circuit is obtained by adding NAND based SR 
latches to the combinational circuit as shown in Fig. 18.

9.4  Design of Pulse Mode Asynchronous Sequential Circuits
In pulse mode asynchronous sequential circuits the inputs are pulses of sufficient duration for the 
output to change for a given input pulse. Here, also only one input is allowed to change at a time, but 
the input pulse will be available only for a short duration sufficient for transition from one stable state to 
another stable state.
The following procedural steps can be followed for the design of pulse mode asynchronous sequential 
circuits from system specifications. 
●  Develop a state diagram and hence state table from the system specifications.
●  If necessary minimize the number of states in the state table.
●  Assign race-free n-bit binary codes to states.
●  The n-bit code will have n state variables and so choose n flip-flops to the state variables.
●  Determine the flip-flop inputs for next state output using excitation table of flip-flop.
●  Draw maps for flip-flop inputs.
●  Form prime implicants by considering adjacent 1’s in each column.
●  Determine the SOP form of Boolean equations for flip-flop inputs.
●  Draw the logic circuit using the Boolean equations.

Example 9.19
Design a pulse mode asynchronous sequential circuit with two inputs x1 and x2 and an output Z such that output 
pulse is produced only when an input sequence x1-x2-x1 is detected and output is 0 for any other input sequence.
Implement the logic circuit i) using D filp-flop, ii) T flip-flop, iii) JK flip-flop, iv) SR flip-flop.
Solution
The circuit requires three states S 0, S1 and S 2 to detect the sequence x 1-x2-x1 as 
shown in Fig. 1. 
 While in S0, if an input pulse x2 is received the circuit remains in S0 itself. But if an input 
pulse x1 is received the circuit go to next state S 1. In both the cases the output is 0 as shown 
in Fig. 2.
While in S1 if an input pulse x 1 is detected the circuit remains in state S 1 itself. But if 
an input pulse x2 is detected the circuit go to state S2. In both the cases output is 0 as shown 
in Fig. 3.
While in S2 if an input pulse x1 is received then the circuit go to state S0 and output 
1 to indicate the detection of sequence x1-x2-x1. But if an input pulse x2 is detected then the 
circuit go to state S0 with output 0 as shown in Fig. 4.
The transitions in Figs. 1 to 4 are combined to get the state diagram of the circuit as shown in Fig. 5.
State Table
Using the state diagram shown in Fig. 5, the state table is formed as shown in Table 1.
Table 1: State Table
There is no identical or equivalent pair of states in the state table with same output and same next state, and 
so there is no need for state reduction. The three states can be formed with two state variables. Let y 1 and y2 be the 
two state variables.

Chapter 9 - Asynchronous Sequential Circuits 9.81
Example 9.20
Design a pulse mode asynchronous sequential circuit with three inputs x1, x2 and x3 and an output Z such that 
output pulse is produced only when an input sequence x1-x2-x3 is detected and output is 0 for any other input sequence.
Implement the logic circuit,
i)   using D filp-flop 
ii)  T flip-flop
iii)  JK flip-flop
iv) SR flip-flop
Solution
The circuit requires four states S0, S1, S2 and S3. Let initial state be S0, 
 While in S 0, if an input pulse x 2 and x 3 is received the circuit remains in S 0 itself. But if an 
input pulse x1 is received the circuit go to next state S1 to detect next input pulse of the sequence. In 
all the cases the output is 0 as shown in Fig. 1.
While in S 1 if an input pulse x 2 is received then the circuit go to next state S 2 to 
detect next input pulse of the sequence and if an input pulse x3 is received then the circuit 
go to state S0. In all the cases the output is 0. But if an input pulse x1 is received the circuit 
remains in S1 itself to start detecting next sequence and the output is 0 as shown in Fig. 2.
 While in S2 if an input pulse x3 is received then the circuit go to next state 
S3 and output 1 to indicate the detection of sequence x1-x2-x3. But if an input pulse 
x1 is detected then the circuit go to state S 1 with output 0 and if an input pulse 
x2 is detected then the circuit go to state S 0 with output 0 to start detecting next 
sequence as shown in Fig. 3. 
While in S3, if an input pulse x2 and x3 is received the circuit remains in S3 itself. But if 
an input pulse x1 is received the circuit go to next state S 1 to start detecting next sequence. 
In all the cases the output is 0 as shown in Fig. 4.
The transitions in Figs.1 to 4 are combined to get the state diagram of the circuit.

∴ y1 = Q1   ⇒  Y1 = Q1 (t + 1)
    y2 = Q2   ⇒  Y2 = Q2(t + 1)

Y1 = D1
Y2 = D2

9.5  Summary of Important Concepts
1. The combinational logic circuits with feedback and without clock are called asynchronous sequential 
 circuits.
2. The present and next state variables of asynchrono us sequential circuit are called secondary and excitation  
 variables.
3. The circuit will attain a stable condition when excitation (or next state) variables are same as secondary  
 (or present state) variables.
4. In asynchronous sequential circuit, the state table is called transition table.
5. A state is a circuit condition represented by a set of variables called state variables.
6. In a state transition, if the next state is not equal to present state then the corresponding state is called  
 unstable state.
7. All possible combinations of state variables and inputs are called total states of the circuit. 
8. The continuous change between two unstable states is also called metastability which refers to an  
 equilibrium condition in an unstable circuit.
9. The flow table lists all state transitions from present state to next state along with output for all possible  
 changes in input.

Chapter 9 - Asynchronous Sequential Circuits 9.91
10. When there is only one stable state in each row of a flow table then it is called a primitive flow table. 
11. The diagrammatic way of representing all possible state transitions between unstable states in every row  
 of transition table is called transition diagram.
12. The race condition is classified into critical and noncritical race condition. 
13. In a state transition, if the final stable state depends on the order of change in state variables, then the  
 race is called critical race. 
14. In a state transition, if the final stable state does not depends on the order of change in state variables,  
 then the race is called noncritical race.
15. When the state transitions in a circuit go through a unique sequence of unstable states then that condition  
 is called a cycle. 
16. Races can also be avoided by using cycles, which terminate on a stable state. 
17.  Two binary codes are said to be adjacent if they differ by only one variable.
18.  Assigning adjacent codes to states to avoid critical races is called race-free assignment. 
19. In fundamental mode asynchronous sequential circuits the inputs are level triggered inputs.  
20. In asynchronous sequential circuits, the state reduction is performed via an implication table or merger 
 table.
21. State pairs that have same next state and output for the same input are equivalent states.
22. State pairs having different next state and output for same input are not equivalent states.
23. If a pair of state having same outputs for the same inputs and go to same equivalent next state then the  
 pair is said to be implied pair.
24. A merger diagram or merger graph is a circle with dots representing the states and every equivalent pair  
 of states is connected by a straight line. 
25. Asynchronous circuits with incompletely specified s tates, the states can be reduced by identifying  
 compatible pairs. 
26. Maximum compatible states is a group of compatible states that includes all possible combinations of  
 compatible states.
27. The closed-covering condition refers to set of compatibles that covers all the states and satisfy covering  
 condition.
28. The set of compatibles that satisfy the closed-covering condition form the minimal set of compatibles.
29. Rows of reduced flow table can be formed by taking one element of each of the minimal compatible set.  
30. The latches are used as memory elements in asynchronous circuits.
31. SR latch is constructed using two cross coupled NOR gates or two cross coupled NAND gates. 
32. In fundamental mode asynchronous sequential circuits the inputs are level triggered inputs.
33. In pulse mode asynchronous sequential circuits the inputs are pulses of sufficient duration for the output  
 to change for a given input pulse.

9.6  Short-Answer Questions
Q9.1 Define asynchronous sequential circuits.
 The combinational logic circuits with feedback and  without clock are called asynchronous sequential circuits. 
Q9.2 What are the characteristic of asynchronous sequential circuits?
 The changes in internal states occur immediately when there is a change in input and hence the response in 
 an asynchronous sequential circuit will be fast. In the asynchronous sequential circuit the change in input  
 may lead to races and unstable condition and therefore, sufficient care must be taken to avoid races and  
 instablity. 
Q9.3 List the difference between asynchronous and synchronous sequential circuits.
Q9.4 What are secondary and excitation variables.
 The present and next state variables of asynchronous sequential circuits are called secondary and excitation 
 variables.
Q9.5 Draw the general model of asynchronous sequential machine (ASM).
Q9.6 Explain stable and unstable states.
 The asynchronous sequential circuit will change from one state to another state when there is a change in 
 input. During a state transition when the next state is same as present state then the circuit attains a stable  
 condition and the corresponding state is called a stable stable. On the other hand in a state transition, if the  
 next state is not equal to present state then the corresponding state is called an unstable state.
             Synchronous Sequential Circuit                             Asynchronous Sequential Circuit
1.  Provided with clock                               1.  Do not have a clock
2.  Changes in internal states occur in                 2.  Changes in internal states occur when there is a
     response to clock.                                    change in input variables. 
3.  Memory elements are clocked flip-flops.      3.  Memory elements are either latches (unclocked 
                                                                                 flip-flops) or time-delay elements.

Q9.7 Define total states.
 All possible combinations of state variables and inputs are called total states of the circuit. 
Q9.8 Define metastable state.
 The continuous change between two unstable states is also called metastability (or metastable state) which 
 refers to an equilibrium condition in an unstable circuit.
Q9.9 What is difference between an internal state and a total state?
 When the excitation variables are fedback to input they are called internal states or secondary variables. The 
 excitation variables are called external states. 
 The internal states along with inputs are called total states.
Q9.10 Define flow table in asynchronous sequential circuit.
 The listing of all state transitions from present state to next state along with output for all possible changes 
 in input is called flow table.
Q9.11 What is primitive flow table. 
 A flow table may have one or more stable states in a row. When there is only one stable state in each row 
 of a flow table then it is called a primitive flow table. 
Q9.12 What is cycle?
 When the state transitions in a circuit go through a unique sequence of unstable states then that condition is 
 called a cycle.
Q9.13 What is meant by race? (or What is race around condition?)
 In an asynchronous sequential circuit, when there are changes in two or more state variables due to change 
 in input, a race condition may exist, in which changes in variables may occur at different timings due to  
 difference in delay in the feedback paths. This leads to unpredictable transition paths during a change in  
 state which in turn settle at different stable state.
Q9.14 Define critical race and non critical race.
 The race condition may be classified into critical and noncritical race. 
 Critical race : In a state transition, if the final stable state depends on the order of change in state variables, 
 then the race is called  critical race.
 Noncritical race : In a state transition, if the final stable state does not depends on the order of change in 
 state variables, then the race is called noncritical race.
Q9.15  Distinguish between noncritical and critical race.
 In noncritical race the final stable state will be same irrespective of the order of changes in state variables 
 and hence final stable state will be same for a change in input. 
 But in critical race the final stable state depends on the order of changes in state variables and hence the  
 final stable state will be different for a change in input. 
Q9.16 What is meant by race-free condition in sequential circuit?
 During state transitions if the order of changes in internal states does not affect the final stable state then the 
 condition is called race-free condition.

 Assigning adjacent codes to states to avoid critical races is called race-free assignment. Two binary codes 
 are said to be adjacent if they differ only in one variable.
