12.1  Basic Concepts of Memory
Memory is a storage device used to store binary information. The memory is manufactured using 
semiconductors in the form of ICs (Integrated Circuits). The basic storage unit in a memory device is called 
memory cell or binary cell. A memory cell can store one bit of binary information. 
Binary information is stored in group of bits called byte or word. Byte is 8-bit binary information. 
Word is 16-bit binary information. Larger size binary information are multiples of a word.
Standard larger size binary information with reference to memory storage are 32 bits, 64 bits and 
128-bits. The 32-bit binary is called double word and has 4 bytes. The 64-bit binary is called long word 
and has 8 bytes.
Byte becomes the standard size to denote memory cap acity because the human-machine 
communication is performed using ASCII (American Standard Code for Information Interchange) which 
is 8-bit binary code. A memory device will have large number of storage cells arranged in groups of 8 
cells to store a byte and the group of 8 cells is called a location or memory location. In general, a memory 
location can store m bits and the size of binary information that can be stored in a memory location is 
called memory word size and the stored binary information is called memory word.  
The process of storing binary information in a memory location is called write operation. The 
process of reading back the stored information from the memory location is called read operation. The 
read operation is non-destructive which means that after the read operation the memory content remains 
same until it is rewritten with new information.
Each memory location has a unique binary number called address. The address is used to access 
the location for read and write operation. The number of addresses for memory locations depends on size 
of binary used to generate addresses. We know that with n-bit binary we can generate 2 n different binary 
codes. Therefore, with n-bit binary we can generate 2n different binary addresses.
n = 1,  21 = 2       n = 4,   24 = 16      n = 7,  27 = 128
n = 2,  22 = 4       n = 5,   25 = 32      n = 8,  28 = 256
n = 3,  23 = 8       n = 6    26 = 64      n = 9,  29 = 512
n = 10,   210  =  1024 = 1 kilo
n = 11,   211  =  2048   =  2 ×1024  =  2 kilo
n = 12,   212  =  4096   =  4 ×1024  =  4 kilo
n = 16,   216  =  65536  = 64 × 1024  =  64 kilo   and so on.

A memory with 1 kilo locations that can store one byte in each location is called 1 kB (kilo-byte) 
memory. This memory will have 8 data lines and 10 address lines. Apart from that it will have read control, 
write control and chip select/enable signal as shown in Fig. 12.1.
In general, a memory will have m data lines and n address lines as shown in Fig. 12.2. The capacity of 
memory is 2n × m bits. Here, m is always multiple of 8, so that memory capacity can be expressed in bytes.

12.1.1  Types of Semiconductor Memories
The semiconductor memories can be broadly classified into two major types.
1.  RAM (Random Access Memory)
2.  ROM (Read Only Memory)
The RAM is also called RWM (Read/Write Memory). The RAM memory can be read or write in the 
system it is fitted or connected. But ROM memory can be only read in the system it is fitted or connected. 
For writing ROM memory a separate system called ROM programmer is needed.
The random access refer to accessing any location of memory with same time duration. Alternatively, 
the time to read or write any memory location is same in semiconductor memory. This feature is called 
random access.
Note: In magnetic memories like hard disc, CD, etc., the time to read/write a memory location 
will not be same.
All semiconductor memories has random access feature for read operation. For write operation only 
RAM memory has random access feature and so it is called RAM. (ROM also has random access features 
for read operation but not for write operation)
The RAM memory can be again classified into DRAM and SRAM
DRAM: Dynamic RAM
SRAM: Static RAM
Both DRAM and SRAM are volatile memories. In volatile memories , the information will be 
retained as long as power supply is ON. When power supply is OFF, the stored information will be lost 
in RAM memory.
In DRAM, the memory content has to be refreshed periodically to retain the stored information even 
when power is ON. Therefore, in all DRAM memory device an in-build refreshing logic will be available, 
which will read the memory content periodically and write into same location.

But in SRAM, refreshing is not required. Once information is stored in SRAM, it will be retained 
as long as power is ON.
The ROM memory can be classified into OTP-ROM, EPROM and EEPROM/EAPROM.
OTP-ROM is one-time programmable and once programmed the content cannot be altered and can 
only read by the system. For programming OTP-ROM separate programmer system is needed.
EPROM is Erasable Programmable ROM. For erasing the EPROM memory an UV (Ultra Violet) 
erasure is needed. It has to be exposed to UV light for 20 to 30 minutes. Then it can be reprogrammed 
using a separate programmer system.
Both ROM and EPROM can be read in the system it is fitted like a RAM memory, but differs only 
in write operation.
The EEPROM/EAPROM memory can be erased by passing an electrical current of specified value. 
They can be erased in the system they are fitted, and so no separate system is needed for erasing. The read 
and write operation is similar to RAM.
12.1.2  Functional Block Diagram of Semiconductor Memory
A typical semiconductor memory IC will have n address pins (lines) and m  data pins (lines). The 
capacity of the memory will be 2 n × m bits. Figure 12.3 shows a simplified functional block diagram of 
semiconductor memory. The functional blocks of semiconductor memory are Row address decoder, Column 
address decoder, Memory array, Input buffer and Output buffer.  
The input and output buffers are used to hold the data until the valid time and also takes care of 
the signal current level matching (Impedance matching). The  n address lines are split into q lines and r 
lines, such that q + r = n. The q address lines are applied as input to the row decoder and r address lines 
are applied as input to the column decoder.

The output lines of the row and column decoders are used to form a matrix array of size, 2 q × 2r 
consisting of 2n crossing points as shown in Fig. 12.4. Each crossing point is called memory cell or binary 
cell and can store one bit of binary information. A typical memory array will consist of m layers of matrix 
array as that of Fig. 12.4 and all of them are wired in parallel. 
When an address is send to memory IC, the row and column decoder will select one line each, which 
in turn select one memory cell in each layer. Thus, m memory cells are selected by an address. Then using 
read or write control signals, the data can be read or stored in the selected memory cells.
In the first version of semiconductor memory, the memory cells were made of passive elements 
like resistors and capacitors. Later, diodes were used instead of passive elements. With advancement 
in semiconductor technology, bipolar and MOS transistors were used to form memory cells. The latest 
technology used for fabricating memory cells are CMOS and HMOS which offer very low power and 
high-speed operation. 
A memory unit is designed to work with microprocessor or microcontroller system. Basically the 
microprocessor/controller will do data transfer with memory. Data transfer from memory to microprocessor 
is called read operation. Data transfer from microprocessor to memory is called write operation. The 
connection of memory with microprocessor is shown in Fig. 12.5.
For proper data transfer three standard control signals are used,
1.  Chip enable/Memory enable
2.  Write control
3.  Read Control
Read Operation
The microprocessor will output or send address first.
Then microprocessor will activate or send chip enable and Read control signal.
In response the memory will output data on data lines.
The microprocessor will read data from data lines.
All these operation are governed by a clock and completed in 3 to 4 clock pulses/periods.

Read Operation in SR Flip-Flop based Binary Cell

12.1.4  Address Decoding in Memory
A 2n × m-bit memory will have 2n storage locations that can be selected using n-bit address and each 
location will have m number of binary cells (BC). So that in each location m-bit memory word can be stored.
A schematic with linear address decoding scheme is shown in Fig. 12.10.
A n-to-2n decoder is employed to generate 2n control signals to select 2n rows.
Each row has m number of BCs. When an n-bit address is send to decoder it will select only one of 
the 2n rows and so data can be read/write only with the selected row.

12.8                                              Digital Logic Circuits
Coincident Decoding
The drawback in linear address decoding is that it require a single large decoder. This can be overcome 
in coincident decoding. In coincident address decoding the address bits are divided into two groups (nearly 
two equal groups). Two decoders are employed to decode the address bits. 
The output of decoders are used to form rows and columns of a matrix array (or two dimensional 
array). The data bits of a memory word is stored at the intersection of a row and column.
In the example shown in Fig. 12.11, a 10-bit address is divided into two groups of 5-bits and named 
A and B. Two 5-to-25 (5-to-32) decoders are employed to decode A and B.
Each decoder generate 32 lines. So a two dimensional array is formed with 32 rows and 32 columns. 
32 × 32 = 1024, so there will be 1024 crossing points of rows and columns. A typical memory will have 
m such arrays wired in parallel. Therefore, at each crossing point a m-bit data is stored.
12.1.5  Address Multiplexing in Memory
A memory IC with memory capacity 2 n × m bits will have n address pins. The concept of address 
multiplexing refer to supplying n-bit address to memory IC with capacity 2 n × m using less number of 
address pins. With less number of address pins it is possible to address larger size memory.
In one type of address multiplexing, a single set of address pins can be used to address row decoder 
and column decoder at different timing as shown in Fig. 12.12. In this scheme, there will be a row decoder 
address select and a column decoder address select signal.
In Fig. 12.12, there are two control signals: 
RAS - Row Address Select and CAS - Column Address 
Select. In order to access a memory location, first  RAS is activated and row address is send. Then CAS 
is activated and columns address is send.
An 8-to-28 (8-to-256) decoder is employed for row address decoding and another 8-to-28 decoder for 
column address decoding. Using these two decoder outputs a 256 × 256 two dimentional array is formed. 
(256 × 256 = 28 × 28 = 28+8 = 216 = 24 × 210 = 16 × 1024 = 16k). A typical memory will have m such arrays 
wired in parallel. At intersection of each row and column of the array a m-bit data is stored.

12.2  ROM and PROM
ROM is a semiconductor memory which permits only a read access. ROM functions as a memory 
array whose contents once programmed, are permanently fixed and cannot be altered by the microprocessor 
to which the memory is interfaced. Other names for this type of memory are dead memory, fixed memory, 
permanent memory and Read-Only Store (ROS). 
ROM is a nonvolatile memory, i.e., loss of power or  system malfunction does not change the 
contents of the memory. Also, the ROM memories have the feature of random access for read operation, 
which means that the access time (or read time) for a given memory location is same as that for all other 
locations. The process of storing information in ROM is called programming. The technique employed 
for storing information in the ROM provides a convenient method for classifying ROMs into one of the 
following three categories: 
1.   Custom programmed or Mask programmed ROM (ROM).
2.   Programmable or Field programmable ROM (PROM).
3.   Reprogrammable or Erasable-Programmable ROM (EPROM).
The custom programmed ROMs are programmed by the manufacturer as specified by the user during 
fabrication and the contents cannot be changed after packaging. The programmable ROMs are one-time 
programmable by the user. 
The reprogrammable ROMs have facilities for programming as well as for erasing its content and 
reprogramming the memory. The reprogrammable ROMs are erased either by passing electrical current 
or Ultraviolet light.
The programming of ROMs can be carried out using ROM (EPROM) programmer. Usually the ROM 
programmer is a digital system interfaced to a Personal Computer (PC). The information to be programmed 
are first stored as a file in the PC and converted to the required binary format using a conversion software. 
Then the information is transferred from the PC to ROM programmer.
12.2.1  Custom or Mask Programmed ROM
ROM devices are programmed during manufacturing as per customers requirements. After 
manufacturing the content of ROM connot be altered. The ROM device will have n-bit address input and 
m-bit data output as shown in Fig. 12.13.
In mask programmed ROM memory, the memory cell (storage unit) will have a MOS transistor 
either with open gate or closed gate as shown in Fig. 12.14. The transistors with closed gate represent 
1’s and with open gate represent 0’s. Since the configuration is fixed, they permanently store 1’s and 0’s.
A simple structure of a 4 × 4 bit ROM using a single MOS transistor for each shell is shown in 
Fig. 12.15.

12.2.2  Programmable or Field Programmable ROM
The programmable ROMs are one-time programmable (OTP) by 
the user. Hence it is also called OTP-ROM. The structure of PROM cells 
will be same as ROM but instead of permanent open or close a fusible 
link is provided in each memory cell. The fusible link can be left intact 
to store a 1 and can be blown open by passing high current to store a 0 
and this process is irreversible. 
Usually, the fusible link is provided in the source connection in 
order to pass higher current to blow the fuse. A simple MOS transistor 
based PROM cell is shown in Fig. 12.16. The PROM devices will have 
n-bit address input and m-bit data output similar to ROM device as shown 
in Fig. 12.13. The programming of PROM device is carried by fixing the PROM in a programming device 
and send an address to select a row and then passing current pulses through data lines where ever 0 has to 
be stored. This process is repeated for all rows one by one.

12.2.3  EPROM
The Read Only Memory (ROM) which has reprogrammable features is called EPROM (Erasable-
Programmable Read Only Memory). The EPROM memory is nonvolatile and also has the feature of 
random access for read operation. In an EPROM, the binary informations are entered using electri cal 
impulses and the stored information is erased using  ultraviolet rays. Typical erase time varies between 
10 to 30 minutes.
In EPROM, the memory cell (storage location of a bit) consists of a MOS transistor with isolated 
or floating gate. The isolated gate is located between the normal control gate and the source/drain region 
of a MOS transistor. 
The isolated gate has no electrical connection and so it can store electrical charge permanently. The 
1 and 0 of data bits are represented by presence or absence of charge in the isolated gate. 
The isolated gate may be charged with electrons dur ing the programming operation and when 
charged with electrons, the transistor is permanently turned OFF. The state of the isolated gate, charged or 
uncharged, is permanent because the gate is isolated in an extremely pure oxide.
A charged isolated gate represents a 0 and uncharged 
isolated gate represents a 1. When 0 is stored the channel 
will be completely OFF but when 1 is stored the cha nnel 
can be turned ON by applying a gate pulse. Hence for a read 
operation, select/address bit is applied to gate and the channel 
will turn ON if 1 is stored otherwise OFF. When channel is 
turned ON, the current flowing through the channel will create 
a voltage drop in an active load connected in series with the 
channel which is read as 1. When channel is OFF there is no 
voltage in active load which is read as 0. A single EPROM 
cell read operation is shown in Fig. 12.18. 
The cells are connected in rows and columns. The number of columns depends on the size of data 
stored in each row and hence each column will have an active load. The number of rows depends on the 
capacity of EPROM.
The charge on the isolated gate may be removed if the device is irradiated with ultraviolet light. The 
ultraviolet light allows the electrons to recombine and discharge through the control gate. The process of 
charging and discharging is repeatable.

The EPROM is programmed by inserting the EPROM chip into the socket of a PROM programmer and 
providing addresses and voltage pulses at the appropriate pins of the chip. Usually, the PROM programmer 
is interfaced to a Personal Computer (PC) and the information to be programmed is downloaded from PC.
EPROMs are manufactured by many semiconductor industries like INTEL, Hitachi, Toshiba, Cypress, 
etc. The manufacturers have a common industry standard, so that a product from different industry will be 
pin-to-pin compatible and slightly differ in electrical and switching characteristics.
The various features of 2764 (8kB EPROM) manufactured by Cypress semiconductor corporation 
are discussed in this section.
CY27C64 (Cypress Make CMOS 2764)
The CY27C64 is a high performance 8192 byte (8192 = 8 × 1024 = 8 kB) CMOS EPROM. It has 
power down mode, in which the device will enter a low-power standby mode when it is not enabled (or 
deselected).
The logic block diagram of CY27C64 is shown in Fig.12.19 and the pin configuration during read 
mode is shown in Fig. 12.20. [The pin configuration of CY27C64 will be different to that of Fig. 12.20 
during programming or write mode.] 
The chip has thirteen address inputs denoted as a0- a12. The address is used to access any one of the 
8 kilo (213 = 23 × 210 = 8 × 1024 = 819210) locations within the chip. 
The eight output lines, O0 to O7 are used to output data from the chip. The chip will be in standby 
mode when 
CE is inactive. The CE is  activated for selecting the chip and OE is activated for enabling 
the output buffer during the read operation.
The CY27C64 EPROM is available with maximum access time of 70, 90, 120, 150 or 200 ns 
(nanosecond). The electrical characteristics or ratings of the EPROM are listed in Table 12.1.

 change 
The CY27C64 EPROM is equipped with an erasure window. When the window is exposed to UV light, 
the contents of EPROM are erased and then it can be reprogrammed. Wavelengths of light less than 4000 A° 
(Angstrom unit) begin to erase the EPROM if the EPROM is exposed to sunlight or fluorescent lighting for 
a very long time. Hence, an opaque label should be placed over the window
The recommended dose of UV light for erasure is a wavelength of 2537 A° for a minimum dose (UV 
intensity multiplied by exposure time) of 25 W-sec/cm2. For an UV lamp with a 12 mW/cm2 power rating, 
the exposure time would be approximately 35 minutes. 
The EPROM has to be placed within a distance of 1 inch from the lamp during erasure. Permanent 
damage may result if EPROM is exposed to high intensity UV light for a very long time. (Maximum 
dosage is 7258 W-sec/cm2).
12.2.4  EEPROM/EAPROM
EEPROM/EAPROM is a nonvolatile read/write memory. They are also called flash memory. These 
memory devices are electrically erasable in the system, but require more time to erase than a static RAM. 
Therefore, they are called EEPROM (Electrically Erasable Programmable ROM) or EAPROM (Electrically 
Alterable Programmable ROM).

Chapter 12 - Memory and Programmable Logic Devices 12.17
The drawback in EEPROMs is that it takes longer time for the system to erase and write. The 
maximum number of write operations that can be performed in most of the EEPROMs is about 10,000 
operations.
INTEL and XYCOR have released their versions of nonvolatile RAMs, which does not have the 
drawbacks of EEPROMs. (The drawbacks of EEPROM are high write time and limited number of write 
cycles.) This type of nonvolatile RAMs consists of a high speed static RAM and a corresponding EEPROM 
on a single chip. For this  reason, it is also called shadow RAM. 
In these devices for each cell of static RAM, there is one EEPROM cell. A typical example of shadow 
RAM is INTEL 2004 and XYCOR’s X2004. The 2004 has a special pin called nonvolatile enable (NE). 
Normally, this pin is high and read or write operation is performed with static RAM. When NE is asserted 
low, the data in the static RAM cells are written into the corresponding EEPROM cells.
12.3  RAM
12.3.1  Static RAM
The static RAM (Random Access Memory) is a read/write memory. In static RAM, the memory 
cell (storage location for each bit of information) consists of a flip-flop or similar device constructed using 
four to eight MOS transistors. [Even though ROM memories are also technically random access memory, 
the read/write memories are called RAM.] Besides random access feature, the static RAMs are volatile in 
nature. The stored information is retained in the memory cell as long as power is supplied to the circuit. 
A typical SRAM cell is made up of six NMOS 
transistors is shown in Fig. 12.22 and it is called a 
6T SRAM cell. Four transistors M1, M2, M3 and M4 
that form two cross-coupled inverters are used to 
store a data bit and its complement. This storage 
cell has two stable states which are used to denote 
0 and 1.Two additional access transistors serve to 
control the access to a storage cell during read and 
write operations.
Access to the cell is enabled by the address 
bit which controls the two access transistors M 5 
and M6 which, decides whether the cell should be 
connected to the data bit lines and its complement. They are used to transfer data for both read and write 
operations. Although it is not strictly necessary to have two bit lines, both the signal and its inverse are 
typically provided in order to improve noise margin.
During read/write accesses, the bit lines are actively driven high and low by the inverters in the 
SRAM cell. This improves SRAM bandwidth.
The static RAMs are manufactured by many semiconductor companies like Motorola, Hitachi, 
Toshiba, Cypress, etc. The manufacturers have a common industry standard, so that a product from different 
companies will be pin-to-pin compatible and only slightly differ in electrical and switching characteristics. 
The various features of 6264 (8 kB RAM) manufactured by Cypress semiconductor corporation are discussed 
in this section.
(RGPV , Jun'22, 3 Marks)(VTU, Aug/Sep'20, 5 Marks)

CY6264 (Cypress Make CMOS 6264)
The CY6264 is a high performance CMOS static RAM organized as 8192 bytes (8192 = 8 × 1024 
= 8 kB). The device has a power down mode. When CY6264 is not enabled (deselected), it will enter the 
power down mode and in this mode the power consumed is reduced to 30% of active mode power.
The logic block diagram and the pin configuration of  CY6264 are shown in Figs. 12.23 and 12.24. 
The chip has 13 address inputs denoted as a0- a12. The address is used to access any one of the 8 kilo (8192) 
locations within the chip. It has eight IO pins for reading/writing the data and they are denoted as IO0-IO7.
The chip has four control signals CE 1, CE2, WE and OE. When CE 1 and WE inputs are both low 
and CE2 is high, data on the eight data pins (IO0 through IO7) is written into the memory location addressed 
by the address pins (a0 through a12).
When CE 1 and OE are both low and CE2 is high, the content of the memory location addressed by 
the address pins will be loaded on the eight data pins, IO0 to IO7.
The CY6264 RAM is available with maximum access time of 55 or 70 ns (nanosecond). The electrical 
characteristics or ratings of the RAM are listed in Table 12.3.

The read operation is carried out in the following steps:
 1.  Place the address of the location to be read on the address pins a 0- a12.
 2.  Enable the chip by asserting Chip Enable-1 ( CE 1) as low and Chip Enable-2 (CE2) as high.
 3.  Assert the Output Enable ( OE) signal low.
 4.  When OE signal is asserted low, the data can be read from the input/output lines (IO0 - IO7) 
                      after a delay time of tDOE (35 ns). 
When the address is placed on the address line, the memory will take a time of tAA to place the data on 
the output lines, provided the CE 1 and OE are asserted low and CE2 is asserted high at the appropriate time.
The timing diagram (or switching waveform) of CY6264 for write operation is shown in Fig. 12.26. 
The diagram shows some important timings of write cycle. 
For detailed discussions on timing diagram, refer to the manufacturer’s data sheet. The timings of 
various signals are listed in Table 12.5.
The write operation is carried out in the following steps :
 1.  Place the address of the location to be written on the address pins a 0 - a12.
 2.  Enable the chip by asserting CE1 signal as low and after a small delay assert CE2 signal as high.
 3.  Assert the write enable WE signal as low.
 4.  Place the data to be written on the IO 0-IO 7 lines immediately after WE is asserted low.
After the address is placed on the address lines and CE 1, CE2 and WE are asserted appropriately, 
the data has to be placed on the data lines within the time t SD (data set-up to write end).

12.3.2  DRAM
DRAM (Dynamic RAM) is a read/write memory in which the 
information is stored in the form of electric charg e on the gate-to-
substrate capacitance of a MOS transistor. This charge dissipates in a few 
milliseconds and the element must be refreshed periodically. A simplified 
MOS transistor based DRAM cell is shown in Fig. 12.27. The write, 
read and refreshing operations on a DRAM cell are shown in Fig. 12.28.
DRAMs are volatile and have random access feature. Dynamic RAMs are important because fewer 
elements are required to store a bit, so that more bits can be packed into an IC of a given physical area. 
They are also faster than the static RAM and consume less power in the quiescent state.
Refreshing of DRAMs needs extra circuitry and so the interfacing of DRAMs are more complex 
than the interfacing of static RAMs. The recent versions of DRAMs have internal refreshing circuit. The 
manufacturing of DRAMs will be cheaper only for very large capacity memories. Therefore, smaller 
memories are generally static elements (up to 256 kB) and large memories (> 1 MB) are typically dynamic.

Write Operation in DRAM
The procedure to write a 1 (data bit = 1) in the DRAM cell is as follows,
●  The refresh line is disabled by asserting low.
●  The control signal, R/W is enabled for write operation by asserting low.
●  Input data line, dIN is made high to write a 1 in DRAM cell.
●  The row line is asserted high to turn ON the transistor.
Now, the output and refresh buffers are disabled and input buffer is enabled. The transistor will act 
as a short circuit and connect the input data line to capacitor, so that the high on the data input line will 
charge the capacitor as shown in Fig. 12.28(a). 
The procedure to write a 0 (data bit = 0) in the DRAM cell is as follows,
●  The refresh line is disabled by asserting low.
●  The control signal, R/W is enabled for write operation by asserting low.
●  Input data line, dIN is made low to write a 0 in DRAM cell.
●  The row line is asserted high to turn ON the transistor.
Now, the output and refresh buffers are disabled and input buffer is enabled. The transistor will act 
as a short circuit and connect capacitor to the input data line, so that the low on the data input line will 
discharge the capacitor as shown in Fig. 12.28(b).

Read Operation in DRAM
The procedure to read a data bit from the DRAM cell is as follows,
●  The refresh line is disabled by asserting low.
●  The control signal, R/W is enabled for read operation by asserting high.
●  The row line is asserted high to turn ON the transistor.
Now, the input and refresh buffers are disabled and output buffer is enabled. The transistor will 
act as a short circuit and connect the output data line to capacitor, so that the high/ low voltage in the 
capacitor will appear on the output data as shown in Fig. 12.28(c). Here, the output buffer will only sense 
the voltage level on the capacitor and will not allow the capacitor to discharge and so the output buffer is 
also called sense amplifier. 
Refreshing Operation in DRAM
The charge in the capacitor of DRAM cell is refreshed by reading the data bit and then writing into 
same cell. The procedure to refresh a stored 1 (data bit = 1) in the DRAM cell is as follows,
●  The refresh line is enabled by asserting high.
●  The control signal, R/W
 is enabled for read operation by asserting high.
●  The row line is asserted high to turn ON the transistor.
Now, the input buffer is disabled and refresh and output buffers are enabled. The transistor will act 
as short circuit and connect the output data line to capacitor, so that the high/low voltage in the capacitor 
will appear on the output data line which is also input to refresh buffer. The refresh buffer output will 
charge the capacitor through the transistor as shown in Fig. 12.28(d).
12.3.3  Content-Addressable Memory (CAM)
CAM is a type of semiconductor memory that is designed for high-speed searching and retrieval 
of data. In a traditional memory, data is accessed by specifying an address, but in a CAM data retrieval is 
based on the actual content of the data itself. 
In a standard semiconductor memory, the user supplies a memory address and the memory returns 
the data word stored at that address. But in a CAM the user supplies a data word and the CAM searches its 
entire memory and if the data word is found, then the CAM returns an address where the word is stored. 
A CAM implements the lookup-table function in a single clock cycle using dedicated comparison 
circuitry. CAMs are especially popular in network routers for packet forwarding and packet classification, 
but they are also beneficial in a variety of other applications that require high-speed table lookup.
CAM is sometimes referred to as associative memory because it associates data content with its 
corresponding address, allowing for associative searches based on content rather than location.
CAM consists of a large array of memory cells, with each cell storing a bit of data (content). A 
CMOS binary CAM Cell consists of a 6T SRAM cell and in addition 4 comparison transistors as shown in 
Fig. 12.29. Every cell is connected to one data bit line (BL) and its complement (BL' ) so that data can be 
stored in cells using write control signal. For search operation, every cell is connected to one data search 
line (SL) and its complement (SL' ) so that data can be searched through read or search control signal.

When the data on the search lines (SL) differs from the data stored in the cell through the bit lines 
(BL), the match line (ML) will be pulled low to indicate a mismatch. If none of the cells on a match line 
indicate a mismatched bit, the match line will remain high at the precharge level to indicate a word match.
The architecture of CAM (Content-Addressable Memory) consists of conventional semiconductor 
memory (usually SRAM) with added comparison circuitry that enables a search operation to complete in 
a single clock cycle. 
The basic data storage in a CAM consists of a large array of memory cells, with each cell storing 
a bit of data (content). The position of cell in the array is the address of the cell. Each CAM cell contains 
a data bit along with associated comparison circuitry. The cells are arranged in rows and columns with 
each row store a word and number columns in each row determine the word size. In general, m × n, CMA 
will store m words of size n-bits each. The simplified architecture of m × n CAM is shown in Fig. 12.30.

 CAM uses match lines to indicate whether a match has been found during a search operation. These 
match lines are connected to the comparison circuitry and are used to identify memory cells where the 
stored data matches the input data.
When a search operation is initiated, the input data (search data) is loaded in search register of 
CAM. The comparison circuitry then compares this input data with the data stored in all memory cells in 
parallel. If a match is found, the corresponding match line is activated, and a  priority encoder is employed 
to generate the address or location of the matching data.
Example 12.3
Explain the logical construction of a 256 × 8 RAM using 64 × 8 RAM.  
Solution
The 256 × 8 memory will have 256 memory locations with 8-bit data per location. Since, 256 = 28, 8-bit address 
is required to address 256 memory locations.
The 64 × 8 memory will have 64 memory locations with 8-bit data per location. Here, 256/64 = 4, hence 4 
numbers of 64 ×8 memory is required to implement 256 × 8 memory.
Since, 64 = 26, 6-bit address is required to address 64 memory locations. In the 8-bit address of 256 × 8 memory, 
the lower 6-bits are common to all the four 64 × 8 memory. The upper two bits are decoded using a 2-to-4 decoder 
to generate four chip enable signals which are used as enables of 64 × 8 memory so that only one 64 × 8 memory is 
selected at any time. The logical diagram of 256 × 8 RAM using 64 × 8 RAM is shown in Fig. 1. 
Example 12.4
Design a 16 × 8 CAM using 8 × 2 CAM chips.  
Solution
The 8 × 2 CAM has a capacity of 8 words each of size 2-bits. The 16 × 8 CAM has a capacity of 16 words each 
of size 8-bits. In order to increase the word bit size to 8-bits, 4 numbers of 8 × 2 CAM should be connected in parallel 
to achieve an 8 × 8 CAM. The word capacity can be increased to 16 words by using two numbers of 8 × 8 CAM. The 
organization of 16 × 8 CAM using 8 × 2 CAM is shown in Fig. 1 (d).

The 8-bit data is split into group of 2-bits and each group is connected to one of the 8 × 2 CAM. Each 8 × 2 CAM 
will provide a 3-bit address when a 2-bit match data is found in that CAM. The 3-bit addresses of all the 8 × 2 CAM has

decode the 3-bit address of the 8 numbers of 8 × 2 CAM. The outputs corresponding to same row of CAMs are logically 
ANDed to combine the decoded output and then encoded using 16-to-4 encoder to generate a unique 4-bit address 
of the identified search data.
12.4  Programmable Logic Devices
The digital ICs (Integrated Circuits) can be broadl y classified into fixed function ICs and 
programmable ICs. The fixed function ICs are manufactured to perform a fixed logical function. Examples 
of fixed function ICs are flip-flops, decoders, mul tiplexers, counters, etc. The programmable ICs are 
designed to be programmed by the user to implement a variety of logical functions. 
Some of the programmable logical devices are,
●  PROM (Programmable ROM)
●  PLA (Programmable Logic Array)
●  PAL (Programmable Array Logic)
●  SPLD (Sequential Programmable Logic Device)
●  CPLD (Complex Programmable Logic Device)
●  FPGA (Field Programmable Gate Array)
The PROM, PAL and PLA are one-time programmable and consists of programmable logic gate 
arrays and can be used to implement only combinational logic functions. The SPLD, CPLD and FPGA 
devices are reprogrammable and consists of programmable logic gate arrays and flip-flops and so can be 
used to implement both combinational and sequential logic functions. 
The advantages of using PLDs to implement a logical function are,
●  PLDs require smaller chip and board area to implement a logic circuit.
●  Logical functions can be easily altered or modified without rewiring and changing the board.
●  Implementation is much faster when compared to fixed function ICs.
12.5  PROM as PLD
The inputs-outputs of a combinational circuit are fixed and can be listed in a truth table. Any fixed 
truth table can be implemented in a PROM device discussed in Section 12.2.2. 
The inputs of a combinational circuit can be used as address of PROM. The output of combinational 
circuit can be permanently stored in fusible links of PROM in which a 0 is blown fuse and 1 is intact fuse. 
An example of 16 × 8-bit PROM is shown in Fig. 12.31 in which 4 address lines (16 = 24) and 8 data 
lines are provided. ROM has a internal decoder (4-to-16 decoder) to decode the 4-bit address to 16 rows. 
Each row has 8 storage locations to store 8-bit data and 8 column lines are provided to access the 8-bit 
data. The columns are terminated on OR gates which act as output data buffers. Hence the memory will 
have 16 × 8 array. Each crossing point is a fusible link and 0's and 1's are permanently stored at these point.

--- Page 1011 ---
12.28                                              Digital Logic Circuits
A permanent 0 can be made by disconnecting the crossing point permanently which is called fuse 
opened or blown. A permanent 1 can be made by leaving the fussible link at the crossing point without open 
or kept intact. The 1 and 0 pattern stored in PROM will be specified by a truth table as shown in Table 12.6.
A typical truth table for programming the PROM is shown in Table 12.6 and the corresponding 
PROM is shown in Fig. 12.31. In Table 12.6, inputs are address bits (4-bit address), outputs are data bits 
(8-bit data) stored in PROM. A stored 1 is shown by × in Fig. 12.31. A stored 0 is shown by a simple 
crossing point of row and column.

12.6  PLA (Programmable Logic Array)
The PLA is a one-time programmable device to implement a Boolean function in sum of products 
form. The PLA will have an array of AND gates followed by an array of OR gates. In PLA, the AND gates 
are provided to implement product terms and OR gates are provided to implement sum of the product terms.
In order to minimize the gate requirements it is common practice to simplify the Boolean function 
to minimum literal form before implementation.
A typical PLA device will have,
●  n number of inputs
●  k number of AND gates
●  m number of OR gates
●  m number of XOR gates
Every input is provided with a buffer and an inverter. PLA will have facility to connect every input/ 
inverted input to array of the AND gate. Therefore, AND gates will have 2n inputs.

Similarly, the PLA will have facility to connect the output of any of the AND gate to all of the OR 
gate. Therefore, OR gates will have k inputs and the product terms generated by AND gates can be routed 
to any OR gate. XOR gates are used to generate normal /complement of output. 
Let, the output of OR gate be F and it is connected to one of the input of an XOR gate. The other 
input of XOR gate can be connected to 0 or 1. When the other input of  XOR is connected to 0, the output 
of XOR gate is F and when connected to 1, the output of XOR gate is F '. This can be verified from the 
truth table of XOR operation of function, F with 0 and 1 (Table 12.7).
The structure of PLA with three inputs, 
five AND gates, three OR gates and three XOR 
gates is shown in Fig. 12.32. In PLA device 
the connections to AND gates and OR gates 
are programmable. 
The structure of PLA in Fig. 12.32 
can be simplified as shown in Fig. 12.33 by 
combining the input buffers to a single buffer 
with two outputs and multiple input lines to 
gates by a single input line. 
A bubble is placed in one of the output of input buffer to indicate that this output will be inverted 
value of input. A slash with a number in the input line to gate indicates the number of input lines in that gate.

12.6.1  Implementation of Combinational Circuit using PLA
Consider the following two Boolean equations of a combinational circuit.
F1 = A' B + AB' C + ABC
F2 = (AB' C + B' C)'       ⇒      F2 = AB' C + B' C 
The Boolean equations has three variables and four product terms. When three input variables are 
complemented we get six inputs and so we require four numbers of six inputs AND gates to implement 
the four product terms. Here, there are two outputs, F1 and F2. Hence we require two OR gates to sum up 
the product terms to get two outputs. 
The structure of PLA with four AND gates two OR gates and two XOR gates is shown in Fig. 12.34. 
The connected inputs to AND gate are marked by x. The connected output of AND gate to input of OR 
gate are marked by x. The connections to 0 or 1 of one of the inputs of XOR gate are also shown by x. 
Here, F1 in expressed in SOP form and F2 in complement of SOP form. Therefore, the output of OR gate 
that generate SOP form of F1 is XORed with 0 to get F1. The output of OR gate that generates SOP form 
of F2 is XORed with 1 to get F2.
The simplified structure of the combinational circuit implemented in PLA is shown in Fig. 12.35.
A PLA programming table can be formed as shown in Table 12.8 to provide informations regarding 
the implementation of combinational circuit. Here, T refers to True output of a function and C refers to 
complement output of a function.

Example 12.8
Implement the following two Boolean functions with a PLA.
F1 = AB' C' + ABC' + ABC    and      F2 = (A' BC + AB' C + ABC)'  
Solution
The given Boolean equations are simplified as shown below:
F1 = AB' C' + ABC' + ABC
    = AB' C' + ABC' + ABC' + ABC = (ABC + ABC' ) + (ABC' + AB' C' )
     = AB(C + C' ) + AC' (B + B' ) = AB + AC'
F2 = (A' BC + AB' C + ABC)' 
    = (A' BC + AB' C + ABC + ABC)' = ((ABC + A' BC) + (ABC + AB' C))' 
    = (BC(A + A' ) + AC(B + B' ))' = (BC + AC)'
Now the simplified Boolean equations are,
F1 = AB + AC'
F2 = (BC + AC)'      ⇒      F2 = BC + AC
Using the above two simplified Boolean equations the PLA programming table is developed as shown in Table 1.  
The structure of programmed PLA using Table 1 is shown in Fig. 1. 
The simplified Boolean equations has three variables and four product terms. When three input variables are 
complemented we get six inputs and so we require four numbers of six inputs AND gates to implement the four product 
terms. Here, there are two outputs, F1 and F2. 
Hence we require two OR gates to sum up the product terms to get two outputs. The connected inputs to AND 
and OR gates are marked by ×. The connections to 0 or 1 of one of the inputs of XOR gates are also shown by ×. Here, 
F1 is expressed in SOP form and F2 in complement of SOP form. Therefore, the output of OR gate that generates SOP 
form of F1 is XORed with 0 to get F1. The output of OR gate that generates SOP form of F2 is XORed with 1 to get F2.

12.7  PAL (Programmable Array Logic)
PAL is a programmable logic device to implement a Boolean function in sum of products form. PAL 
will have programmable AND gate array followed by a fixed OR gate. A typical PAL device will have m 
sets of AND-OR array with each array having k number of AND gates and one OR gate. In PAL device 
one set of AND-OR array combination is used to independently implement one function. 
The only difference between PLA and PAL is that the OR gate array is programmable or not. In PLA 
device, the OR array is programmable but in PAL device the connections to OR array is fixed. In order 
to minimize the gate requirements, it is common practice to simplify the Boolean function to minimum 
literal form before implementation.

In PAL, the AND array is used to generate product terms. The product terms of AND array is routed 
to fixed OR gate in PAL, so that product terms of one function cannot be directly connected to another 
function. Whereas in PLA the product terms generated by AND gates can be routed to any OR gate. The 
PAL will have programmable facility to connect the output of an AND-OR array as input to AND gate 
of any other AND-OR array. This facility can be used to cascade the AND-OR array so that the cascade 
combination can be used to implement a larger number of product terms than permitted by a single AND-
OR array. 
A typical PAL device will have,
●  n number of inputs   ●  m number of OR gates
●  k number of AND gates                        ●  m number of XOR gates

Every input is provided with a buffer and an inverter. PAL will have facility to connect every input/ 
inverted input to any of the AND gate. XOR gates are used to generate True/complement of output. 
The output of each OR gate is connected to one of the inputs of an XOR gate. The other input of 
XOR gate can be connected to 0 or 1. When the other input of XOR is connected to 0 we get True output 
and when connected to 1 we get complemented output. This can be verified from Table 12.7.
The internal structure or architecture of PAL devic e with n inputs and m outputs is shown in  
Fig. 12.36. One set of AND-OR combination has 3 AND gates and so only three product terms can be 
generated. The three product terms are summed up using an OR gate. When we need a larger number of 
product terms, the output of an AND-OR array can be connected as input to any AND gate so that cascade 
connection of AND-OR array will have sum of all the product terms. The number of inputs to AND gate 
will be 2(n + m).  
In some of the PAL devices, the outputs of PAL will have tristate logic with active low output and 
provided with complement facility using XOR gate similar to PLA.

12.8  Sequential Programmable Logic Device (SPLD)
The SPLD includes flip-flops, in addition to the AND-OR array, within the integrated circuit chip. 
The block diagram of a SPLD is shown in Fig. 12.38. In a SPLD, a PLA or PAL is modified by including 
a number of flip-flops connected to form registers. The circuit outputs can be taken from the OR gates or 
from the outputs of the flip-flops. Additional programmable connections are available to include the flip-
flop output in the product terms formed with the AND array. The flip-flops may be D or JK type.
A PAL that includes flip-flops is also known as a registered PAL, to signify that the device contains 
flip-flops in addition to the AND-OR array. The SPLD will have a number of sections of registered PAL 
and these sections of a SPLD are called macrocells.
Fig. 12.39 shows the logic of a basic macrocell. The AND-OR array is the same as in the combinational 
PAL. The output is driven by an edge-triggered D flip-flop connected to a common clock input. The ouput 
of the flip-flop is connected to a three-state buffer (or inverter) controlled by an output enable (OE) signal. 
The output of the flip-flop is fed back into one of the inputs of the programmable AND gates to provide 
the present-state condition for the sequential circuit. A typical SPLD has 8 to 10 macrocells.
In addition, a macrocell may have other programming features like ability to either use or bypass 
the flip-flop, the selection of clock edge polarity, the selection of preset and clear for the register, and the 
selection of the true value or complement of an output. An XOR gate is used to program a true/complement 
condition.     
(JNTUH, Nov/Dec'20, 7 Marks)

12.9  Complex Programmable Logic Device (CPLD) 
A CPLD integrates a number of PLDs in a single device so that large complex combinational and 
sequential digital systems can be implemented in a CPLD.
The CPLDs of different manufactures differ in architecture and functionality but have some common 
features. The common basic architecture of a CPLD is shown in Fig. 12.40. 
A CPLD consists of three main components: programmable logic blocks, programmable interconnect 
channel and I/O block. Each programmable logic block of a CPLD consists of a fully programmable 
AND-OR array similar to a PAL/PLA and a bank of macrocells. A simplified block diagram of a typical 
programmable logic block is shown in Fig. 12.41.
The AND/OR array is reprogrammable and can perform a large number of logic functions. 
Macrocells are functional blocks with flip-flop, data selector and other control logic circuits that can perform 
combinatorial or sequential logic. Macrocells also have the added flexibility for true or complement output, 
along with feedback paths. Each macrocell has multiple configurations and each macrocell can be used in 
cascade, so that more complex combinational and sequential logic functions can be realized. 
Programmable interconnect channels provide intercon nection networks between logic blocks, 
macrocells and input/output pins. The input/output blocks (I/O blocks) provide the interface between the 
internal logic to the I/O pins of the device. In advanced version of CPLDs, embedded array blocks with 
on-chip RAM/ROM are usually provided.

Chapter 12 - Memory and Programmable Logic Devices 12.55
12.10  Field Programmable Gate Array (FPGA)
R.H.Freeman invented the first practical FPGA in 1985.
FPGA is a programmable semiconductor logic device consisting of large number of logic gates which 
can be configured by the user to implement any kind of digital circuit or system. FPGAs are manufactured 
with thousands to millions of logic gates. The programming of logic gates of FPGA is called configuration 
and FPGAs are reprogrammable (or reconfigurable). 
The configuration of the FPGA is generally performed using a Hardware Description Language 
(HDL). The popular HDLs are Verilog and VHDL. 
FPGAs store their customized configuration data in SRAM-type internal latches. Depending on the 
device size and user-design implementation options the number of configuration bits varies from 1 Mb to 
33 Mb or even more in modern FPGAs. 
The internal SRAM is volatile and so the configurations bits will be erased whenever power is turned 
OFF. Therefore, when an FPGA is powered up the configuration storage must be reloaded. Usually, the 
modern FPGA based systems will have serial EEPROM as boot loader, so that the configuration bits are 
permanently stored in boot loader and whenever power is turned ON the configuration bits are serially 
transmitted from EEPROM to configuration SRAM in FPGA.
Xilinx and Altera are two major manufacturers of FPGA holding nearly 90% of market share. The 
discussions in this section are with reference to Xilinx FPGAs. Altera FPGAs may also have resources 
similar to Xilinx FPGAs but there will be differences in architecture and functionality.  
12.10.1  Basic Architecture of FPGA 
FPGAs are evolved from gate arrays and early versions of FPGA basically have simple Configurable 
Logic Blocks (CLB) and small number of inputs and outputs as shown in Fig. 12.42. Each CLB will consist 
of a Look-Up Table (LUT) and a Flip-Flop (FF). The basic idea of FPGA’s is to inter-connect small “truth 
tables” to emulate complex digital circuits. In an FPGA, these tables are called “Lookup Table” (LUT).
The basic architecture of an FPGA is shown in Fig. 12.43.
The FPGA architecture consists of four major components
●  Programmable/Configurable Logic Blocks
●  Programmable switch blocks
●  Programmable Routing (interconnect lines)
●  I/O blocks

12.56                                              Digital Logic Circuits
A configurable logic block (CLB) is the basic logic resource on an FPGA. The configurable logic 
block (CLB) includes logic and look-up tables (LUTs) that can be configured to implement combinational 
logic circuits. When CLBs are linked together by routing resources (carry chain), the components in CLBs 
execute complex logic functions, implement memory functions and synchronize code on the FPGA. The 
block diagram of a typical CLB in an FPGA is shown in Fig. 12.44. 
The CLB shown in Fig. 12.44 contain look-up-table (LUT), carry logic, flip-flop (FF) and multiplexer. 
It also has a clear/preset and clock control unit. A  LUT can speed up processing by providing the output 
for a given input without logical processing. A flip-flop is a primitive storage device that can store a single 
bit of information. 
Carry look-ahead logic is implemented in each CLB with a combination of dedicated multiplexer 
and XOR gates that are used within the carry/cascade chain. The carry/cascade chain logic in an individual 
CLB is the circuit that directly connects a column of CLBs together. It is possible to cascade a carry chain 
across multiple CLBs in order to quickly implement addition, subtraction, and multiplication operations 
on operands that are too large to be processed by a single CLB.

Chapter 12 - Memory and Programmable Logic Devices 12.57
The programmable routing are the wiring resources in FPGAs. The programmable routing establishes 
a connection between logic blocks and Input/Output blocks to complete a user-defined design unit. It 
consists of multiplexers pass transistors and tri-state buffers. Pass transistors and multiplexers are used in 
a logic cluster to connect the logic elements.
The programmable switches are user-programmable switch that can connect a logic element to an 
interconnect wire and/or one interconnect wire to another. The programmable I/O pads are used to interface 
the logic blocks and routing architecture to the external components. The I/O pad and the surrounding logic 
circuit form as an I/O cell. These cells consume a large portion of the FPGA’s area. And the design of I/O 
programmable blocks is complex, as there are great differences in the supply voltage and reference voltage.
Modern FPGAs contain a heterogeneous mixture of different blocks like dedicated memory blocks, 
multiplexers. Configuration memory is used throughout the logic blocks to control the specific function 
of each element.
Advantages of FPGA
●  FPGAs can implement faster and parallel processing.
●  FPGAs are programmable IC, programmed by software and can be re-programmed or reused any 
number of times. 
●  Since FPGA ICs are programmable the solution is available faster to the market. 
●  FPGA development is cheaper due to non recurring expenses. 
●  In FPGA, software takes care of routing, placement and timing and so manual intervention is lesser. 
Disadvantages of FPGA
●  Programming the FPGA requires the knowledge of VHDL/Verilog programming languages and 
digital system fundamentals.
●  Programmers do not have any control on power optimization.
●  Development resources are more specific for specific FPGA. 
●  FPGAs are costly for large quantity production.
Comparison of CPLD and FPGA
●  FPGA is more suitable for structures with large number of flip-flops, while CPLD is more suitable 
for structures with limited flip-flops and rich product terms.
●  The continuous wiring structure of CPLD determines that its timing delays are uniform and 
predictable, while the segmented wiring structure of FPGA determines the unpredictability of its delays.
●  CPLD is programmed by modifying the logic function with fixed interconnect circuit, while 
FPGA is programmed by changing the wiring of internal wires.
●  FPGA can be programmed under the logic gate, while CPLD is programmed under the logic 
block. Hence, CPLDs are faster than FPGAs and have greater time predictability.
●  FPGAs are more integrated than CPLDs and have more complex wiring structures and logic 
implementations.

--- Page 1041 ---
12.58                                              Digital Logic Circuits
● CPLD is programmed using internal EEPROM or FASTFLASH technology, no external memory 
chip is needed. While the FPGA programming information needs to be stored in external memory, and 
transferred to internal RAM during switch ON.
●  CPLD is mainly based on EEPROM or FLASH memory programming, which can be programmed 
up to 10,000 times, and has the advantage that the programming information is not lost even when the 
system is powered off.
12.10.2  Xilinx FPGA Family of Devices
Xilinx has released a number of families of FPGA devices with a large number of internal logical 
devices in each family with enhanced and variable features. XC2000 series is the first family of FPGA 
devices released by Xilinx in the year 1985 manufactured using 2000 nm (nano-meter) process. 
Note: The nano-meter manufacturing process refer to the size of fundamental transistor in the 
FPGA IC. Xilinx started with 2000 nm process and realized up to 7 nm process in their latest Versal 
family of FPGAs. 
This is followed by XC3000, XC4000, XC5200, XC6200 and XC8100 series of FPGA devices 
released over a period of 10 years, from 1985, with enhanced features in every family of devices. These 
FPGA devices are outdated and no longer manufactured by Xilinx. 
The Family of Xilinx FPGA devices released after 19 95 are named as Spartan, Artix, Kintex, 
Virtex and Versal. The evolution of various families of FPGA devices has made improvements in density, 
performance, power consumption, voltage levels, IO support and other functionality. The various Xilinx 
FPGAs are listed in Appendix 7. A brief discussion about Spartan-6 family of FPGAs is presented in the 
following section. 
12.10.3  Spartan-6 Family of FPGA
The Spartan-6 family includes thirteen types of FPGA devices with logic cell densities ranging 
from 3,840 to 1,47,443 logic cells and manufactured using 45 nm low-power copper process technology. 
The specific features of Spartan-6 family members are summarized in Tables 12.10 and 12.11. The salient 
features of Spartan-6 family of FPGAs are, 
●  Dual-register 6-input lookup table (LUT) logic.
●  18 kB (2 x 9 kB) block RAMs.
●  Second generation DSP48 slices.
●  SDRAM memory controllers.
●  Enhanced mixed-mode clock management blocks.
●  Select IO technology.
●  Power optimized high-speed serial transceiver blocks.
●  PCI Express compatible Endpoint blocks.
●  Advanced system-level power management modes.
●  Auto-detect configuration options.
●  Enhanced IP security with AES and Device DNA protection.

CLBs, Slices and LUTs
Each configurable logic block (CLB) in Spartan-6 FPGAs consists of two slices, arranged side-by-
side as two vertical columns. There are three types of CLB slices in the Spartan-6 architecture: SLICEM, 
SLICEL and SLICEX. Each slice contains four LUTs, eight flip-flops and other control logic. The LUTs 
are used to implement combinational and sequential logic functions. 
In the total slices in Spartan-6 FPGA, 25% of slices are SLICEMs. Each of the four SLICEM LUTs 
can be configured as either a 6-input LUT with one output, or as dual 5-input LUTs with identical 5-bit 
addresses and two independent outputs. These LUTs can also be used as distributed 64-bit or 32-bit RAM, 
or as a single 32-bit shift register, or as two 16-bit shift registers. Each LUT output can be registered in a 
flip-flop within the CLB. For arithmetic operations, a high-speed carry chain propagates carry signals in 
a column of slices.
In the total slices in Spartan-6 FPGA, 25% of slices are SLICELs, which contain all the features of 
the SLICEM except the memory/shift register function.
In the total slices in Spartan-6 FPGA, 25% of slices are SLICEXs. The SLICEXs have the same 
structure as SLICELs except the arithmetic carry option and the wide multiplexers.
Clock Management
Spartan-6 have up to six clock management tiles (CMTs), each consisting of two digital clock 
managers (DCMs) and one phase lock loop (PLL). The DCM provides four phase shift of the input 
frequency (CLKIN): 0°, 90°, 180°, and 270°. It also provides a doubled clock frequency output and its 
complement output. 
The PLL can act as a frequency synthesizer and as a filter for input clock in combination with the 
DCMs. V oltage-Controlled Oscillator (VCO) is the heart of the PLL with a frequency range of 400 MHz to 
1,080 MHz. PLL have of programmable frequency dividers to divide the clock generated clock to convert 
to clock at different clock rates. 
Block RAM
Every Spartan-6 FPGA has between 12 and 268 dual-port block RAMs, each with a capacity of  
18 kB. Each block RAM has two independent ports that share the stored data.
Each memory access is controlled by the clock. All the inputs, data, address, clock enables, and 
write enables are stored in registers. The data output retains data until the next operation.
The memory data width is programmable and hence, each port can be configured as 16K × 1, 8K × 
2, 4K × 4, 2K × 9 (or 8), 1K × 18 (or 16), or 512 x 36 (or 32).  Parity bits are included in the x9, x18, and 
x36 configurations. 

--- Page 1045 ---
12.62                                              Digital Logic Circuits
Memory Controller Blocks
Spartan-6 devices have dedicated memory controller blocks (MCBs) for interfacing external DRAM 
and support access rates up to 800 Mb/s. The MCB has dedicated routing to predefined I/Os. If the MCB 
is not used, these I/Os are used as general purpose I/Os. The MCB can be connected to 4 -, 8-, or 16-bit 
external DRAM. The MCB provides a faster DRAM interface.
The memory controller offers a complete multi-port arbitrated interface to the logic inside the 
Spartan-6 FPGA. Commands and data can be pushed to and poped from independent built-in FIFOs, using 
conventional FIFO control signals. 
Digital Signal Processing-DSP48 Slice
Spartan-6 FPGAs have many dedicated DSP slices consisting of binary multipliers and accumulators 
to support DSP computations. Each DSP48 slice consists of a dedicated 18 × 18 bit two's complement 
multiplier and a 48-bit accumulator.
The DSP48 slice provides extensive pipelining and extension capabilities that enhance speed and 
efficiency of many applications, such as wide dynamic bus shifters, memory address generators, wide bus 
multiplexers and memory-mapped I/O register files. The accumulator can also be used as a synchronous 
up/down counter. The multiplier can perform barrel shifting.
Input/Output Banks
The number of I/O pins varies from 102 to 576, depending on device and package size. Each I/O 
pin is configurable and can comply with a large number of standards, using up to 3.3 V. 
With the exception of supply pins and a few dedicated configuration pins, all other package pins 
have the same I/O capabilities. All user I/Os are bidirectional. All I/O pins are organized in banks, with 
four banks on the smaller devices and six banks on the larger devices.
Serial Transceiver
Spartan-6 LXT devices have 2 to 8 transceiver circuits. Each transceiver is a combined transmitter 
and receiver capable of operating at data rates up to 3.2 Gb/s. The transmitter and receiver are independent 
circuits that use separate PLLs to multiply the reference frequency input by certain programmable numbers 
between 2 and 25, to become the bit-serial data clock. 
The transmitter is fundamentally a parallel-to-serial converter with a conversion ratio of 8, 10, 16, 
or 20. The transmitter output drives the PC board with a single-channel differential current-mode logic 
(CML) output signal. The receiver is fundamentally a serial-to-parallel converter, changing the incoming 
bit serial differential signal into a parallel stream of words, each 8, 10, 16, or 20 bits wide.
Integrated Endpoint Block for PCI Express Designs
The PCI Express standard is a packet-based, point-t o-point serial interface standard. The PCI 
Express Base Specification 1.1 defines bit rate of 2.5 Gb/s per lane, per direction (transmit and receive). 
The Spartan-6 LXT devices include one integrated Endpoint block for PCI Express technology that is 
compliant with the PCI Express Base Specification Revision 1.1.

12.11  Summary of Important Concepts
1. The digital ICs (Integrated Circuits) can be broadly classified into fixed function ICs and programmable  
 ICs. 
2. PROM, PAL and PLA are one-time programmable and consists of programmable logic gate arrays and  
 so can be used to implement only combinational logic functions. 
3. CAM is a type of semiconductor memory that is designed for high-speed searching and retrieval of data.
4. CAM consists of a large array of memory cells, with each cell storing a bit of data (content).
5. FPGA devices are reprogrammable and consists of programmable logic gate arrays and flip-flops and so  
 can be used to implement both combinational and sequential logic functions. 
6. PLA is a one-time programmable device to implement a Boolean function in sum of products form.
7. PAL device will have m sets of AND-OR array with each array having k number of AND gates and one  
 OR gate. 
8. A CPLD integrates a number of PLDs in a single device.
9. A CPLD consists of three main components: programmable logic blocks, programmable inter connect  
 channel and I/O block. 
10. Each programmable logic block of a CPLD consists of a fully programmable AND-OR array similar to  
 a PAL/PLA and a bank of macrocells.
11. FPGA is a programmable semiconductor logic device consisting of large number of logic gates.
12. The programming of logic gates of FPGA is called configuration and FPGAs are reprogrammable (or  
 reconfigurable). 
13. FPGAs store their customized configuration data in SRAM-type internal latches.
14. The basic idea of FPGA’s is to inter-connect small “truth tables” to emulate complex digital circuits.
15. The FPGA architecture consists of four major components: programmable/configurable logic blocks,  
 programmable switch blocks, programmable routing (interconnect lines), I/O blocks.
16. A configurable logic block (CLB) is the basic logic resource on an FPGA. 
17. The configurable logic block (CLB) includes logic and look-up tables (LUTs) that can be configured to  
 implement combinational logic circuits. 
18. Carry look-ahead logic is implemented in each CLB with a combination of dedicated multiplexer and  
 XOR gates.
19. The programmable routing are the wiring resources in FPGAs. 
20. The programmable switches are user-programmable sw itch that can connect a logic element to an  
 interconnect wire and/or one interconnect wire to another. 
21. The digital ICs (Integrated Circuits) can be broadly classified into fixed function ICs and programmable  
 ICs. 
22. PROM, PAL and PLA are one-time programmable and consists of programmable logic gate arrays and  
 so can be used to implement only combinational logic functions. 
23. FPGA devices are reprogrammable and consists of programmable logic gate arrays and flip-flops and so  
 can be used to implement both combinational and sequential logic functions.

24. PLA is a one-time programmable device to implement a Boolean function in sum of products form.
25. PAL device will have m sets of AND-OR array with each array having k number of AND gates and one  
 OR gate. 
26. The SPLD includes flip-flops, in addition to the AND-OR array, within the integrated circuit chip. 
27.  A CPLD integrates a number of PLDs in a single device.
28. A CPLD consists of three main components: programmable logic blocks, programmable inter connect

12.12  Short-Answer Questions
Q12.1   Distinguish between a memory address and memory's addressability?
 The memory address is the identification number in binary for a memory location.
 The memory's addressability is the size of binary that can be stored in a memory location.
 For example in 6264 RAM memory, the memory address range is 0000 H to 1FFF H with addressability of 
 8-bits i.e., each memory location can store 8-bit binary information.
Q12.2   A memory unit is 16-bit addressable and has 12 k locations. How many bits of storage does the memory  
 consist of?
 The storage capacity of the memory will be 12 k × 16-bit = 192 kilo-Bits.
Q12.3 Define memory address and memory word.
 Each memory location has a unique binary number called address. The address is used to access the location  
 for read and write operation.
 In general, a memory location can store m bits and the size of binary information that can be stored in a  
 memory location is called memory word size and the stored binary information is called memory word.

--- Page 1048 ---
Chapter 12 - Memory and Programmable Logic Devices 12.65
Q12.4   Give two advantages of machine language programming over high-level language programming?
 i)  Machine language program can be directly executed in a machine and does not require conversion using 
 assembler/compiler. Hence execution of machine language program will be much faster than any other  
 language program.
 ii) The machine language program can be written using only two symbols '0' and '1'.
Q12.5   What are the types of semiconductor memories?
 The semiconductor memories can be broadly classified into two major types,
 1.  RAM (Random Access Memory)
 2.  ROM (Read Only Memory)
Q12.6 What is a RAM?
 RAM is a semiconductor memory. The RAM is also called RWM (Read/Write Memory). The RAM memory 
 can be read or write in the system it is fitted or connected.
Q12.7 What is a ROM?
 ROM is a semiconductor memory. ROM memory can be only read in the system it is fitted or connected. 
 For writing ROM memory a separate system called ROM programmer is needed.
Q12.8 List the types of ROM.
 1.  Programmable Read Only Memory (PROM)
 2.  Erasable Programmable Read Only Memory (EPROM)
 3.  Electrically Erasable Programmable Read Only Memory (EEPROM).
Q12.9 What is Read and Write operation?
 The binary information can be stored in a memory location which is called write operation.
 The stored information can be taken back from the memory loaction which is called read operation. 
Q12.10 Define memory location.
 A memory device will have large number of storage cells arranged in groups of 8 cells to store a byte and  
 the group of 8 cells is called location or memory location.
Q12.11    What are the characteristics of ROM memory ?
    1.  ROM is non-volatile memory.
   2.  The contents of ROM can be read by the processor but it cannot perform a write operation.
   3.  The ROM has the feature of random access for read operation.
   4.  The memory cell has a MOS transistor either with an open gate or a closed gate.
Q12.12    How are ROMs classified?
    ROMs can be classified into the following three categories based on the method of programming. 
   1.  Custom programmed or Mask programmed ROM.
   2.  Programmable or Field programmable ROM.
   3.  Reprogrammable or Erasable-programmable ROM.

Q12.15    Write a short note on the memory cell of EPROM.
    The memory cell of EPROM contains a MOS transistor with isolated or floating gate. The isolated gate is     
   located between the normal control gate and the source/drain region of transistor. The information is stored    
   as a charge or no charge in the isolated gate. 
Q12.16   What is NVRAM?
     The non-volatile read/write memories are called NVRAM. The various types of  NVRAMs are flash memory,     
   EEPROM and Shadow RAM. 
Q12.17   List the features of static RAM.
  1. Static RAMs are read/write memories.
   2. They are volatile and have random access feature for both read and write operations.
   3. The memory cell is a flip-flop constructed using 6 to 8 MOS transistors. 
Q12.18    What is DRAM ?
    DRAMs are read/write semiconductor memories in which the information is stored in the form of electric      
   charge on the gate to substrate capacitance of a MOS transistor. 
Q12.19    List the characteristics of DRAM.
   1. The DRAMs are volatile and have random access feature.
   2. They are read/write memories.
   3. The contents of DRAM has to be refreshed periodically using refreshing circuits. 
   4. The memory cell of DRAM will have 3 to 4 MOS transistor.

Q12.24  How many address bits are required for a 512 × 4 memory?
   A 512 × 4 memory has 512 locations with 4-bit data stored in each location. Here, 512 = 29, and hence with 
               9-bit address it is possible to generate 512 addresses in order to address all the 512 locations.
   ∴ Address bits = 9
Q12.25   A microprocessor uses RAM chips of 1024 × 1 capacity.   
    a) How many chips will be required and how many a ddress lines will be connected to provide a capacity of 
          1024 bytes?
    b)  How many chips will be required to obtain a memory of capacity of 16 K bytes?
Solution:
                    a)    A 1024 × 1 memory will have 1024 storage locations with 1-bit stored in each location. A memory with 1024 
               bytes (1024 × 8) will have 1024 storage locations with 8-bit stored in each locations. Therefore, 8 memory  
                    ICs of capacity 1024 × 1 are connected to common address lines. Here, 1024 = 210, and hence 10 address lines 
              are required to address all the 1024 locations.

Q12.26 What is programmable logic array? How it differs from ROM?
 The PLA is a device to implement Boolean function in sum of products form. The PLA will have an array  
 of AND gates to implement product terms followed by an array of OR gates to implement the sum of the  
 products. 
 ROM is a storage device used to store the truth table of a Boolean function. But PLA is used to implement  
 the SOP form of a Boolean function.  
Q12.27 What is the difference between PLA and PAL? 
 The only difference between PLA and PAL is that the OR gate array is programmable or not. In PLA device, 
 the OR array is programmable but in PAL device the connections to OR array is fixed.
Q12.28 Explain about combinational PLD's.
                    PLDs without flip-flops are also called combinational PLDs and they are used to implement only combinational  
                        logic circuits. The PROM, PAL and PLA are combinational PLDs.
Q12.29 What are the basic internal components of CPLD?
 A CPLD consists of three main components. 
●  Programmable logic blocks. 
●  Programmable inter connect channel. 
●  I/O block.
Q12.30 What is FPGA?
 FPGA is a programmable semiconductor logic device consisting of large number of logic gates which 
 can be configured by the user to implement any kind of digital circuit or system. FPGAs are manufactured  
 with thousands to millions of logic gates. The programming of logic gates of FPGA is called configuration  
 and FPGAs are reprogrammable (or reconfigurable).
Q12.31 What are basic internal components of FPGA?
 The FPGA architecture consists of four major components.
●  Programmable/Configurable Logic Blocks
●  Programmable switch blocks
●  Programmable Routing (interconnect lines)
●  I/O blocks
Q12.33 What is configuration in FPGA?
 The programming of logic gates of FPGA is called co nfiguration and FPGAs are reprogrammable (or 
 reconfigurable). The configuration of the FPGA is generally performed using a Hardware Description  
 Language (HDL). The popular HDLs are Verilog and VHDL.

Q12.34 What are the difference between CPLD and FPGA?
 ●  FPGA is more suitable for structures with large number of flip-flops, while CPLD is more suitable for 
      structures with limited flip-flops and rich product terms.
 ●  The continuous wiring structure of CPLD determines that its timing delays are uniform and predictable,  
        while the segmented wiring structure of FPGA determines the unpredictability of its delays.
 ●  CPLD is programmed by modifying the logic function with fixed interconnect circuit, while FPGA is  
      programmed by changing the wiring of internal wires.
 ●   FPGA can be programmed under the logic gate, while CPLD is programmed under the logic block.
Q12.35 Differentiate between word capacity and word size.
 The word capacity refers to number storage locations in a memory. The word size refers to the size of binary 
 that can be stored in a memory location. For examp le, a memory of capacity 1024 × 16, has the word capacity 
 of 1024 locations with word size of 16-bits, so that 1024 numbers of 16-bit binary words can be stored in  
 1024 × 16 memory.

DATA CONVERTERS
13.1  Introduction
Processing of various types of signals is an important requirement in engineering. Since the real 
world signals are analog in nature, before the invention of digital systems the signals were processed by 
analog systems. After the invention of digital systems, it becomes more convenient to process signals by 
digital systems. 
In order to process signals by digital systems the analog signal has to be converted to digital signal 
and after processing, the processed digital signal has to be converted back to analog signal for real world 
application. The conversion of analog to digital signal is performed using a device called Analog to Digital 
Converter (ADC). The conversion of digital to analog signal is performed using a device called Digital to 
Analog Converter (DAC). In general, the ADC and DAC are referred to as data converters.  
The ADC will generate an n-bit binary corresponding to analog input voltage signal. The n-bit binary 
can have 2n different binary values. Every ADC will have a positive and negative voltage reference. The 
input analog voltage should be within this reference value. The ADC will divide the difference between 
positive and negative reference into 2n - 1 steps and it can generate a unique n-bit binary for each step of 
reference value. When the input analog value matches one of the steps of reference value the ADC will 
output the corresponding n-bit binary. 
The DAC will generate an analog voltage or current signal corresponding to input n-bit binary. The 
n-bit binary can have 2 n different binary values. Every DAC will have a positive and negative voltage/
current reference. The generated output analog voltage/current will be within this reference value. The 
DAC will divide the difference between positive and negative reference into 2 n - 1 steps which can be 
matched to 2n - 1 binary values of n-bit excluding zero. For every input n-bit binary, the DAC will generate 
the correspond step of analog value.
Note: Since one of the 2 n binary value is 0, the reference value is divided into 2 n
 - 1 steps and 
matched to 2n
 - 1 binary values.
