13.2                                              Digital Logic Circuits
The ADC is also known as A/D converter and the DAC is known as D/A converter. The process of 
analog to digital conversion is also referred to as A/D process. Similarly the process of digital to analog 
conversion is referred to as D/A process.
Since, different methods are available for analog-to-digital conversion and vice-versa, there are 
large number of types of ADCs and DACs.  
Some of the popular types of ADCs are, 
●  Flash type ADC
●  Counter type ADC
●  Tracking type ADC
●  Dual slope ADC
●  Successive Approximation ADC
Some of the different types of DACs are, 
●  R-2R ladder type DAC
●  Weighted resistor type DAC
●  Switched-current source type DAC
●  Switched capacitor type DAC
13.1.1  Parameters of Data Converters
Quantization: The process of dividing the reference value is called quantization and each step of 
analog value is also called quantization step or simply step size. In n-bit binary representation the step size 
is determined by dividing the reference voltage by number of possible binary values, 2n.
∴ Step size = VREF 2
1
n#  
Coding: Attaching a unique n-bit binary code to each quantization step is called coding.
Reference value: The data converter will have a positive and negative reference analog voltage/
current to indicate the maximum value of positive and negative analog value it can handle for conversion 
from analog to digital or vice-versa. The analog value handled by data converters should be within the 
range of positive and negative reference value. The difference between the positive and negative reference 
is the reference value. In unipolar data converters the negative reference is ground or 0 volt and hence 
reference value is equal to positive reference.
Let,  VREF(+) =  Positive reference value
        VREF(-) =  Negative reference value
∴ VREF = VREF(+) - VREF(-)
Resolution: It is the minimum value that can be handled or detected by a data converter. In ADC, 
it is the minimum analog value that can be converted to digital value. In DAC, it is the minimum analog 
value that can be generated for a change in digital input. The resolution is same as the step size. In n-bit 
binary representation the step size is determined by dividing the reference voltage by number of possible 
binary values, 2n.  
∴ Resolution = VREF 2
1
n#

The resolution of a DAC is also defined as the product of reciprocal of the number of discrete steps 
and the full-scale output of the DAC. 
∴ Resolution = scale value scale value- -
Number of steps

Full

Full scale value: It is the maximum value of analog voltage or current that can be represented in 
digital by a data converter. Full scale value will be one step lesser than reference value.  
∴ Full scale value = VREF - Resolution 
Since number of steps of analog values is 2 n - 1 the full scale value is also given by product of 
number of steps and resolution.  
∴ Full scale value = Number of steps × Step size = (2n - 1) × Step size
Conversion time: It is the time taken by data converter to convert an analogue signal to digital or 
vice-versa. The conversion time depends on the type of ADC/DAC.  
Settling Time: It is the minimum time required for converted signal to settle at a stable value for 
a change in input.
Accuracy: It refers to closeness of converted value to true value. With smaller resolution higher 
accuracy can be achieved. For smaller resolution the binary data size, n of the converter should be increased. 
For example, a 10-bit converter will have more accuracy than 8-bit converter.
Linearity: It refers to direct proportionality between input and output. For linear relationship, the 
relation between input and output should follow a straight line.   
13.2  Digital to Analog Converter (DAC)
The DAC will accept a digital (binary) input and convert to analog voltage or current. Every DAC 
will have n input data lines and an analog output line. The DAC requires a reference analog voltage (VREF) 
or current (IREF) source. The reference value is the difference between positive and negative reference value. 
The smallest possible analog value that can be represented by the n-bit binary code is called resolution. 
The resolution of DAC with n-bit binary input is 2
1
n  of the reference analog value. 
∴ Resolution = 2
1 VREFn #
In general, for an n-bit DAC, the number of different binary values will be 2 n including zero and 
therefore, the number of analog steps will be 2n - 1. The greater the number of bits, the greater will be the 
number of steps and the smaller will be the step size, and therefore, the finer will be the resolution. Of 
course the cost of the DAC increases with the number of input bits.
Every analog output will be a multiple of the resolution. For example, consider an 4-bit DAC with 
reference analog voltage of 5 Volts. Now the resolution of the DAC is (1/2 4 ) × 5 Volts. The 4-bit digital 
input can take, 24 = 16 different values which is given by the product of decimal value of digital input and 
resolution. The analog values for all possible digital inputs are as shown in Table 13.1.

The time required for converting the digital signal to analog signal is called conversion time. It 
depends on the response time of the switching transistors and the output amplifier. The digital data (signal) 
should remain at the input of DAC, until the conversion is complete. Hence, to hold the data a latch is 
provided at the input of DAC. 
13.2.2  Weighted-Resistor DAC
The diagram of the weighted-resistor DAC is shown in Fig. 13.3. The operational amplifier act as 
an adder (or summer) and it generates a weighted sum of the digital inputs. The resistor values are weights 
which are proportional to the weights of the bit positions of inputs. 
Since the operational amplifier is connected as an inverting amplifier, each input is amplified by a 
factor equal to the ratio of the feedback resistance divided by the input resistance to which it is connected. 
The output of operational amplifier will be a negative voltage and hence the output voltage is inverted by 
connecting an analog inverter or sign changer.
(IKGPTU, May'20, 5 Marks)(GTU, May'19, 7 Marks)

13.2.5  DAC0800
The DAC0800 is an 8-bit, high speed, current output DAC with a typical settling time (conversion 
time) of 100 ns. It produces complementary current output which can be converted to voltage by using a 
simple resistor load. The DAC0800 employs binary weighted resistors to convert digital data to analog 
current. The DAC0800 is available as a 16-pin IC in DIP. The pin configuration of DAC0800 is shown

and the digital input will decide the analog output current, which can be converted to a voltage by simply 
connecting a resistor to output terminal or by using an op-amp I to V converter.

5.3  Analog to Digital Converter (ADC)
The Analog-to-Digital (A/D) conversion is the process of converting an analog signal to digital 
signal. The A/D conversion involves sampling and quantization. The analog signals vary continuously and 
are defined for any interval of time. The digital signals (or data) can take only finite values and defined 
only for discrete instant of time. If the digital data is represented by an n-bit binary then it can have 2 n 
different values including zero. In A/D conversion the given analog signal has to be divided into steps (or 
quantization steps) of 2n - 1 values, and each step is represented by one of the 2n - 1 values excluding zero. 
The resolution of the converter is the minimum analog value that can be represented by the digital 
data. If the ADC gives n-bit digital output and the reference voltage is VREF, then the resolution is given by,
Resolution = 2
1
n  VREF Volts
The analog input signal can be divided by resolution to get number of quantization steps. The analog 
input signal will not be an exact multiple of quantization step and so the division of input by resolution 
will give number of quantization steps plus error. The quantization steps will be the integer part of quotient 
and error is the fraction part. Therefore, the binary value of the integer part of quotient is the digital data 
corresponding analog input voltage, Vin. 
∴ Digital data = 
/Resolution
V Error V 2
V Error V
V 2 Errorin

Note: Since A/D process is basically a quantization process, the above equation for digital data 
can be used to compute the output of all types of ADC.
The error will be in the range 0 to 1. The error is zero when V in is an exact multiple of resolution 
and error is 1 when Vin is equal to V REF. Therefore if Vin = VREF take error as 1 in above equation and for 
other values the error is the fraction part.   
In an ADC, another critical parameter is conversion time. The conversion time is defined as the total 
time required to convert an analog signal into its digital equivalent. It depends on the conversion technique 
and the propagation delay in various circuits.

Chapter 13 - Data Converters 13.11
The analog-to-digital converters can be classified into two groups based on the technique involved 
for conversion. The first group includes successive approximation, counter and flash-type converters. The 
technique involved in these devices is that the given analog signal is compared with internally generated 
analog signal. The second group includes integrator converters. In the devices of the second group, the 
given analog signal is converted to time and compared with the known values to produce digital signal.
The trade-off between the two techniques is based o n accuracy versus speed. The successive 
approximation and the flash type are faster but generally less accurate than the integrator type converters. 
Also, the flash type is costlier. The successive approximation type converters are used for high speed 
conversion and the integrating type converters are used for high accuracy.
13.3.1  Flash Type ADC
The flash type A/D converter employs parallel differential comparators that compare various steps 
of reference voltages with the analog input voltage. The n-bit flash type converter will have 2n resistors and 
2n
 - 1 comparators. Fig. 13.9(a) shows n-bit flash type ADC. The 2n resistors are connected in series with 
reference voltage as voltage divider network in order to divide the reference voltage into 2n - 1 steps. Every 
step voltage will be connected as one of the input to comparators and the input analog voltage is applied 
as another input to comparator. Now, the outputs of comparators will be high if the input is greater than 
the step value of reference otherwise low. All outputs of comparator are connected to a priority encoder so 
that the encoder will generate an n-bit binary corresponding to highest order output of comparator whose 
output is 1.  
The flash type ADC is one of the fastest ADC converters. The main advantage of this type of converter 
is the conversion time is less, but the disadvantage is that, an n-bit converter of this type requires 2 n - 1 
comparators, 2n resistors, and a 2 n to n priority encoder. The flash converter does not use a clock signal 
and the conversion takes place continuously. The conversion time depends on the delay in the comparators 
and the priority encoder. 
3-bit Flash Type ADC  
Fig. 13.9(b) shows a 3-bit flash type A/D converter which employs 7 comparators (2 3
 - 1 = 7). A 
reference voltage VREF is connected to a resistive voltage divider network with 8 equal value resistors that 
divides the reference voltage into seven equal increment levels. Each level is compared to the analog input 
by a voltage comparator. All comparator outputs are connected to an 8 to 3 priority encoder. The encoder 
produces a 3-bit digital output corresponding to the input having the highest priority. The higher priority 
input to encoder corresponds to output of comparator with largest value of input. The digital output for 
various values of analog input is listed in Table 13.2.

8-bit Flash Type ADC  
Fig. 13.10 shows the block diagram of a modified 8-bit flash type A/D converter in which 8-bit 
conversion is performed using two 4-bit flash type c onverters. An 8-bit flash type ADC require 255  
comparators (28 - 1 = 255) but a 4-bit flash type ADC requires 13 comparators (2 4 - 1 = 13) so that two 
4-bit flash type ADC require only 30 comparators to perform the task of 8-bit conversion.
In this method, one of the 4-bit flash type converters is used to generate the four most significant 
bits (MSBs) and output through an 8-bit latch as bits D7 to D4. Also, these four bits are converted back to 
an analog voltage by a DAC and this voltage is subtracted from the analog input. This difference in voltage 
is the analog voltage corresponding to the four least significant bits (LSBs). Therefore, this difference 
in voltage is converted to the four least significant bits by another 4-bit flash type converter and output 
through the 8-bit latch as bits D3 to D0.

13.3.2  Counter Type ADC
The counter type ADC consists of a sample and hold (S/H) circuit, a comparator, a counter, a DAC, 
an AND gate, a latch and the control circuit as shown in Fig. 13.12. The binary counter generate all possible 
value of n-bit binary and convert every binary value to analog and compare with input analog signal. The 
binary count that generates matched analog value is output as digital value of the analog signal. 
The counter is controlled by a clock so that the counter will keep counting as long as clock is active. 
Initially, the counter is reset and clock is allowed to start count. The output of counter is converted to analog 
by the DAC and compared with input analog.

13.14                                              Digital Logic Circuits
The analog signal to be converted is sampled by S/H (Sample and Hold) circuit and applied to the 
non-inverting terminal of the op-amp comparator. The S/H circuit is enabled by a start of conversion (SOC) 
signal to initiate the sampling of analog signal. The output of the DAC is applied to the inverting terminal 
of the op-amp. Whenever the analog input signal is greater than the DAC output, the output of the op-amp 
is high and whenever the output of the DAC is greater than the analog signal, the output of the comparator 
is low. The comparator output serves as an active-low end of the conversion signal (EOC) which is used 
to stop the counter and enable the S/H circuit to take next sample of analog input.
The value of binary in the counter at this instant is the value of digital signal and latch is enabled 
to output this counter value as digital value. The principal disadvantage of this type of converter is that, 
the conversion time depends on the magnitude of the analog input. The larger the input, the more will be 
the number of clock pulses that must pass to reach the proper count, and, therefore, the larger will be the 
conversion time. For each conversion, the counter has to start from reset only and count up to the point 
at which the generated analog is one step higher than the analog input voltage. This type of converter is 
considered quite slow in comparison with the other types.
13.3.3  Tracking Type ADC
The tracking-type ADC employ an up/down counter and is faster than the counter type ADC. The 
counter is not reset after each sample of analog signal, but counts up or down from its last count to its new 
count. Thus the total number of clock pulses required to perform a conversion is proportional to the change 
in the analog input between counts and hence it is called tracking type ADC.
Figure 13.13 shows the logic diagram of a tracking type ADC. As long as the DAC generated 
reference voltage is less than the analog input, the comparator output is high putting the counter in the up 
count mode. When the generated reference voltage is higher than the analog input, the comparator output 
switches low and puts the counter in the down count mode. Thus the counter effectively track the input.
The conversion time of this ADC is the time interval between the start of the conversion (SOC) and 
the time the generated analog voltage is equal to sampled analog input voltage. The end of conversion is 
indicated by either a high to low (for up count) or a low to high (for down count) comparator output. The 
control logic will detect this transition and generates an end of conversion (EOC) signal. 
At the end of conversion, the output latch is enabled to latch the current count value as digital output.

13.3.4  Dual-slope Type ADC
A dual-slope ADC uses an operational amplifier based integrator to generate a ramp signal and a 
binary counter to generate digital output. The integrator employs two components R and C to generate the 
ramp voltage. The ramp voltage controls the length of time that the binary counter is allowed to count and 
the binary value of the counter is proportional to input analog voltage. 
Figure 13.14 shows the functional block diagram of a dual-slope ADC. In dual slope type ADC, the 
integrator performs two integrations in order to generate two different ramps one with negative slope and 
the other with positive slope. Initially the counter is reset and the analog input Vin is connected to input of 
integrator. In unipolar dual slope ADC, the input is a positive analog voltage. In the first integration the 
integrator generates a ramp with negative slope proportional to analog input voltage, Vin. The capacitor is 
allowed to charge for fixed time T1 as shown in Fig. 13.16. Let the capacitor charged to a voltage of V rx.  
This phase is also called measuring phase.  
At time, T1 the integrator input is connected to a reference voltage VREF, having a polarity opposite 
to that of the analog input which is in this case a negative reference voltage. Therefore, the output of the 
second integration is a positive going ramp (or ramp with positive slope) proportional to negative reference 
value. Also, the counter is reset at time T 1 and the AND gate is enabled to allow the clock to counter to 
start a new count.

The dual-slope converter is one of the slowest converters. But it is relatively inexpensive because 
it does not require a DAC. Another advantage of the dual-slope ADC is its low sensitivity to noise and to 
variations in its component values caused by temperature changes. 
13.3.5  Successive Approximation ADC
A successive approximation ADC consists of D/A converter, successive approximation register and 
comparator. Figure 13.18 shows the functional blocks of a typical successive approximation A/D converter.
The analog signal to be converted is sampled by S/H (Sample and Hold) circuit and applied to 
the non-inverting terminal of the op-amp comparator. The S/H circuit is enabled by a start of conversion 
(SOC) signal to initiate the sampling of analog signal. On receiving the SOC, the control unit of the ADC 
will give a start command to the successive approximation register and it starts generating digital signal 
by the successive approximation method. The generated digital data is converted to analog signal by the 
D/A converter and then compared with the input analog signal.

(IKGPTU, May'20, 10 Marks)

Chapter 13 - Data Converters 13.17
When the analog signals are equal, the comparator output informs the control unit to stop generation 
of digital signal. The digital data available at this instant is given as output through output register. Also, 
the control unit generates a signal to indicate the End Of Conversion (EOC) process.
Successive Approximation Method of Conversion
In this method, the MSD (Most Significant Digit) is first set to “1” and all other digits are reset to 
“0”. The analog signal generated for this digital data is compared with the given analog signal. (Initially, 
the comparator output will be high. After comparison the output of the comparator remains in high state 
if the input analog signal is higher than the generated analog signal. Otherwise, if the input signal is less 
than the generated signal then the output of the comparator changes from high to low state.) If the output 
state of the comparator changes then the MSD is reset to “0” otherwise it is retained as “1”. 
Then the above process is repeated by setting the next higher order bit to “1”. The process is 
continued for each bit starting from MSD to LSD. (During a process, the higher order bits are the bits 
determined in earlier steps and the lower order bits are reset to “0”.) After one complete cycle through 
MSD to LSD, the data available on the successive approximation register will be the digital equivalent of 
the input analog signal.

The internal block diagram of ADC0809 is shown in Fig. 13.20. The various functional blocks of

register, output buffer, address latch and decoder.

The Successive Approximation Register (SAR) performs eight iterations to determine the digital 
code for input analog voltage. The SAR is reset on the positive edge of the START pulse and start the 
conversion process on the falling edge of START pulse. A conversion processs will be interrupted on 
receipt of a new START pulse. The End Of Conversion (EOC) will go low between 0 and 8 clock pulses 
after the positive edge of the START pulse.
The ADC can be used in continuous conversion mode by tying the EOC output to the START input. 
In this mode an external START pulse should be applied whenever power is switched ON.
The 256R resistor network and the switch tree is shown in Fig. 13.21. The 256R ladder network has 
been provided instead of conventional R/2R ladder because of its inherent monotonicity, which guarantees 
no missing digital codes. Also, the 256R resistor network does not cause load variations on the reference 
voltage.
In ADC conversion process, the input analog value is quantized and each quantized analog value 
will have a unique binary equivalent. The quantization step or resolution in ADC0809 is given by,

other values the error is the fraction part.

13.4  Summary of Important Concepts
1. Analog to Digital Converter (ADC) and Digital to Analog Converter (DAC) are referred to as data  
 converters.
2. The ADC will convert analog signal to digital signal and the DAC will convert digital signal to analog  
 signal.
3. The process of analog to digital conversion is also referred to as A/D process
4. The process of digital to analog conversion is referred to as D/A process.
5. The ADC will divide the reference voltage into 2 n - 1 steps and it can generate a unique n-bit binary for 
 each step of reference value.
6. The DAC will divide the reference value into 2 n - 1  and for every input n-bit binary, the DAC will generate 
 the corresponding step of analog value.
7. The process of dividing the reference value is called quantization and each step of analog value is also  
 called quantization step or simply step size.
8. Attaching a unique n-bit binary code to each quantization step is called coding.
9. In data converters, the difference between the positive and negative reference is the reference value.
10. Resolution is the minimum value that can be handled or detected by a data converter. 
11. In ADC, resolution is the minimum analog value that can be converted to digital value. 
12. In DAC, resolution is the minimum analog value that can be generated for a change in digital input.
13. Full-scale value is the maximum value of analog voltage or current that can be represented in digital by  
 a data converter. 
14. Conversion time is the time taken by data converter to convert an analogue signal to digital or vice-versa.
15. Settling time is the minimum time required for converted signal to settle at a stable value for a change  
 in input.

--- Page 1085 ---
13.24                                              Digital Logic Circuits
16. Accuracy in data converter, refers to closeness of converted value to true value.
17. Linearity in data converters refers to direct relationship between input and output signals.
18. The R-2R ladder type DAC employs only two values of resistors.
19. In weighed resistor type DAC, the resistor values are proportional to the weights of the bit positions of  
 inputs.
20. In switched current source type DAC, the currents flows through resistors will be proportional to binary  
 weights.
21. In switched capacitor type DAC, the capacitor valu es are proportional to binary weights of the bit positions  
 of inputs.
22. The flash type A/D converter employs parallel differential comparators that compare reference voltages  
 with the analog input voltage. 
23. The n-bit flash type converter will have 2 n resistors, 2n - 1 comparators and 2n-to-n priority encoder
24. The counter type ADC employs a counter and DAC to generate an analog signal internally and compare  
 with input analog to determine the binary value of analog input.
25. The dual slope ADC employs integrator whose capacitor is charged by input voltage and the discharge  
 time of the capacitor voltage is proportional to binary value of analog input.
13.5  Short-Answer Questions
Q13.1 What is resolution in DAC?
 The resolution in DAC is the smallest possible analog value that can be generated by the n-bit binary input. 
 If the reference voltage in n-bit DAC is V REF , then the resolution is  (1/2n) × VREF Volts.
Q13.2 What are the internal devices of a typical DAC?
 The internal devices of a DAC are R-2R resistive network, an internal latch and current to voltage converting 
 amplifier. 
Q13.3 What is settling or conversion time in DAC?
 The time taken by the DAC to convert a given digital data to a corresponding stable analog signal is called  
 conversion or settling time. 
Q13.4 What are the different types of ADC?
 The different types of ADC are successive approximation ADC, counter-type ADC, flash-type ADC, tracking  
 type ADC and dual slope ADC. 
Q13.5 What is conversion time in ADC?
  The conversion time in ADC is defined as the time required to convert a sample of analog signal into its  
 digital equivalent.
Q13.6 What do meant by analog quantity?
 An analog quantity or signal is a physical quantity like voltage, current, temperature, etc., that can take on 
 continuous values with respect to independent variable time. The analog quantity is defined for any instant of  
 time.

--- Page 1086 ---
Chapter 13 - Data Converters 13.25
Q13.7    What do you meant by digital quantity?
  A digital quantity or signal is a physical quantity like voltage, current, temperature, etc., that can take on 
  discrete values with respect to discrete instants of independent variable time. The digital values are the  
  quantized and coded value of discrete values repr esented by n-bit binary. The discrete instants of independent  
  variable time is also represented by discrete instants of time called sampling time. 
Q13.8    What is the need of ADC and DAC in controlling a process?
  When a process is controlled by a digital system all the control variables should be in digital. But, the control 
  variables of a process will be analog in nature. Hence, the analog control variables are converted into  
  digital signals using ADC. These digital signals are processed by the digital system to generate processed  
  digital control signals. But the process requires only processed analog signals and so the processed digital  
  control signals are converted into processed analog control signals using DAC. 
Q13.9  What is the function of ADC and DAC?
  The function of ADC is to convert an analog signal to digital signal and the function of DAC is to convert  
  digital signal to analog signal. Therefore, the ADC proforms the reverse function of DAC.
Q13.10   What is meant by D/A conversion?
  The D/A conversion refer to the process of converting an digital signal represented in binary code into  
  analog voltage or current proportional to the value of binary code.
Q13.11  Is the output of DAC a true analog quantity?
  The output of a DAC will be a stepped analog quantity with each step represented by the quantized analog  
  value. The output will be closer to true analog value if the quantized analog value is represented by large  
  number of steps.
Q13.12  How many different output voltages can an 8-bit DAC produce?
  An n-bit binary will take 2n different binary values which can be converted to 2 n - 1 steps of analog value 
  by a DAC. Therefore, an 8-bit DAC can produce 2 8 - 1 = 255 different output voltages.
Q13.13  What is the advantage of smaller (finer) resolution?
  The advantage of smaller (finer) resolution is that the analog value can be represented by large number of  
  quantized steps and the quantized analog quantity will be closer to true analog value.
Q13.14  Distinguish between unipolar and bipolar DAC?  
  In unipolar DAC, the negative reference will be tied to ground or 0 V olt and hence it can generate an output  
  analog voltage or current in the range 0 to positive reference (V REF(+)  / IREF(+) ).
  In bipolar DAC, the negative reference will be tied to a negative reference voltage/current (V REF(-) /  IREF(-)) 
  and hence it can generate an output analog voltag e or current in the range negative reference (VREF(-)/ IREF(-)) 
  to positive reference (V REF(+) / IREF(+)).
Q13.15  What is the advantage of the R-2R ladder DAC over the weighted resistor type DAC?
  The advantage of R-2R ladder type DAC over the weighted resistor type DAC is that only two values of  
  resistors are required for R-2Rladder DAC. Therefore standard resistors can be used. But in weighed  
  resistor type DAC, different values of resistors proportional to binary weights are required. Therefore,  
  high precision resistors are employed for better accuracy in weighed type DAC.
(IKGPTU, Dec'19, 2 Marks)

--- Page 1087 ---
13.26                                              Digital Logic Circuits
Q13.16  A certain 6-bit DAC uses binary weighted resistor s. If the MSB resistor is 40 kΩ, what is the LSB resistor?
  The resistor in binary weighed type DAC should be proportional to binary weights. The binary weights  
  for 6-bit DAC are 2 5, 2 4, 2 3, 2 2, 2 1 and 2 0. The MSB resistor is proportional to 2 0 and LSB resistor is 
  proportional to 2 5.  
  LSB resistor = 2 5 × 40 = 1280 kΩ
Q13.17  Why the current switch type DAC is faster than voltage switch type DAC?
  The ON and OFF characteristics of current operate d switches are much faster than voltage operated switches  
  and hence the current switch type DAC is generally faster than voltage switch type DAC
Q13.18  Which is the simplest type ADC? What is its other name?
  The counter-type ADC is the simplest type of ADC. It is also called a digital ramp ADC.
Q13.19  Write the advantage and disadvantage of a counter-type ADC.
  The advantage of counter-type ADC is that it is the simplest ADC. 
  The disadvantage of counter-type ADC is that, the  conversion time depends on the magnitude of the analog  
  input.
Q13.20  Why does the conversion time increase with the value of the analog input voltage in a counter type ADC?
  In a counter-type ADC, the conversion time increases with the value of the analog input voltage because  
  the larger the input, the more will be the number of clock pulses that must pass to reach the proper count.
Q13.21  Why is the tracking-type ADC faster than the counter type ADC?
  The counter-type ADC is slow because the counter resets itself after each conversion. The tracking-type  
  ADC uses an up-down counter and is faster than the counter type ADC because the counter is not reset  
  after each sample, but tends to track the analog input, i.e. counts up or down from its last count to its new  
  count.
Q13.22  Why is the name tracking-type ADC and what is it other name?
  Since the counter starts count from previous value for any change in input, the ADC is called the tracking- 
  type ADC. The tracking-type ADC is also called the continuous conversion type ADC.
Q13.23  What is the main disadvantage of a flash-type ADC?
  The main disadvantage of a flash-type ADC is the complexity of the circuit. An n-bit converter requires  
  2 n - 1 comparators, 2n resistors and a 2n-to-n priority encoder.
Q13.24  Give two advantages of a dual-slope type ADC?
  The advantages of dual-slope ADC are, 
  ●  It is relatively inexpensive  
  ● It is less sensitive to variation in its component values.
Q13.25  Which is the fastest ADC and why?
  The flash type ADC is the fastest ADC because it does not have a clock and counter-DAC circuit to generate  
  an internal analog value and compare with input. The flash type ADC will continuously convert the analog  
  input and the only delay is the delay in comparator and priority encoder. 
(IKGPTU, May'20, 2 Marks)

VHDL
14.1  Introduction to VHDL
VHDL is an acronym for VHSlC (Very High Speed Integrated Circuits) Hardware Description 
Language.
In 1983, VHDL was originally developed by the direction of the U.S. Department of Defense to the 
ASICs (Application Specific ICs) manufacturers in order to standardize the hardware description. Since 
1987, VHDL has been standardized by the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE) as IEEE 
Standard 1076. The latest version of VHDL is IEEE standard 1076-2019.
VHDL is used to model a digital system at multiple levels of abstraction. An abstraction is a 
description of a system with a set of minimum details or components required for modelling the system 
and hiding all other associated details or components of the system. VHDL supports the following four 
levels of abstraction for digital system design.
●  Transistor level
●  Gate level
●  Register-transfer level (RTL)
●  Processor level
The various levels of abstraction will differ in the following aspects of system design.
●  Basic building block
●  Signal representation
●  Time representation
●  Behavioral representation
●  Physical representation
The basic building blocks are the parts or components used in various levels of abstraction. Signal 
and time representations refer to expressing signal values and changes in signal over time. Behavioral and 
physical representations are descriptions concerned with behavioral and physical views.
In transistor level abstraction, basic building blocks are basic electronic components like transistors, 
resistors, capacitors, etc. In gate level abstracti on, basic building blocks are logic gates, flip-flo ps, 
multiplexers, etc. In register-transfer level (RTL)  abstraction, the basic building blocks are modules 
developed using registers, adders, multiplexers, et c. Alternatively, the RTL abstraction can be called 
module-level abstraction. In processor level abstraction, the basic building blocks are processors, memory 
modules, bus interfaces, etc.      
CHAPTER 14

--- Page 1093 ---
14.2                                              Digital Logic Circuits
14.2  Elements of VHDL Language
The VHDL language has been developed by integrating the following languages: 
●  Sequential language 
●  Concurrent language 
●  Net-list language
●  Timing specifications 
●  Waveform generation language
Therefore, VHDL language has constructs to express the concurrent or sequential behaviour of a 
digital system with or without timing, to model the system as an interconnection of components and to 
generate test waveforms in a single model of the system.
The basic elements of the VHDL language are literals, comments, identifiers, data objects and 
operators.
14.2.1  Literals
Explicit data values that are assigned to objects or used within expressions are called literals.
Literals can be classified into following six general categories.
●  Character literals
●  String literals
●  Bit string literals
●  Numeric literals
●  Based numeric literals
●  Physical literals 
Character literals: Character literals are 1-character ASCII values that are enclosed in single-quotes.
Examples of character literals
 '0',  'X',  '$'  
String literals: String literals are collections of one or more ASCII characters enclosed in double-
quote characters.
Examples of string literals  
“my_state”,  “count”, “result” 
Bit string literals: Bit string literals are special forms of string literals that are used to represent 
binary string in 1’s and 0’s  in binary, octal, or hexadecimal numeric data values. Base specifier B, O and 
X are used for binary, octal and hexadecimal respectively.
Examples of bit string literals
B"1111_1101"       -- decimal value 253
O"6144"                -- decimal value 428
O"146_231"           -- decimal value 52,377
X"C300"                 -- decimal value 49,920

--- Page 1094 ---
Chapter 14 - VHDL 14.3
Numeric literals:  Numeric literals are decimal numbers. There are two basic forms of numeric 
literals in VHDL and they are integer literals and real literals.
Integer literals are signed decimal numbers without fraction. The ge neral range of integers is 
- 2,147,483,647 to + 2,147,483,647 (32 bits of precision, including the sign bit).
Real literals are decimal numbers with an integer part and a fraction part separated by a decimal 
point. For large numbers, scientific notation is also allowed using the character 'e', where the number to the 
left of the 'e' represents the mantissa of the real number, while the number to the right of the 'e' represents 
the exponent. The general range of real numbers is - 1.0e38 to +1.0e38.
Examples of numeric literals
5.0
- 12.9
1.6e10
1.2e - 20
Based numeric literals: Based numeric literals are another form of integer or real values, with 
a base specification such as 2, 8 or 16 and enclose the integer or mantissa with a pair of  ‘# ‘ characters. 
Examples of based numeric literals
2#10010001#      --integer value 145
16#FFCC#            --integer value 65,484
2#101.0#E10       --real value 5,120.0
Physical literals: Physical literals are special types of literals used to represent physical quantities 
such as time, voltage, current, distance, etc. Physical literals include both an integer numeric part and a 
unit specification. 
Examples of physical literals
300 ns     --300 nanoseconds
900 ps     --900 picoseconds
40 ma      --40 mille-amperes
14.2.2  Comments 
Comments are texts that are added as explanations, wherever necessary. A comment starts with a 
minimum of two dashes ( -- ) followed by the text to explain the concepts. The comment is provided for 
explaining the various concepts of VHDL program and hence, anything after two or more dashes will be 
ignored while compiling the code.
14.2.3  Identifiers
Identifiers are name of objects that are used in VHDL programs. Identifiers are formed using English 
letters/alphabets, decimal numbers and underscore. Special characters are not allowed in identifiers. 
Reserved words of VHDL language cannot be used as identifiers. The list of reserved words is listed in 
Table 14.1. Identifiers are case insensitive and hence uppercase and lower case letters are equivalent. 
The identifiers have to satisfy the following rules.
●  Identifiers can have only English letters, decimal numbers and underscores. 
●  First character of an identifier must be an alphabet.

--- Page 1095 ---

●  Last character of an identifier cannot be an underscore.
●  Identifiers cannot have two underscore in succession.

14.2.5  Data Types and Subtypes
The data types and subtypes other than predefined data types that can be declared in VHDL programs 
are discussed in this section. In VHDL, each data object has data type and associated operators. The data 
type is declared using a type statement.
Syntax for type declaration
type object_name is data_type;
Example of type declaration
type my_count is (‘2’, ‘4’,  ‘6’, ‘8’);
Subtype is a part or subset of a data type that is specified by a condition or constraint.
Syntax for type and subtype declaration
type object_name is data_type;
subtype subtype_object_name is object_name data_type;
Example of type and subtype
type pin_count is range 0 to 40;
subtype address_pin is pin_count range 25 to 40;
The data types that are used in VHDL programs can be classified into following four groups.
●  Scalar types
●  Composite types
●  Access types 
●  File types 
14.2.6  Scalar Data Types
The scalar data types can be again classified into following four groups.
●  Enumeration
●  Integer
●  Physical
●  Floating point
Enumeration type is associating user defined set of values called enumeration literals to an object. 
The values of enumeration literals are formed using alphabets and numeric character literals.
Example of enumeration data type
type my_state is (S0, S1, S2, S3, S4);
type rain_sevirity is (green, yellow, orange, red);
Integer type is associating an integer with values within a specified range to an object. 
Example of integer data type
type count_int is range 0 to 64;

--- Page 1098 ---
Chapter 14 - VHDL 14.7
Physical type associates numeric value of a physical quantity such as time, length, mass, voltage, 
current, etc to an object. Each value of a physical type has a position number that is an integer value. Any 
value of a physical type is a straight multiple of the primary unit of measurement for that type.
Syntax for physical type
type type_name is range left_bound to right_bound
units
primary_unit_name;
secondary_unit_name = number primary_unit_name;
secondary_unit_name = number primary_unit_name;
. . .
end units type_name;
Example of physical data type
type length is 0 to 1e3
units
mm;
cm   = 10 mm;
m       = 1000 mm;
inch = 25 mm;
ft       = 12 inch;
end units;
Floating point type is associating a real decimal number within a specified range to an object.
Example of floating point data type
type probability is range 0.0 to 1.0;
type signal_a_is range - 10.0 to +10.0;
14.2.7  Composite Data Types
A composite data type represents a collection of signals or objects. Composite types can be further 
classified into array types and record types. An array type represents a collection of signals or objects 
belong to a same data type. A record type represents a collection of signals or objects belong to same or 
different data types.
Examples of array data type
type word is array (15 downto 0) of bit:
type food is array (1 to 10) of character;
Example of record type
type uart_transmit is record
rx  : std_logic:
cts : std_logic;
tx   :  std_logic;
rts : std_logic;
end record uart_transmit;

14.2.8  Access Data Types
Access type is a pointer to an object of some other data type. 
Example of access data type
type fifo_stack is array (0 to 63, 0 to 7) of bit; 
type fifo_ptr is access fifo_stack;
File Data Types
Data stored as a file in the host environment (the system that simulate and synthesize the code) is 
called file data type. 
Syntax of a file data type declaration
type file_type_name is file of data_type; 
Example of file data type
type input_data is file of bit_vector;
type employee_names is file of string; 
14.2.9  Data Objects (or Objects)
Data object or simply object is an identifier that holds a specific data type, which is declared while 
creating the object. A data object is created by declaring the class, identifier/name, data type and optional 
initial value.
The objects in the VHDL language are classified into the following four categories.  
●  Constants
●  Signals
●  Variables
●  Files
Constant:  A constant object is assigned a fixed value and cannot be changed in other part of the code. 
Syntax for declaring constant
constant  name_of_constant:  data_type  := value_of_constant; 
Examples of constants
constant address_size : integer := 16; 
constant sram : bit_vector (15 downto 0) := X"F0F0";
constant message : string  := "this is a string";
constant error_flag : boolean := true;
Signal:  A signal object is created for intermediate signals in the design entity apart from input and 
output signals. Signals are declared in the architecture and outside the process. Initial value is meaning less 
in signal objects that are assigned a fixed value and cannot be changed in other part of the code.

--- Page 1100 ---
Chapter 14 - VHDL 14.9
Syntax for declaring signal
signal name_of_signal : data_type  := initial_value_of_signal; 
Examples of signals
signal propagation_delay : time := 12ns; 
signal data_size : bit_vector (0 to 15); 
Variable:  An object which takes different values during program execution is called variable. When 
an object is declared as a variable, the value of the variable can be changed in any part of the code using 
an assignment statement. Variables are declared inside a process and they are local to a process.
Syntax for declaring variable
variable  name_of_variable : data_type := initial_value_of_variable; 
Examples of variables
variable propagation_delay: time  := 12ns; 
variable data_size:   bit_vector (0 to 15);  
File: A file with a list of input and/or output data can be declared as an object. The file can used to 
read the stored input data and write the output data while simulating a test bench.
Syntax for declaring a file
type file_type_name is file of data_type;
type file_name: file_type_name is mode “file path”;
Note: mode is either in or out.
Examples of file
type input_data is file of bit_vector;
file sel_values: input_data is in "/usr/home/vhdl_ex";
type employee_names is file of string;
file sel_employee: employee_names is out "/usr/home/vhdl_ex"

14.3  Process and Process Statement
The executable functionality of an entity or a component is defined as a process in behavioral 
modelling. Hence the process is the key programming structure in behavioral modelling. All components 
in the model must be defined using one or more processes inside the architecture. 
The executable statements of a process are enclosed in a process statement. In a single process 
model, the process statement includes all executable statements of the model. In a multi-process model 
each process is defined by a process statement that includes executable statement of the individual process.
Initially, the process will be executed once using the current value of objects in the sensitivity 
list and the process execution will be repeated only when a change occurs in one or more objects in the 
sensitivity list. The process label is optional and made to identify a process in a multi-process model. In 
process without sensitivity list, a wait statement should be provided inside the process statement.
Syntax of process statement
process_label : process (sensitivity list)
                        -- declaration statements; 
                       begin 
                        -- sequential statements;
                       end process (process_label);
Example of process statement
--program segment showing only a process statement
--a, b, c are declared as inputs and z as output in entity
process (a, b, c)
variable m1, m2 : std_logic;
begin
m1 :=  a nand b;
m2 :=  m1 nand c;
z    <= m1 nand m2;
end process;
    Precedence  Operators
Highest **,   abs,   not
            *,   /,   mod,   rem
 +,   - (identity and negation)
 &,   +,   - (addition and subtraction)
 sll,   srl,   sla,   sra,   rol,   ror
 =,   /=,   <,   <=,   >,   >=
Lowest and,   or,   nand,   nor,   xor,   xnor

14.4  Sequential Statements
Sequential statements allow the user to describe signal assignments in an algorithmic fashion. The 
sequential statements are written inside a process statement. All statements in a process are evaluated 
sequentially and therefore the order of the statement is important.
The various types of sequential statement available in VHDL are,
●  Variable assignment statement
●  Signal assignment statement
●  Wait statement
●  If statement 
●  Case statement 
●  Loop statement
●  Null statement
●  Exit statement
●  Next statement
14.4.1  Variable Assignment Statement 
The variable objects will take different values whenever the process is executed and the variable 
assignment statements are used to assign the next value to variable objects.
Syntax of variable assignment statement 
variable_name := value_expression;
Example of variable assignment statement inside a process
--program segment showing only a process statement
--a, b, c are declared as inputs and y, z as outputs in entity
process (a, b, c)
variable m1, m2 : integer range 0 to 10 ;     
-- variables are declared inside the process 
begin
m1 :=  (a +  b) - c;  -- variable assignment statement
y    <= - m1
m2 :=  m1 * 2;        -- variable assignment statement
z    <= m2;
end process;

--- Page 1104 ---
Chapter 14 - VHDL 14.13
14.4.2  Signal Assignment Statement
Signals are assigned values using a signal assignment statement. 
Syntax of signal assignment statement
signal_name <= value expression;
Example of signal assignment statement inside a process
--program segment showing only a process statement
--a, b, c are declared as inputs and y as output in entity
signal m1, m2 : std_logic;    -- signals are declared outside the process
begin
process (a, b, c)
begin
m1 <= a or c;           -- signal assignment statement
m2 <= a and b;        -- signal assignment statement
y <= m1 and m2;
           end process;
14.4.3  Wait Statement 
The wait statement is used to suspend a process without sensitivity list. The wait statement will 
have a condition and the process will resume only when the condition is true. There are three basic forms 
of wait statement.
Syntax of a wait statement
wait on sensitivity_list;
wait until boolean_expression;
wait for time_expression;
Examples of wait statements
wait on a, b, c;        --wait until a change occurs in one or more object ( a, b, c)
wait until (a = b);    --wait until object a is equal to object b
wait for 30 ns;         --Resume the process after a delay of 30 ns
Example of a process with wait statement
--program segment showing only a process statement
--a, b, c, d are declared as inputs and y as output in entity
process
variable m1, m2 : std_logic;
begin
m1 := a and b;
m2 := c and d;
y   <= m1 or m2;
wait on a, b, c, d;
end process;
14.4.4  If Statement
If statement is used to execute one or more statements when a condition specified in the if statement 
is true. The general syntax of the if statement shown below can be used to execute a number of statements 
based on different conditions. 

--- Page 1105 ---
14.14                                              Digital Logic Circuits
An if statement will have one if-condition-then statement, one or more optional elsif-condition-then 
statement and one optional else statement. At any one time only one condition will be true and hence the 
statements followed by the true condition are executed. If no condition is true then the statements followed 
by else will be executed and if there is no else statement then no statement will be executed   
Syntax of if statement when multiple conditions have to be checked 
if condition_1 then 
sequential_statements ;
elsif condition_2 then 
      sequential_statements;
.
.
.
elsif condition_n then 
sequential_statements;
else
sequential_statements;
end if;
Syntax of if statement for only one condition
if condition then 
sequential_statements; 
else 
     sequential_statements;
end if;
Syntax of if statement without else statement for only one condition
if condition then 
sequential_statements; 
end if;
Example of if statement inside a process
--program segment of 4:1 multiplexer based on if statement
--i0, i1, i2, i3 are declared as inputs and y as output in entity
--s is declared as 2-bit std_logic_vector input in entity
process (i0, i1, i2, i3)
begin
if (s = "00") then 
y <= i0;
elsif (s = "01") then 
y <= i1;
elsif (s = "10") then 
y <= i2;
else
y <= i3;
end if;
end process;

14.4.5  Case Statement
A case statement will check the value of an expression or object that can take multiple values. At 
any onetime only one value will be true and one (or a set of) sequential statement after the true case is 
executed. The values of the expression or object are denoted as choice_1 to choice_n.
Syntax of case statement
case_expression is
when choice_1 => 
sequential_statements; 
when choice_2 => 
sequential_statements; 
       .
       .
       .
when choice_n => 
sequential_statements; 
end case;
Example of case statement inside a process
--program segment of 4:1 multiplexer based on case statement
--i0, i1, i2, i3 are declared as inputs and y as output in entity
--sel_in is declared as 2-bit std_logic_vector input in entity
process (i0, i1, i2, i3)
begin
case sel_in is
when "00" =>
y <= i0;
when "01" =>
y <= i1;
when "10" =>
y <= i2;
when others =>
y <= i3;
end case;
end process;
14.4.6  Loop Statement
The loop statement is used to execute a sequential statement (or a set of sequential statements) 
repeatedly with in a process. There are three types of loop statements in VHDL.
●  For-loop
●  While-loop
●  Loop terminated using an exit or next statement

--- Page 1107 ---
14.16                                              Digital Logic Circuits
For-loop
Syntax of for-loop statement 
(loop_label:) for index in loop_range loop
              sequential_statements;
                   end loop (loop_label);      -- loop label is optional
Example of for-loop 
sum_int := 0;
for int_num in 1 to 10 loop
sum_int := sum_int + int_num;
end loop;
VHDL Program 14.1

While-loop
Syntax of while-loop statement 
while Boolean_expression loop
--sequential_statements;
end loop;
Example of while-loop

statements corresponding to for-loop with statements for while-loop.

Loop terminated using an exit or next statement
Syntax of loop statement
loop_label: loop  
            --sequential_statements;
                exit when boolean_expression;
                end loop loop_label;                 -- loop label is optional
Example of simple loop
sum_int := 0;
int_num := 1;
L1: loop 
sum_int := sum_int + int_num;
int_num := int_num + 1;
exit when int_num>10;
end loop L1;
Note: The example program given for for-loop can be run with simple loop, by replacing the 
statements corresponding to for-loop with statements for simple loop.
14.4.7  Exit Statement
The exit statement is a sequential statement that can be used only inside a loop. The exit statement 
will check the specified condition/Boolean_expression and if the condition / Boolean_expression  is true 
then It stops execution of loop statement immediately and jump out of the loop. Hence it is used to terminate 
the iterations in the loop statement.
Syntax of exit statement
exit when Boolean_expression: 
Note: Refer example of simple loop for usage of exit statement.
14.4.8  Next Statement
The next statement is also a sequential statement that can be used only inside a loop. It is used to skip 
a part of statements in the iteration. When a next statement is encountered and if the specified condition is 
true then the execution jump to start of next iteration by skipping the statements after the next statement.
Syntax of next statement 
next when Boolean_expression:
Example of next statement
sum_int := 0;
int_num := 0;
while int_num < 10  loop
int_num := int_num + 1;                  
next when int_num = 14;      --integer 14 will not be added in sum
sum_int := sum_int + int_num;              
end loop;

--- Page 1109 ---
14.18                                              Digital Logic Circuits
14.4.9  Null Statement
The null statement is a sequential statement and used in places where no action is required for a 
particular condition.
Example of null statement
--program segment showing usage of null statement inside a case statement
--a, b, c are declared as inputs and y as output in entity
--opcode is declared as signal in architecture
case opcode is
when "000"    => y <= a and b;
when "000"    => y <= a or b;
when "000"    => y <= a xor b;
when others  => null;
end case;
14.4.10  Assertion Statement
An assertion statement is used to verify a specifie d condition and to report if the condition is 
violated. If the condition is false then the string_expression in the report statement is displayed and the 
string_expression in the severity statement is used to display the severity clause.
Note: During simulation in vivado, the assert statement is included in test bench. The string_
expression in report statement is displayed in log file and the string_expression in severity statement is 
displayed in TCL console. 
Syntax of assertion statement
assert condition report “string_expression “ severity “string_expression”; 
Example of assertion statement   
assert (s = '0') report "se1" severity “error”;
assert (co = '1') report "ce1" severity “error”;

14.5  Concurrent Statements
The concurrent statements are used in dataflow architecture. VHDL supports the following concurrent 
statements.
●  Concurrent signal assignment statement
●  Conditional signal assignment statement
●  Selected signal assignment statement
●  Concurrent assertion statement
14.5.1  Concurrent Signal Assignment Statement
Signal assignment statements that appear outside of a process are called concurrent signal assignment 
statements and they are used to assign a value to an object. The syntax for concurrent signal assignment 
statement is same as that of signal assignment stat ement discussed under sequential statements. An 
architecture body can have any number of concurrent signal assignment statements. Concurrent signal 
assignment statements are event triggered and hence, they are executed whenever there is an event or 
change in a signal that appears in the expression in the statement.
14.5.2  Conditional Signal Assignment Statement
Conditional signal assignment statement assigns different values for the target signal based on the 
specified conditions similar to if statement. 
Syntax of conditional signal assignment statement
signal_name <= value_exp_1 when condition_1 else
                          value_exp_2 when condition_2 else
                              .
                              .
                          value_exp_n
Example of conditional assignment statement in a dataflow architecture
--program segment of 4:1 multiplexer based on 
--conditional assignment statement
--i0, i1, i2, i3 are declared as inputs and y as output in entity
--sel_in is declared as 2-bit std_logic_vector input in entity
y <= i0 when (sel_in = "00") else 
        i1 when (sel_in = "01") else
        i2 when (sel_in = "10") else
        i3;
14.5.3  Selected Signal Assignment Statement
Selected signal assignment statement assigns different values for a target signal based on the value 
of a select_expression similar to case statement.
Syntax of selected signal assignment statement
with select_expression select
signal_name  <=  value_exp_1 when choice_1,
              value_exp_2 when choice_2,
                                     .
                                     .
                                  value_exp_n when choice_n;

--- Page 1112 ---
Chapter 14 - VHDL 14.21
Example of selected signal assignment statement in a dataflow architecture
--program segment of 4:1 multiplexer based on 
--selected signal assignment statement
--i0, i1, i2, i3 are declared as inputs and y as output in entity
--sel_in is declared as 2-bit std_logic_vector input in entity
with sel_in select
y <= i0 when "00", 
        i1 when "01",
        i2 when "10",
        i3 when others;
14.5.4  Concurrent Assertion Statement
Assertion statements that appear outside of a process are called concurrent assertion statements and 
they are used to report the error conditions. The syntax for concurrent assertion statement is same as that 
of assertion statement discussed under sequential statements. 
14.6  VHDL Design Entity (or Model)
In order to describe a design entity (or model), VHDL provides the following five different types 
of primary constructs called design units. 
●  Entity declaration 
●  Architecture body 
●  Configuration declaration 
●  Package declaration 
●  Package body 
In the simplest form, a VHDL design entity (or model) includes an entity declaration and at least 
one architecture body. 
The entity declaration describes the input and output signal names. The architecture body contains 
a set of interconnected components which represents the structure of the entity, or as a set of concurrent 
or sequential statements that represents the behaviour of the entity. Figure 14.1 shows a simple VHDL 
design entity or model. 
Entity declaration: Describes the input output parameter
Architecture body: Describes the functionality of the design
   Entity declaration 
   (List of input, output port  declaration)
   Architecture body
   (Functional description)
                                Fig. 14.1: VHDL design entity (or model)
Hardware
description
of a digital
system
►

--- Page 1113 ---
14.22                                              Digital Logic Circuits
VHDL separates entity declaration and architecture body into two independent design units. 
Configuration is the process of binding a component with an entity and architecture. In a simple VHDL 
program configuration is not needed but configuration will be useful in development and testing of large 
systems. 
A package declaration  is used to store a set of common declarations like  components, types, 
procedures, and functions. These declarations can then be imported into other design units.
A package body is always associated with a package declaration. A package body is used to store 
the definitions of functions and procedures that were declared in the corresponding package declaration 
and also the constant declarations for any constants that appear in the package declaration.
14.6.1  Entity Declaration 
Entity declaration specifies the name of the entity and a set of interface ports. Ports are signals 
through which the entity communicates with the other models in its external environment.
Syntax for entity declaration
entity entity_name is 
port ( list of input_port   :  mode data_type;
          list of output_port :   mode data_type );
end entity_name;        
Note: mode is in, out, inout, buffer.
Port
Each input and output signal in an entity is called a port. Each port should have a name, data type 
and direction (or mode). The mode can be assigned one of the four possible choices: in, out, inout, buffer. 
The set of ports defined in an entity is called port declaration.  
Generic
The generic construct of VHDL is provided to pass information into an entity and a component. 
Generics are like parameters. They are first declared in entity and component declaration and later assigned 
a value during component instantiation. In order to use generics, an additional declaration called generic 
declaration is added in entity.
Syntax for entity declaration with generics
entity entity_name is
generic (list of generic_names : data_types);    --generic declarations
port (list of input_ports : mode data_types;
               list of output_ports : mode data_types);   --port declarations
end entity_name;

--- Page 1114 ---
Chapter 14 - VHDL 14.23
14.6.2  Architecture Body
The internal details of a design/model are specified in architecture body. The different types of 
architecture models are,  
●  Dataflow model 
●  Behavioral model 
●  Structural model 
●  Combination of the above three.
Dataflow Model  
A dataflow model specifies the functionality of a design entity or model without specifying the 
structure of the design. It shows the flow of information through the design entity
Syntax for architecture body of dataflow model
architecture architecture_name of entity_name is
    --architecture item declarations 
begin
        --concurrent statements;
end architecture_name;
Behavioral Model
The behavior of the entity is defined using a set of sequentially executed statements .
A process statement is the main mechanism used to model the behavior of an entity. 
Architecture Body
The architecture body consist of  a set of interconnected components which represents the structure 
of the entity, or as a set of concurrent or sequential statements that represents the behavior of the entity
Syntax for architecture body of behavior model
architecture architecture_name of entity_name is
    --architecture item declarations
begin       
       --concurrent statements ;
process (sensitivity list)
begin 
 --statements
                               .
   .
                               .
end process   
end architecture_name;
Structural Model 
In structural model, a design entity is designed with the set of components connected by signals. 
Components are VHDL modules compiled as separate entity and can be used in any other structural 
model of digital systems.

--- Page 1115 ---
14.24                                              Digital Logic Circuits
Instead of coding a complex design in single VHDL Code, it can be divided into submodules as 
components and combine them using port map technique in a main module.
The component declaration and component instantiation statements are the primary structures used 
to describe the design entity.
14.6.3  Component Declaration 
A component declaration declares the name of the component and a set of interface ports.
The port interface specifies the mode and the type of ports, similar to an entity declaration.
Syntax of component declaration  
component component-name 
port (list_of_interface_ports) ; 
end component;
14.6.4  Component Instantiation 
A component instantiation statement is used to define the subcomponent of the entity in which it 
is appearing. 
It connects the signals in the entity with the ports of the subcomponent.  
The association-list associates signals in the entity called actuals, with the ports of a component, 
called locals.
Syntax for component instantiation
component_label: component_name port map (association_list)
Syntax for architecture body of Structural model 
architecture architecture_name of entity_name is
component component_name1 
port (list_of_interface_ports) ; 
end component;
component component_name2 
port ( list_of_interface_ports ) ; 
end component;
begin
component_label1: component_name1 port map ( association_list1 );
component_label2: component_name2 port map ( association_list2 );
end architecture_name;

The Boolean equations for half adder are,
s  = a ⊕ b
co = a . b
 Where, a and b are 1-bit input data sum and carry are 1-bit output data. The VHDL codes for dataflow 
model of half adder are developed using the above equations. (Refer Chapter 5, Section 5.9.1 for design 
of half adder).

14.7  Subprograms
Subprograms are codes for repeated operations in a VHDL program, similar to any high level language 
programs. Subprograms are part of a main program and cannot be compiled separately. Procedures and 
functions are two types of subprograms supported by VHDL. Procedures and functions are first declared in 
the declaration part of architecture and called later any number of times in the execution part of architecture.
14.7.1  Procedure
Procedures are subprograms written for repeated operations in a main program. Procedure requires 
a declaration which includes inputs, outputs and return values. Any number of values can be returned from 
a procedure. 
VHDL Program 14.4
--example program for usage of procedure
library ieee; 
use ieee.std_logic_1164.all;
use ieee.numeric_std.all;

--- Page 1118 ---
Chapter 14 - VHDL 14.27
entity pro_ex is
    generic (N : integer := 7);
    port ( x, y         : in signed (N - 1 downto 0);
                    sum, dif : inout signed (N - 1 downto 0));
end pro_ex;
architecture arch_pro_ex of pro_ex is
signal p : signed (2 * N - 1 downto 0);
--procedure to add and subtract two numbers
procedure sum_dif ( signal a     : in signed (N - 1 downto 0); 
                                        signal b     : in signed (N - 1 downto 0);
                                       signal s, d   : out signed (N - 1 downto 0)) is
begin
s <= a + b;
d <= a - b;
end sum_dif;                               -- procedure ends, procedure returns two values s and d
begin   
sum_dif ( a => x, b => y, d => dif, s => sum);      -- procedure call
              p <= sum * dif;                                     -- product of sum and difference
end arch_pro_ex;
14.7.2  Functions
Functions are subprograms written for repeated operations in a main program. Function requires 
a declaration which includes inputs and a return value. In a function outputs need not be declared and it 
returns only one value. 
The differences between procedure and function are,
●  In a function, outputs need not be declared whereas in a procedure, the outputs have to be declared.
●  A function will return only one value, whereas a procedure can return multiple values.
VHDL Program 14.5 
--example program for usage of function
library ieee;
use ieee.std_logic_1164.all;
use ieee.numeric_std.all;
entity func_ex is
generic ( N : integer := 7);
port ( x, y  : in signed (N - 1 downto 0);
                sum : inout signed (N - 1 downto 0);
                dif    : inout signed (N - 1 downto 0) );
end func_ex;
architecture arch_func_ex of func_ex is
signal p : signed (2 * N - 1 downto 0);
--function to find sum of two integers
function sum2int ( signal a : in signed (N - 1 downto 0); 
                               signal b : in signed (N - 1 downto 0) );                
      return signed is variable s : signed (N -1 downto 0);

--- Page 1119 ---
14.28                                              Digital Logic Circuits
begin
s := a + b;
return s;
end sum2int;      -- end of function, function returns the value of s.
--function to find difference of two integers
function dif2int ( signal a : in signed (N - 1 downto 0); 
                             signal b : in signed (N - 1 downto 0));                
return signed is variable d : signed (N - 1 downto 0);
begin
d := a - b;
return d;
end dif2int;                                         --end of function, function returns the value of d;
begin   
sum <= sum2int (a => x, b => y);   --function call
dif   <= dif2int (a => x, b => y);      --function call
p     <= sum * dif;                           --product of sum and difference
end arch_func_ex;
14.8  Introduction to Packages
A package provides a convenient method to store and share declarations that are common to many 
design units. A Package is a VHDL file, contains data types, constants, functions, procedures, etc, that can 
be shared across many VHDL designs.  
A package is created by a package declaration and package body. A package declaration contains 
a set of declarations that can be shared by many design units. A package body contains the functions and 
procedures that are declared in the corresponding package. 
A package can be compiled or simulated separately and stored in a default library or in any user 
defined library and called in any other program using package name. The default library in Vivado is 
“xil_defaultlib”. Also, the global include should be activated in Vivado before simulating the package.
Syntax of a package declaration
package package_name is 
-- subprogram declarations 
-- subtype declarations 
-- constant declarations 
-- signal declarations 
-- file declarations 
-- alias declarations 
-- component declarations 
-- attribute declarations 
-- attribute specifications 
-- disconnection specifications 
-- use clauses 
end package [ package_name ];  -- package name is optional

--- Page 1120 ---
Chapter 14 - VHDL 14.29
14.8.1  Package Body
A package body primarily contains the behavior of the subprograms and the values of the deferred 
constants declared in a package declaration. It may contain other declarations as well, as shown by the 
following syntax of a package body. 
Syntax of a package declaration
package body package_name is                         
- subprogram bodies 
- subprogram declarations 
- type and subtype declarations 
- file and alias declarations 
- use clauses 
end package body [ package_name ];  -- package name is optional 
The package body name must be the same as the name of its corresponding package declaration. 
A package body is not necessary, if its associated package declaration does not have any subprogram or 
deferred constant declarations. 
A package body is used to store local declarations that cannot be access by other design, while a 
package declaration is used to store public declarations which can be accessed by other design units.
VHDL Program 14.6
--example program for package declaration and package body
library ieee; 
use ieee.std_logic_1164.all;
use ieee.numeric_std.all;
-- package declaration
package mypackage3 is
-- declare a constant with value 1 
constant k : signed (3 downto 0) := "0001";
-- procedure to add two integers
procedure sum_2int ( signal a      : in signed (3 downto 0); 
                                          signal b      : in signed (3 downto 0);
                                          signal sum : out signed (3 downto 0));
-- declare signals for if loop
signal m : unsigned (2 downto 0):=  (others => '0');
type state_type is (start_state, continue_state, stop_state);
end package mypackage3;
-- package body declaration
package body mypackage3 is
 -- procedure to add two integers
procedure sum_2int ( signal a      : in signed (3 downto 0); 
                                          signal b      : in signed (3 downto 0);
                                          signal sum : out signed (3 downto 0)) is 
begin
sum <= a + b;
end sum_2int;
end package body mypackage3;

--- Page 1121 ---
14.30                                              Digital Logic Circuits
--example program that calls the above package (mypackage3)
library ieee; 
library xil_defaultlib;                                       --mypackage3 is compiled in xil_defaultlib
use ieee.std_logic_1164.all;
use ieee.numeric_std.all;
use xil_defaultlib.mypackage3.all;                 --use clause for mypackage3
entity mypackage3_call is
    port ( clk                             : std_logic;
              x                                : in unsigned (4 downto 0);
              count                         : out unsigned (2 downto 0);
              num1, num2             : in signed (3 downto 0);
              sum_num1_constant : out signed (3 downto 0);
              sum_num1_2             : inout signed (3 downto 0) );
end mypackage3_call;
architecture arch_mypackage3_call of mypackage3_call is
signal current_state : state_type;                       --state_type is defined in package
begin   
-- add constant k to num1
sum_num1_constant <= num1 + k;              --k is defined in package
-- add num1 and num2
sum_2int(num1, num2, sum_num1_2);        --procedure sum_2int is defined in package
--process for start-stop control of a count sequence
process (clk, current_state, m)
begin
if (m <= x) then                                      --m is defined in package
current_state <= continue_state;      --continue_state is defined in package
else
current_state <= stop_state;             --stop_state is defined in package
end if;
end process;
--process to generate a count sequence
process (clk,  current_state) 
begin
if (current_state = continue_state) then
m <= m + 1; 
else 
m <= (others => '0');         
end if;                                                    --if loop end
count <= m;
end process;      
end arch_mypackage3_call;
14.9  Library
A library is a collection of packages that are compiled and stored in a directory in the host environment 
(or personal computer) in which the VHDL software tool is installed. 
A library is a directory and each package is a file in that directory. The package file is a database 
containing information about the components in the package.

--- Page 1122 ---
Chapter 14 - VHDL 14.31
The two most commonly used libraries are IEEE and W ORK. The IEEE library is a standard 
library standardized by IEEE and has a large number of packages. The WORK library is always available 
for user defined library packages. In vivado, the default library for user defined library and packages is 
“xil_defaultlib”. The programmer or user can select either WORK library or “xil_defaultlib” library.
The keyword “library” identifies a library in VHDL followed by the logical library name.
Example
library IEEE;
library WORK;
library xil_defaultlib;
library mylib1;
A library may have large number of packages and all the packages may not be required for a design 
unit. Normally, the library statement shown above has to be combined with use statements to access the 
required packages in the library. In general programming practice, the library and use statements are placed 
in the beginning of the source file.
use ieee.std_logic_1164.all; 
--makes all components in std_logic_1164 library from ieee library visible
use ieee.std_logic-arith.all; 
--makes all components in std_logic_arith library from ieee library visible
use ieee.std_logic_unsigned.all; 
--makes all components in std_logic_unsigned library from ieee library visible
use ieee.std_logic_signed.all;
--makes all components in std_logic_signed library from ieee library visible
use ieee.std_logic_textio.all;
--makes all components in std_logic_textio library from ieee library visible
use ieee.numeric_bit.all;
--makes all components in numeric_bit library from ieee library visible
use ieee.numeric_std.all;
--makes all components in numeric_std library from ieee library visible
Design Library
Users can create small design units (with a design entity and architecture) and compile and store in 
a user defined library so that they can be accessed in any other larger design units. A design unit can be 
compiled or simulated separately and stored in a default library or WORK library or in any user defined 
library and called in any other program using the design entity name. 
The default library in Vivado is “xil_defaultlib”. Also, the global include should be activated in 
Vivado before simulating the design units. In order to use a design entity in another design, the library 
name in which the design unit is available should be included in design in which the library is called and 
use clause statement is not required.

14.10  Test Bench
A test bench is also a VHDL program that is used to verify the correctness of the VHDL program 
of the hardware model. A test bench VHDL program has three main purposes: 
●  Generation of necessary inputs and clock for simulation.
●  Apply this inputs and clock to the entity under test and to monitor the output
●  Comparing the output of VHDL program model with expected output. 
The application of inputs and clock to the entity u nder test is accomplished automatically by 
instantiating the entity in the test bench model and then specifying the appropriate interface signals. 
Format of a test bench that drives an entity under test 
entity test_bench is 
--port
end test_bench; 
architecture tb_behavior of test_bench is 
component entity_under_test 
port (list_of_ports_their_types_and_modes); 
end component; 
local_signal_declarations; 
begin 
generate_waveforms_using_behavioral_constructs; 
apply_to_entity_under_test; 
eut: entity_under_test port map (port_associations); 
monitor_values_and_compare_with_expected_values; 
end tb_behavior; 
VHDL program examples without test bench are presented in Section 14.12 and VHDL programs 
with test bench along with the output waveform are presented in Section 14.13. All the programs are 
simulated in Vivado 2019.2, which is a VHDL tool from XILINX.
