14.11  RTL Design
In the VLSI design flow, the designer describes the behavior of the circuit using a hardware description 
language (HDL) such as VHDL or Verilog. These descriptions are then synthesized into a gate-level netlist, 
which is a representation of the circuit at the level of gates and interconnections. This netlist can be used 
to create a physical layout of the circuit on a FPGA IC using computer-aided design (CAD) tools. 
The various steps in the design of a an IC using VHDL and implementing in FPGA are,
●  Develop the design file and testbench in VHDL.
●  Use the design file as the circuit description, and perform a simulation to verify the functionality  
  of the design.
●  Perform a synthesis and generate a netlist.
●  Use the output netlist file of the synthesizer as the circuit description, and perform a simulation  
   of timing analysis. 
●  Perform placement and routing.
●  Update the timing information to the netlist, and perform a simulation and timing analysis to  
   verify the correctness of the placement and routing.

●  Generate the configuration file and program the FPGA device.
●  Verify the working of FPGA device.
A flowchart for IC design using VHDL and implementing in FPGA is shown in Fig. 14.1.
In IC design, it is important to consider various factors such as timing, power and area constraints. 
Timing constraints refer to the speed at which the circuit must operate, power constraints refer to the amount 
of power the circuit consumes, area constraints refer to the physical size of the IC. These requirements can 
be easily realized by the concept of RTL coding style. 
RTL design is a digital design methodology that focuses on the transfer of data between registers 
within a digital system. At the RTL level, the system functionality and behavior of the system are described 
in terms of registers, data flow and control signals.
A digital system is represented at the register tra nsfer level (RTL) when it is specified by the 
following three elements:
1.  The set of registers in the system.
2.  The operations that are performed on the data stored in the registers.
3.  The control that supervises the sequence of operations in the system.    
RTL Design Key Concepts and Elements
●  Registers: Registers are the building blocks of RTL design. Registers can hold binary values, and 
their outputs can be connected to the inputs of other registers, enabling the flow of data between different 
components.
●  Data Flow: RTL design focuses on the transfer of data between registers. Data flow is typically 
defined using a data path diagram, illustrating the connections between registers and the combinational 
logic blocks.
●  Control Signals: Control signals determine the timing and sequencing of operations within a 
digital system. Control signals can be generated through combinational logic circuits or finite state machines, 
ensuring proper synchronization and operation of the system.
●  Combinational Logic: Combinational logic circuits perform operations on input data to produce 
desired output values. Combinational logic circuits include various components such as arithmetic and 
Boolean operations, multiplexers, decoders, encoders, and logic gates.
The programming structure of RTL design can be broadly classified into data path and control path. 
The basic structure of RTL design is shown in Fig. 14.3. The data path has routing network, combinational 
logic and output registers. The control path has next state logic, registers and output logic.

Advantages of RTL Design
● Performance Optimization:  RTL design allows for performance optimization by carefully 
managing the data flow, control signals and interconnections between registers. 
● Design Validation: RTL design provides a structured approach to validate the functionality of a 
digital system before proceeding to physical implementation. 
● Reusability and Modularity:  Designers can create libraries of RTL blocks, such as adders, 
multipliers, memory controllers, or communication interfaces. These reusable blocks can be easily integrated 
into new designs. 
RTL Design Methodologies
●  Manual RTL Design:  In manual RTL design, designers explicitly specify the behavior and 
functionality of the digital system using a hardware description language (HDL) such as Verilog or VHDL. 
The designer defines the registers, data flow, control signals, and interconnections. Manual RTL design 
allows for precise control over the system implementation and provides in-depth understanding of the 
design details. Some examples of manual RTL design are presented in Section 14.14.
●  RTL Synthesis: RTL synthesis is an automated process that transforms a behavioral description 
written in VHDL into RTL description using a VLSI s oftware tool. The synthesis tool translates the 
algorithmic representation into a register-level implementation, optimizing the design for area, power, and 
timing considerations. The Vivado tool used to synthesize the VHDL codes in this book will follow this 
automated process of RTL simulation and synthesis. All the example VHDL programs in Sections 14.12, 
14.13 and 14.14 are simulated in Vivado 2019.2 as RTL project and outputs are verified.

14.11.1  Combinational Logic
A combinational circuit, by definition, is a circuit whose output, is a function of current input. It has 
no internal state and therefore, it is system without memory about the past events (or past inputs). 
Combinational RTL design involves the specification of circuits that perform logical operations on 
input signals to produce output signals, without any internal memory or state. Even though a digital system 
requires a clock for functioning, it is not mandatory to include clock signals in combinational logic circuit 
design. But the combinational digital system working will depend on FPGA IC default clock. 

--- Page 1127 ---
14.36                                              Digital Logic Circuits
Combinational logic circuits can be designed using VHDL concurrent and sequential statements in 
dataflow or behavioral or structural architectures. Examples of combinational logic circuits are half adder, 
full adder, multiplexers, demultiplexers, etc. The RTL synthesisable VHDL codes for some combinational 
logic circuits are presented in Example programs in Section 14.12 and 14.13. All the example programs 
are simulated in Vivado 2019.2 as RTL project and outputs are verified. 
14.11.2  Sequential Circuit
A sequential circuit has an internal state, or memory. Its output is a function of current input as 
well as the internal state. The internal state essentially "memorizes" the effect of the past input values. 
Sequential RTL design involves the specification of circuits that perform logical operations on input signals 
to produce output signals, with internal memory or states.
In addition, the operations of a sequential circuit depend on a clock signal. The "event" attribute of 
VHDL can be attached to a signal named "clk" to create a clock dependent process in a sequential circuit 
design. An example VHDL program of D flip-flop using positive edge triggered clock signal is given below:   
Note: The attribute is an advanced feature in VHDL. An attribute is a value or function or type 
or range or signal or a constant that can be associated with certain names in a VHDL description. The 
name can be an entity name or an architecture name or a label or a signal.
VHDL Program 14.8
--VHDL program for positive edge triggered D flip-flop
library ieee;
use ieee. std_logic_1164.all;
entity pos_dff  is
port ( clk : in std_logic;
                d    : in std_logic;
                q    : out std_logic );
end pos_dff ;
architecture arch of pos_dff is
begin
process (clk)
begin
if (clk' event and clk = '1') then
q <= d;
end if;
end process;
end arch;
In the above program, the key expression that creates clock sensitive process is,
if (clk' event and clk = '1') then
          q <= d;
end if;
The 'event term is a VHDL attribute returning true when there is a change in clk signal value  
(i.e., an event). When the clk = ’1’ expression is true, it means that the new value of clk is '1' . If statement 
states that at the rising of the clk signal, q gets the value of d. Since there is no else branch, it means that 
q keeps its previous value otherwise. 
In the above program, the clock can be modified to have negative edge sensitivity by using the 
following if statement.

--- Page 1128 ---
Chapter 14 - VHDL 14.37
if (clk' event and clk = '0') then
          q <= d;
end if;
Sequential logic circuits can be designed using VHDL concurrent and sequential statements in 
dataflow or behavioral or structural architectures. Examples of sequential logic circuits are flip-flops, 
counters, shift registers, etc. The RTL synthesisable VHDL codes for some sequential logic circuits are 
presented in Example programs in Section 14.12 and 14.13. All the example programs are simulated in 
Vivado 2019.2 as RTL project and outputs are verified.

VHDL Program 14.9
Simplify the Boolean function F by means of K-map and write a dataflow and structural HDL 
to implement the reduced Boolean function.
f(a, b, c, d) = ∑m(0, 6, 7, 9, 11, 13, 15),  d(a, b, c, d) = ∑m(2, 5, 8, 10)
To find Boolean Equation using K-map
The given function has four variables and so a 4-variable 
K-map with 16 squares (24 = 16) is drawn as shown in Fig. 1. The 
function is defined as sum of minterms m0, m6, m7, m9, m11, m13 
and m 15 and so a "1" is filled in the corresponding squares in 
K-map. The function also has don’t-care outputs for the minterms 
m2, m 5, m 8 and m 10 and so a "x" is filled in the corresponding 
squares in K-map and the remaining squares are filled with "0". 
For NAND implementation, the Boolean function should 
be formed in SOP form. In the K-map of Fig. 1, by considering the 
don’t-care condition in m2 and m5 as "1", three prime implicants 
can be formed with four adjacent 1's and the corres ponding 
product terms are ab', bd, a' bc and b' d'. The simplified Boolean 
function is given by sum of these three product terms. 
∴  f = ab' + bd + a' bc + b' d'
Using the above Boolean function the logic circuit using only NAND gates is drawn as shown in Fig. 2.

VHDL Program 14.11
Write VHDL code for dataflow, behavioral and structural models of a 2-to-4 decoder. 
Program Logic for Dataflow and Behavioral Model
 The Boolean equations for 2-to-4 decoder are,
Y0 = I1' . I0'
Y1 = I1' . I0
Y2 = I1 . I0'
Y3 = I1 . I0 
 Where, I1 and I0 are 1-bit input data and Y0, Y1, Y2 and Y3 are 1-bit output data. The VHDL codes for 
dataflow and behavioral model of 2-to-4 decoder are developed using the above equations. (Refer Chapter 5, 
Section 5.4.1 for design of 2-to-4 decoder).
VHDL Program for Dataflow Model of 2-to-4 Decoder
library ieee;
use ieee.std_logic_1164.all;
entity decoder_2_4 is
port ( i1, i0             : in std_logic;
         y0, y1, y2, y3 : out std_logic );
end decoder_2_4;
architecture dfm_decoder_2_4 of decoder_2_4 is
signal m1, m2 : std_logic;
begin
m1 <= not i1;
m2 <= not i0;
y0    <= m1 and m2;
y1    <= m1 and i0;
y2    <= i1 and m2;
y3    <= i1 and i0;
end dfm_ decoder_2_4;
VHDL Program for Behavioral Model of 2-to-4 Decoder using “case” Statement
library ieee;
use ieee.std_logic_1164.all;
entity decoder_2_4 is
port ( i                    : in std_logic_vector (1 downto 0);
         y0, y1, y2, y3 : out std_logic );
end decoder_2_4;

--- Page 1134 ---
Chapter 14 - VHDL 14.43
architecture bm_decoder_2_4 of decoder_2_4 is
signal m1, m2 : std_logic;
begin
process (i) 
begin
m1 <= not i(0);         
m2 <= not i(1);
case i is
when “00”     => y0 <= m1 and m2;
when “01”     => y1 <= m1 and i(1);
when “10”      => y2 <= i(0) and m2;
when others => y3 <= i(0) and i(1);
end case;
end process;
end bm_decoder_2_4;
VHDL Program for Behavioral Model of 2-to-4 Decoder using “if elsif” Statement
library ieee;
use ieee.std_logic_1164.all;
entity decoder_2_4 is
port ( i                              : in std_logic_vector (1 downto 0);
          y0, y1, y2, y3  : out std_logic );
end decoder_2_4;
architecture bm_decoder_2_4 of decoder_2_4 is
signal m1, m2 : std_logic;
begin
process (i) 
begin
m1<= not i(0);
m2<= not i(1);
if i = “00” then
y0 <= m1 and m2;
elsif i = “01” then
y1 <= m1 and i(1);
elsif i = “10” then
y2 <= i(0) and m2;
else
y3 <= i(0) and i(1);
end if;
end process;
end bm_decoder_2_4;

Program Logic for Behavioral Model
The VHDL code for behavioral model of 3-to-8 decoder are developed using the truth table of 3-to-8

VHDL Program for Behavioral Model of 3-to-8 Decoder
library ieee;

           y : out bit_vector (7 downto 0) );

begin

elsif I = "101" then

end process;   
end bm_decoder3_8;

Y1 = I2 + I3   ;   Y0 = I1 + I3
Where, I0, I1, I2 and I3 are 1-bit input data, Y0 and Y1 are 1-bit output data. The VHDL code for dataflow 
model of 4-to-2 encoder is developed using the above equations. (Refer Chapter 5, Section 5.5.1 for design 
of 4-to-2 encoder).

end encoder_4_2;

VHDL Program 14.14
Write a VHDL code for dataflow model of priority encoder.
Program Logic for Dataflow Model
Boolean equations for priority encoder with I3 having highest priority and I0 having lowest priority are,
Y1 = I2 + I3     ;     Y0 = I1.I2' + I3     ;     v = I0 + I1 + I2 + I3
Where, I0, I1, I2 and I3 are 1-bit input data and Y0, Y1 and v are 1-bit output data. The VHDL code for 
dataflow model of priority encoder is developed using the above equations. (Refer Chapter 5, Section 5.6.2 
for design of priorioty encoder).
VHDL Program for Dataflow Model of Priority Encoder
library ieee;
use ieee.std_logic_1164.all;
entity priority_encoder is
port ( i0, i1, i2, i3 : in std_logic;
          y0, y1, v      : out std_logic );
end priority_encoder;
architecture dfm_priority_encoder of priority_encoder is
signal m1 : std_logic;
begin
m1 <= not i2;
y1   <= i2 or i3;
y0   <= (i1 and m1) or i3;
v     <= i0 or i1 or i2 or i3;
end dfm_priority_encoder;

VHDL Program 14.17
Write a VHDL code for dataflow and structural model of a 1*4 demultiplexer.
Program Logic for Dataflow Model
The Boolean equations for 1*4 demultiplexer are,
Y0 = Ii.S1' .S0'    ;   Y1 = Ii.S1' .S0     ;     Y2 = Ii.S1.S0'     ;     Y3 = Ii.S1.S0 
Where, S1 and S0 are 1-bit selection input and Y0, Y1, Y2 and Y3 are 1-bit output data. The VHDL code 
for dataflow model of 1*4 demultiplexer is developed using the above equations. (Refer Chapter 5, Section 
5.8 for design of 1*4 demultiplexer).
VHDL Program for Dataflow Model of 1*4 Demultiplexer
library ieee;
use ieee.std_logic_1164.all;
entity demux_1_4 is
port ( ii, s0, s1          : in std_logic;
          y0, y1, y2, y3  : out std_logic );
end demux_1_4;
architecture dfm_demux_1_4 of demux_1_4 is
signal m1, m2 : std_logic;
begin
m1 <= not s0;
m2 <= not s1;
y0  <= ii and (m1 and m2);
y1  <= ii and (m1 and s1);
y2  <= ii and (s0 and m2);
y3  <= ii and (s0 and s1);
end dfm_demux_1_4;

VHDL Program 14.18
Write VHDL code for dataflow and structural models of a full adder. 
Program Logic for Dataflow Model
 The Boolean equations for full adder are,
 s = a ⊕ b ⊕ ci
 co = (a b) + (b ci) + (ci a)
 Where, a, b and ci are 1-bit input data, sum (s) and carry (c o) are 1-bit output data. The VHDL code for 
dataflow model of full adder is developed using the above equations. (Refer Chapter 5, Section 5.9.2 for design 
of full adder).

VHDL Program for Dataflow Model of Full Adder
library ieee;
use ieee.std_logic_1164.all;
entity full_adder is
port ( a, b, ci  : in std_logic;
          s, co      : out std_logic );
end full_adder;
architecture dfm_fa of full_adder is
signal m1, m2, m3 : std_logic;
begin
s       <= a xor b xor ci;
m1 <= a and b;
m2 <= b and ci;
m3 <= ci and a; 
co   <= m1 or m2 or m3;
end dfm_fa;

VHDL Program 14.20
Write a VHDL code for dataflow model of a 4-bit CLA (Carry look ahead adder).
Program Logic for Dataflow Model
si = pi ⊕ ci            ;           ci+1 = gi + pi ci
pi = ai ⊕ bi            ;           gi = ai bi 
Where, p i is carry propagate from i th stage and g i is carry generate of i th stage. The VHDL code for 
dataflow model of 4-bit CLA is developed using the above equations. (Refer Chapter 5, Section 5.9.4 for design 
of 4-bit CLA).
VHDL Program for Dataflow Model of 4-bit CLA
library ieee;
use ieee.std_logic_1164.all;
entity cla_4bit is
port ( a3, a2, a1, a0     : in std_logic;
          b3, b2, b1, b0     : in std_logic;
          c0                       : in std_logic;
          c4, s3, s2, s1, s0  : out std_logic);
end cla_4bit;
architecture dfm_cla_4bit of cla_4bit is
signal m1, m2, m3, m4, m5, m6, m7  : std_logic;
signal p0, p1, p2, p3 : std_logic;
signal g0, g1, g2, g3 : std_logic;
begin
p0  <= a0 xor b0;    p1  <= a1 xor b1;   p2   <= a2 xor b2;    p3   <= a3 xor b3;
g0   <= a0 and b0;   g1  <= a1 and b1;   g2  <= a2 and b2;   g3  <= a3 and b3;
m1 <= g0 or (p0 and c0);
m2 <= g1 or (p1 and g0) or (p1 and p0 and c0);
m3 <= g2 or (p2 and g1) or (p2 and p1 and g0) or (p2 and p1 and p0 and c0);
s0   <= p0 xor c0;
s1   <= p1 xor m1;
s2   <= p2 xor m2;
s3   <= p3 xor m3;
m4 <= p3 and g2
m5 <= p3 and p2 and g1
m6 <= p3 and p2 and p1 and g0
m7 <= p3 and p2 and p1 and p0 and c0 
c4  <= g3 or m4 or m5 or m6 or m7;
end dfm_cla_4bit;

VHDL Program 14.21
Write VHDL code for dataflow and structural models of a half subtractor. 
Program Logic for Dataflow Model 
 The Boolean equations for half subtractor are,
d = a ⊕ b = ab' + a' b
co = a' b
 Where, a and b are 1-bit input data, difference (d) and borrow (co) are 1-bit output data. The VHDL code 
for dataflow model of half subtractor is developed using the above equations. (Refer Chapter 5, Section 5.10.1 
for design of half subtractor).
VHDL Program for Dataflow Model of Half Subtractor
library ieee;
use ieee.std_logic_1164.all;
entity half_subtractor is
port ( a, b  : in std_logic;
         d, co : out std_logic );
end half_subtractor;
architecture dfm_hs of half_subtractor is
signal m1 : std_logic;
begin
d      <= a xor b;

VHDL Program 14.22
Write VHDL code for dataflow and structural models of a full subtractor. 
Program Logic Dataflow Model 
 The Boolean equations for full subtractor are,
d = a' b' ci ⊕ a' bci' ⊕ a' bci' ⊕ abci
 co = (a' b) + (b ci) + (ci a' )
 Where, a, b and c i are 1-bit input data, difference (d) and borrow (c o) are 1-bit output data. The VHDL 
code for dataflow model of full subtractor is developed using the above equations. (Refer Chapter 5, Section 
5.10.2 for design of full subtractor).
VHDL Program for Dataflow Model of Full Subtractor
library ieee;
use ieee.std_logic_1164.all;
entity full_subtractor is
port ( a, b, ci  : in std_logic;
          d, co      : out std_logic );
end full_subtractor;
architecture dfm_fs of full_subtractor is
signal m1 : std_logic;
begin
d       <= a xor b xor ci;
m1 <= not a;
co   <= (m1 and b) or (b and ci) or (ci and m1);
end dfm_fs;

 The VHDL code for structural model of full subtractor is

VHDL Program 14.23
Write a VHDL code for dataflow model of 1-bit magnitude comparator.
Program Logic for Dataflow Model 
Let a and b are 1-bit binary numbers.
The Boolean equations for 1-bit magnitude comparator are,
if a = b,  then (a ⊕ b)'  = 1
if a > b,  then a b'  = 1
if a < b,  then a' b = 1
The VHDL codes for dataflow model of 1-bit magnitude comaparator are developed using the Boolean 
equations. (Refer Chapter 5, Section 5.12 for design of 1-bit magnitude comparator).
VHDL Program for Dataflow Model of 1-bit Magnitude Comparator
library ieee;
use ieee.std_logic_1164.all;
entity comparator_1bit is
port ( a, b                              : in std_logic;
          a_eq_b, a_lt_b, a_gt_b : out std_logic );
end comparator_1bit;
architecture dfm_comparator_1bit of comparator_1bit is
signal a_bar, b_bar : std_logic;
begin
a_bar   <= not a;             
b_bar   <= not b;
a_eq_b <= not (a xor b);
a_gt_b  <= a and b_bar;
a_lt_b   <= a_bar and b;
end dfm_comparator_1bit;

VHDL Program 14.24
Write a VHDL code for dataflow model of a 3-bit comparator.
Program Logic for Dataflow Model 
Let a and b are 3-bit binary numbers.
The Boolean equations for 3-bit magnitude comparator are,
if a = b,  then (a0 ⊕ b0)' . (a1 ⊕ b1)' . (a2 ⊕ b2)' = 1
if a > b,  then (a2 . b2) + ((a2 ⊕ b2)' . a1 . b1) + ((a2 ⊕ b2)' . (a1 ⊕ b1)' . a0 . b0) = 1        
if a < b,  then (a2 . b2) + ((a2 ⊕ b2)' . a1 . b1) + ((a2 ⊕ b2)' . (a1 ⊕ b1)' . a0 . b0) = 1
The VHDL codes for dataflow model of 3-bit magnitude comparator are developed using the Boolean 
equations. (Refer Chapter 5, Section 5.12.2 for design of 3-bit magnitude comparator).
VHDL Program for Dataflow Model of 3-bit Comparator
library ieee;
use ieee.std_logic_1164.all;
entity comparator_3bit is
port ( a0, a1, a2, b0, b1, b2  : in std_logic;
          a_gt_b, a_lt_b, a_eq_b  : out std_logic );
end comparator_3bit;
architecture dfm_comparator_3bit of comparator_3bit is
signal a0bar, a1bar, a2bar, b0bar, b1bar, b2bar : std_logic;
signal m0, m1, m2, m3, m4, m5, m6, m7, m8 : std_logic;
begin
m0 <= not (a0 xor b0);
m1 <= not (a1 xor b1);
m2 <= not (a2 xor b2); 
m3 <= a2 and b2bar;
m4 <= m2 and a1 and b1bar; 
m5 <= m2 and m1 and a0 and b0bar; 
m6 <= a2bar and b2; 
m7 <= m2 and a1bar and b1;
m8 <= m2 and m1 and a0bar and b0;
a0bar <= not a0;   a1bar <= not a1;   a2bar <= not a2;
b0bar <= not b0;   b1bar <= not b1;   b2bar <= not b2;
a_eq_b <= m0 and m1 and m2;
a_gt_b  <= m3 or m4 or m5;
a_lt_b   <= m6 or m7 or m8;
end dfm_comparator_3bit;

VHDL Program 14.27
Write a VHDL code for dataflow, behavioral and structural model of a SR flip-flop using NAND 
gates.
Program Logic
The following Boolean equations for SR flip-flop ar e 
developed from Fig. 1.
m1 = (s . clk)'
m2 = (r . clk)'
q = (m1 . q' )'
q' = (m2 . q)'
 Where, s and r are 1-bit input data, q and q ' (qbar) are 1-bit output data. 
The VHDL code for dataflow model of SR flip-flop is developed using the above 
equations. The behavioral model of SR flip-flop is developed using the truth table of 
SR flip-flop. The VHDL code for structural model of SR flip-flop is developed using 
the logic circuit shown in Fig. 1. In structural model, each component involved in 
the SR flip-flop are coded separately and then the components are added in the 
code for SR flip-flop. (Refer Chapter 6, Section 6.2.2 for design of SR flip-flop).
VHDL Program for Dataflow Model of SR Flip-Flop
library ieee;
use ieee.std_logic_1164.all;
entity sr_ff is
port ( s, r, clk   : in std_logic;
          q, qbar    : inout std_logic);
end sr_ff;
architecture dfm_sr_ff of sr_ff is
signal m1, m2, m3, m4 : std_logic;
signal q1       : std_logic := '0';
signal q1bar : std_logic := '1';
begin
m1 <= not(s and clk);
m3 <= not(m1 and q1bar); 
m2 <= not(r and clk);
m4 <= not(m2 and q1);
q <= m3;
qbar <= not(q);
end dfm_sr_ff;

VHDL Program for Behavioral Model of JK Flip-Flop
library ieee;
use ieee.std_logic_1164.all;
entity jk_ff is
port ( j, k          : in std_logic;
          clk, reset : in std_logic;
          q, qbar    : out std_logic);
end jk_ff;
architecture bm_jk_ff of jk_ff is
begin
qbar <= not q;
process (clk, reset)
begin
if (reset = '1') then
q <= 0;                qbar <= 1;
elsif (clk' event and clk = '1') then
if (j = '0' and k = '0') then 
q <= q;                qbar <= qbar;
if (j = '0' and k = '1') then
q <= 0;                qbar <= 1;
if (j = '1' and k = '0') then
q <= 1;                qbar <= 0;
else
 q      <= qbar;     qbar <= not q;
end if;
end if; 
end if;
end if;
end process;
end bm_jk_ff;

Write a VHDL code for behavioral model of a D flip-flop.

VHDL Program 14.31
Write a VHDL code for behavioral model of a 2-bit up/down counter.
Program Logic for Behavioral Model
A selection bit, a is required to select up count when a = 1 and down count when a = 0. Initial count 
is kept 0 and increment by 1 for up count and decrement by 1 for down count for every clock pulse. (Refer 
Chapter 8, Section 8.2.3 for design of up/down counter).
VHDL Program for Behavioral Model of 2-bit up/down Counter
library ieee;
use ieee.std_logic_1164.all;
use ieee.std_logic_arith.all;
use ieee.std_logic_unsigned.all;
entity updown_2bit is
port ( clk, a : in std_logic;
          dout   : out std_logic_vector (1 downto 0) );
end updown_2bit;
architecture bm_updown_2bit of updown_2bit is
signal m1 : std_logic_vector (1 downto 0) := "00";
begin
process (clk)
begin
if (clk = '1') then
if a = '1' then 
m1   <= m1 + "01";
dout <= m1;
else 
m1   <= m1 - "01";
dout <= m1;
end if;
end if;
end process;
end bm_updown_2bit;

VHDL Program 14.32
Write VHDL code for dataflow model of a binary to gray code converter. 
Program Logic for Dataflow Model
The following procedure will be useful for bit-by-bit conversion of n-bit binary to n-bit gray code.
Step 1:  The most significant bit of binary and gray code are same. Hence retain the most significant 
bit of binary as most significant bit of gray code.
Step 2:  Starting from most significant bit of binary, add two consecutive bits of binary and record the 
sum as bit of gray code and discard the carry in every addition.
The VHDL code for dataflow model of binary to gray code converter is developed using the above 
procedure.(Refer Chapter 5, Section 5.3 for design of binary gray code).
VHDL Program for Dataflow Model of Binary Gray Code
library ieee;
use ieee.std_logic_1164.all;
entity binary_gray is
port ( b3, b2, b1, b0 : in std_logic;
          g3, g2, g1, g0  : out std_logic );
end binary_gray;
architecture dfm_binary_gray of binary_gray is
begin
g3 <= b3;
g2 <= b3 xor b2;
g1 <= b2 xor b1;
g0 <= b1 xor b0;
end dfm_binary_gray;

VHDL Program 14.35
Write VHDL code for dataflow model of a 4*1 multiplexer. 
Program Logic for Dataflow Model 
The Boolean equations for 4*1 multiplexer are,
Y = S0' .S1' .I0 + S0' .S1.I1 + S0.S1'. I2 + S0.S1.I3 
Where, S0 and S1 are 1-bit selection input, Y is 1-bit output data. The VHDL code for dataflow model 
of 4*1 multiplexer is developed using the above equations. (Refer Chapter 5, Section 5.7 for design of 4*1 
multiplexer).
VHDL Program for Dataflow Model of 4*1 Multiplexer
library ieee;
use ieee.std_logic_1164.all;
entity mux_4_1 is
port ( s0, s1          : in std_logic;
          i0, i1, i2, i3 : in std_logic;
                     y                  : out std_logic );
end mux_4_1;
architecture dfm_mux_4_1 of mux_4_1 is
signal ns0, ns1              : std_logic;
signal m1, m2, m3, m4 : std_logic;
begin
ns0 <= not s0;
ns1 <= not s1;
m1  <= ns0 and ns1 and i0;
m2  <= ns0 and s1 and i1;
m3  <= s0 and ns1 and i2;
m4  <= s0 and s1 and i3;
y     <= m1 or m2 or m3 or m4;
end dfm_mux_4_1;

library ieee;
use ieee.std_logic_1164.all;
entity demux_1_4 is
port ( s1, s0            : in std_logic;
          ii                           : in std_logic;
         y0, y1, y2, y3 : out std_logic );
end demux_1_4;
architecture bm_demux_1_4 of demux_1_4 is
begin
process ( s1, s0, ii ) 
begin
 if s0 = '0' and s1 = '0' then
y0 <=  ii;        y1 <= '0';       y2 <= '0';       y3 <= '0';
elsif s0 = '0' and s1 = '1' then
y0 <=  '0';       y1 <= ii;         y2 <= '0';       y3 <= '0';
elsif s0 = '1' and s1 = '0' then
y0 <=  '0';       y1 <= '0';       y2 <= ii;         y3 <= '0';
else 
y0 <= '0';       y1 <= '0';        y2 <= '0';       y3 <= ii;
end if;
end process;
end bm_demux_1_4;

Chapter 14 - VHDL 14.91
VHDL Program 14.39
Write VHDL code for behavioral model of a half subtractor. 
Program Logic for Behavioral Model 
 The Boolean equations for half subtractor are,
 d = a ⊕ b      ;        co = a' b
 Where, a and b are 1-bit input data, difference (d) and borrow (c o) are 1-bit output data. The VHDL code for 
behavioral model of half subtractor is developed using the above equations. (Refer Chapter 5, Section 5.10.1 for 
design of half subtractor).
VHDL Program for Behavioral Model of Half Subtractor
library ieee;
use ieee.std_logic_1164.all;
entity half_subtractor is
port ( a, b  : in std_logic;
          d, co : out std_logic );
end half_subtractor;
architecture bm_half_subtractor of half_subtractor is
signal m1 : std_logic;
begin
process ( a, b ) 
begin
d <= a xor b;       m1 <= not a;       co <= m1 and b;
end process;
end bm_half_subtractor;

VHDL Program for Behavioral Model of 4-bit ALU
library ieee;
use ieee.std_logic_1164.all;
use ieee.std_logic_arith.all;
use ieee.std_logic_unsigned.all;
entity alu_4bit is
port ( clk    : in std_logic; 
                      reset : in std_logic; 
          a, b   : in std_logic_vector   (3 downto 0);
                ci       : in std_logic_vector   (1 downto 0);
                      sel     : in std_logic_vector (2 downto 0);
    f         : out std_logic_vector (3 downto 0) );
end alu_4bit;
architecture bm_alu_4bit of alu_4bit is
begin
process (clk, reset) 
begin
if (reset'event and reset = '0') then
f <= "0000";
elsif (clk'event and clk = '1') then 
case (sel) is
when "000" => f <= "0000";
when "001" => f <= b - a;
when "010" => f <= a - b;
when "011" => f <= a + b;
when "100" => f <= a xor b;
when "101" => f <= a or b;
when "110" => f <= a and b;
when others => f <= "1111";
end case;
end if;
end process;
end bm_alu_4bit;

VHDL Program 14.42
Write VHDL code for behavioral model of the Mealy FSM given below.
Program Logic for Behavioral Model
The given Mealy FSM has four states. Here, case statement is used to select a current state and the next 
state is decided based on output and input in each case. (Refer Chapter 7, Section 7.2.1 for design of Melay_fsm).
VHDL Program for Behavioral Model of Mealy_FSM
library ieee;
use ieee.std_logic_1164.all;
entity melay_fsm is
port ( x, clk : in bit;
          y        : out bit );
end melay_fsm;
architecture bm_melay_fsm of melay_fsm is
type s_type is (s0, s1, s2, s3);
signal c_s, n_s : s_type;
begin
process (clk)
begin
if (clk = '1' and clk' event) then
c_s <= n_s;
end if;
end process;
process (x, c_s, n_s)
begin
case c_s is
when s0 => if x = '1' then
n_s <= s1;       y <= '0';
else
n_s <= s2;       y <= '1';
end if;
when s1 => if x = '1' then
n_s <= s2;       y <= '0';
else
n_s <= s0;             y <= '1';
end if;

VHDL Program 14.45
Write VHDL code for behavioral model of a MOD6 counter.
Program Logic for Behavioral Model
Initially the count value is kept 0. MOD6 counter is basically an up counter and hence the count value 
is incremented by 1 for every clock pulse. When the count reaches 101 the count value is clear to 0. (Refer 
Chapter 8, Section 8.2.6 for design of MOD6 counter).
VHDL Program for Behavioral Model of MOD6 Counter
library ieee;
use ieee.std_logic_1164.all;
use ieee.std_logic_arith.all;
use ieee.std_logic_unsigned.all;
entity mod6_counter is
port ( clk    : in std_logic;
          dout  : inout std_logic_vector (2 downto 0));
end mod6_counter;
architecture bm_mod6_counter of mod6_counter is
signal m1 : std_logic_vector (2 downto 0) := "000";
begin
process (clk)
begin
if (clk = '1') then
if m1 = "101" then
m1 <= "000";             dout <= m1;
  else
m1 <= m1 + "001";    dout <= m1;
end if;

VHDL Program 14.46
Write a VHDL code for behavioral model of 8-bit SISO right shift register.
Program Logic for Behavioral Model 
In the VHDL code, an 8-bit buffer is declared to store the 8-bit data. The LSB (Least Significant Bit) of 8-bit 
buffer is output as serial output data. The shift operation is performed by concatenation of input data bit as 
MSB (Most Significant Bit) and upper 7-bit of buffer.  (Refer Chapter 8, Section 8.6.1 for right shift SISO register.
VHDL Program for Behavioral Model of 8-bit SISO Right Shift Register
library ieee;
use ieee.std_logic_1164.all;
entity RS_reg is
port ( clk                   : in std_logic;
           reset                : in std_logic;
                 ser_data_in     : in std_logic;
                ser_data_out   : out std_logic;
                 rightshift_reg : buffer std_logic_vector(7 downto 0));            
end RS_reg;
architecture bm_RS_reg of RS_reg is
begin
process (clk, reset)
begin 
if (reset'event and reset = '0') then 
rightshift_reg <= "11110000"
elsif (clk'event and clk = '1') then 
ser_data_out <= rightshift_reg(0);    
rightshift_reg <= ser_data_in & rightshift_reg(7 downto 1);     
end if;
end process;   
end bm_RS_reg;

14.14  VHDL Programs in RTL Methodology
VHDL Program 14.49
Write a VHDL program to perform addition of four 8-bit unsigned integer numbers by using 
RTL design methodology.
RTL Design Program Logic for Sum of Four Integers
Let a, d, c and d is the four integers.
Now, sum of four integers can be expressed as.
Sum = ((a + b) + c) + d
 In RTL implementation, the computation task is breakdown into a sequence of steps, each one involving 
only a single addition and each operation is executed sequentially.  
sum = 0   sum = sum + a
sum = sum + b  sum = sum + c
sum = sum + d 
Now the logic components required in data path module are one adder, a register to hold the value 
of sum in-between operations, a multiplexer to select the input to be added, and a circuit to clear sum at the 
start of computation. A simple block diagram showing data and control path of RTL design is shown in Fig. 1.
The RTL design is implemented in three modules: rtl_adder_data_path, rtl_adder_control_path , rtl_adder.  
The rtl_adder_data_path and rtl_adder_control_path are compiled separately and used as in rtl_adder which 
is the top module. The VHDL programs for the three modules are given below: 
VHDL Program for Adder
--rtl_adder_data_path.vhd
library ieee;
use ieee.std_logic_1164.all;
use ieee.std_logic_arith.all;
entity rtl_adder_data_path is
port ( a, b, c, d            : in unsigned (7 downto 0); 
          sum                  : out unsigned (7 downto 0); 
          sel                    : in std_logic_vector (1 downto 0);
          load, clear, clk : in std_logic ); 
end rtl_adder_data_path;

architecture arch_rtl_adder_data_path of rtl_adder_data_path is
signal mux_out, sum_reg, next_sum_reg : unsigned (7 downto 0);    
constant sum_zero                                  : unsigned (7 downto 0) := "00000000";  
begin
-- mux to select input data
with sel select mux_out <= 
a when "00",     
b when "01",     
c when "10",    
d when others; 
-- mux to select register input
next_sum_reg <= 
sum_reg + mux_out when load = '1' else 
sum_zero when clear                = '1' else 
sum_reg; 
-- process to load sum_reg 
process (clk) 
begin 
if clk'event and clk = '1' then 
sum_reg <= next_sum_reg ; 
end if;
 end process;
--output reg_sum 
sum <= sum_reg ; 
end arch_rtl_adder_data_path;
--rtl_adder_control_path.vhd
library ieee;
use ieee.std_logic_1164.all;
entity rtl_adder_control_path is
port ( update        : in std_logic;
                sel               : out std_logic_vector (1 downto 0);
                load, clear  : out std_logic;
                clk               : in std_logic );
end rtl_adder_control_path;
architecture arch_rtl_adder_control_path of rtl_adder_control_path is
type states is (clr, add_a, add_b, add_c, add_d, hold); 
signal cs, holdns, ns : states;
signal tmp                : std_logic_vector (3 downto 0);
begin
-- select next state
with cs select ns <=
add_a   when clr,
add_b   when add_a,
add_c   when add_b,
add_d   when add_c,
hold     when add_d,
holdns  when others;

--- Page 1216 ---
Chapter 14 - VHDL 14.125
--process to decide current state (cs)        
process (clk)
begin
if clk' event and clk = '1' then
cs <= ns;
end if;
end process;        
--output control signal to select mux input         
with cs select sel<=
"00" when add_a,         "01" when add_b,
"10" when add_c,         "11" when others;
--output control signal to clear register
holdns <=
clr when update = '1' else
hold;   
load  <= '0' when cs = clr or cs = hold else '1';
clear <= '1' when cs = clr else '0';
end arch_rtl_adder_control_path;
--rtl_adder.vhd, top module of VHDL program
--rtl_adder_data_path.vhd and rtl_adder_control_path.vhd are added as components in this top module

use ieee.std_logic_arith.all;

                sum              : out unsigned (7 downto 0);
                update, clk : in std_logic );
end rtl_adder;

port ( a, b, c, d           : in unsigned (7 downto 0);
                      sum                  : out unsigned (7 downto 0);
                      sel                    : in std_logic_vector (1 downto 0);
                      load, clear, clk : in std_logic );
end component;
component rtl_adder_control_path
port ( update        : in std_logic;
                sel               : out std_logic_vector (1 downto 0);
                load, clear  : out std_logic;
                clk              : in std_logic );
end component; 
begin
d1 : rtl_adder_data_path port map (a => a, b => b, c => c, d => d, sum => sum,
                                                                     sel => sel, load => load, clear => clear, clk => clk);
c1: rtl_adder_control_path port map (update => update, sel => sel, load => load,
                                                                        clear => clear, clk => clk );
end arch_rtl_adder;

VHDL Program 14.50
Write a VHDL program to generate a pulse of width equal to width of four input clock pulse 
using RTL design methodology.
RTL Design Program Logic for Pulse Genereation
A simple block diagram showing data and control path 
of RTL design is shown in Fig. 1. The data path has a count 
register that counts the input clock pulses and com pares 
the count with a specified pulse width count. Three input 
control signals start, stop and reset are used control the pulse 
generation process. The reset can be used as general system 
reset. The stop signal is used to stop the process at any desired 
time. The program is designed to generate an output pulse for 
a specified width whenever the start pulse goes high.  
The RTL design is implemented in three modules: 
rtl_pulse_gen_data_path, rtl_pulse_gen_control_path , 
rtl_pulse_gen.  The rtl_pulse_gen_data_path and rtl _pulse_
gen_control_path are compiled separately and used a s in 
rtl_pulse_gen which is the top module. The VHDL programs 
for the three modules are given below:
VHDL Program for Pulse Genereation
--rtl_pulse_gen_data_path.vhd
library ieee;
use ieee.std_logic_1164.all;
use ieee.std_logic_arith.all;
use ieee.std_logic_unsigned.all;
entity rtl_pulse_gen_data_path is
port ( clk, reset   : in std_logic;
           start, stop : in std_logic;
           pulse         : out std_logic ); 
end rtl_pulse_gen_data_path;
architecture arch_rtl_pulse_gen_data_path of rtl_pulse_gen_data_path is
constant pulse_width : integer := 4;
type state_type is (idle, delay);
signal state_reg, state_next    : state_type;
signal count_reg, count_next : unsigned (3 downto 0);
begin
-- next_state logic & datapath functional units/routing
process (state_reg, start, stop, count_reg)
begin
pulse <= '0';       count_next <= count_reg;
case state_reg is
when idle =>
if (start = '1') then
state_next <= delay;
else
state_next <= idle;

when delay =>

type state_type is (idle, delay);

begin
if (reset = '1') then
state_reg   <= idle;                 count_reg <= (others => '0');

state_reg  <= state_next;       count_reg <= count_next;
end if;
end process;
end arch_rtl_pulse_gen_control_path;

begin
d1 : rtl_pulse_gen_data_path port map (clk => clk, reset => reset, start => start, stop => stop, 
                                pulse => pulse);
c1 : rtl_pulse_gen_control_path port map (clk => clk, reset => reset);
end arch_rtl_pulse_gen;
VHDL Program 14.51
Write a VHDL program to design a UART receiver using RTL design methodology.
RTL Design Program Logic for UART receiver
Universal asynchronous receiver and transmitter (UART) is a scheme that sends bytes of data through 
a serial line. Normally, the serial line is in the ‘1’ state when it is idle and the start of reception is indicated by 
asserting this line ‘0’, which is considered as start bit. The start bit is followed by eight data bits and ended 
with a stop bit, which is ' 1'. 
UART receiver uses an oversampling scheme to ensure that the data bits are retrieved at the right point. 
This scheme utilizes a high-frequency sampling signal to estimate the middle point of a data bit and then 
retrieve data bits at these points. Here, the sampling rate is 16 times the baud rate 1200 and hence, there are 
16 sampling pulses for each received bit. The program uses a sampling pulse counter of size 16 bits. 
The procedure to retrieve the incoming data bits is follows:
Step-1: When the serial line goes ‘0’ indicating beginning of the start bit, initiate the sampling pulse 
counter.
Step-2: When the counter reaches 7, clear it to 0 and restart. At this point, the incoming signal reaches 
about a half of the start bit (or the middle point of the start bit).
Step-3: When the counter reaches 15, clear it to 0 and rest art. At this point, the incoming signal 
progresses for one bit and reaches the middle of the first data bit. The data in the serial line should be 
retrieved and shifted into a register.
Step-4: Repeat Step 3 seven times to retrieve the remaining seven data bits.
Step-5: Repeat Step 3 one more time but without shifting. The incoming signal should reach the middle 
of the stop bit at this point, and its value should be '1'.
Here, the system clock is assumed as 1 MHz and the baud rate is 1200 baud. The frequency of the 
sampling enable pulse should be 16 * 1200, which can be obtained by a mod-52 counter (1 × 106
 ÷ (16 × 1200) 
= 52). The syn_pulse signal is the enable pulse whose frequency is 16 times that of the baud rate. 

--- Page 1220 ---
Chapter 14 - VHDL 14.129
The program uses four states idle, start, data and stop in order to keep track of various activities in 
the data bit receiving process. Note that the system, remains in the same state unless the syn-pulse signal 
is activated. 
There are two counters namely, syn_pulsecount and syn_bitcount registers. The syn_pulsecount register 
keeps track of the number of sampling pulses. 
 The syn_bitcount register keeps track of the number of data bits received in the data state. The retrieved 
bits are shifted into and reassembled in the data bit register. 
The RTL design is implemented in three modules: rtl_uart_rec_data_path, rtl_ uart_rec _control_path, 
rtl_ uart_rec. The rtl_ uart_rec _data_path and rtl_ uart_rec _control_path are compiled separately and used as 
in rtl_ uart_rec which is the top module. The VHDL programs for the three modules are given ahead:
VHDL Program for UART Receiver
--rtl_uart_rec_data_path.vhd
library ieee;
use ieee.std_logic_1164.all;
use ieee.std_logic_arith.all;
use ieee.std_logic_unsigned.all;
entity rtl_uart_rec_data_path is
port ( clk, reset, rec_bit : in std_logic;
           ready                   : out std_logic; 
           pout                      : out std_logic_vector (7 downto 0));
end rtl_uart_rec_data_path;
architecture arch_rtl_uart_rec_data_path of rtl_uart_rec_data_path is
type state_type is (idle, start, data, stop);
signal syn_pulse                                   : std_logic;
signal state_reg, state_next                  : state_type;
signal syn_pulsecount_reg, pulse_next : unsigned (3 downto 0);
signal syn_bitcount_reg, bit_next         : unsigned (2 downto 0);
signal databit_reg, databit_next           : std_logic_vector (7 downto 0);
begin
process (state_reg, syn_pulsecount_reg, syn_bitcount_reg, databit_reg, syn_pulse, rec_bit)
begin
pulse_next    <= syn_pulsecount_reg;
bit_next        <= syn_bitcount_reg;
databit_next <= databit_reg;
ready            <= '0';
case state_reg is
when idle =>
if (rec_bit ='0') then
state_next <= start;
else
state_next <= idle;
end if;
ready <= '1';
when start =>
if (syn_pulse = '0') then
state_next <= start;
elsif (syn_pulsecount_reg = 7) then

--- Page 1221 ---
14.130                                              Digital Logic Circuits
state_next <= data;        pulse_next <= (others => '0');
else
state_next <= start;       pulse_next <= syn_pulsecount_reg + 1;
end if;
when data =>
if (syn_pulse = '0') then
state_next <= data;
elsif (syn_pulsecount_reg = 15) then
pulse_next    <= (others => '0');
databit_next <= rec_bit & databit_reg (7 downto 1);
if (syn_bitcount_reg = 7) then
state_next  <= stop;
bit_next     <= (others => '0');
else
state_next <= data;       bit_next <= syn_bitcount_reg + 1;
end if;
else
state_next <= data;       pulse_next <= syn_pulsecount_reg + 1;
end if;
when stop =>
if (syn_pulse = '0') then
state_next <= stop;
elsif (syn_pulsecount_reg = 15) then
state_next  <= idle;
pulse_next <= (others => '0');
else
state_next <= stop;       pulse_next <= syn_pulsecount_reg + 1;
end if;
end case;
end process;
pout <= databit_reg;
end arch_rtl_uart_rec_data_path;
--rtl_uart_rec_control_path.vhd
library ieee;
use ieee.std_logic_1164.all;
use ieee.std_logic_arith.all;
use ieee.std_logic_unsigned.all;
entity rtl_uart_rec_control_path is
port (clk, reset : in std_logic);
end rtl_uart_rec_control_path;
architecture arch_rtl_uart_rec_control_path of rtl_uart_rec_control_path is
type state_type is (idle, start, data, stop);
signal syn_pulse                                  : std_logic;
signal clk16_reg, clk16_next                : unsigned (5 downto 0);
constant dvsr                                       : integer := 52;
signal state_reg, state_next                  : state_type;
signal syn_pulsecount_reg, pulse_next : unsigned (3 downto 0);
signal syn_bitcount_reg, bit_next         : unsigned (2 downto 0);
signal databit_reg, databit_next           : std_logic_vector (7 downto 0);

--- Page 1222 ---
Chapter 14 - VHDL 14.131
begin
-- free running mod-52 counter, independent of fsmd.
process (clk, reset)
begin
if (reset = '1') then
clk16_reg <= (others => '0');
elsif (clk'event and clk = '1') then
clk16_reg <= clk16_next;
end if;
if (reset = '1') then
state_reg                 <= idle;
syn_pulsecount_reg <= (others => '0');
syn_bitcount_reg     <= (others => '0');
databit_reg              <= (others => '0');
elsif (clk'event and clk = '1') then
state_reg                  <= state_next;
syn_pulsecount_reg <= pulse_next;
syn_bitcount_reg     <= bit_next;
databit_reg              <= databit_next;
end if;
end process;
--next state/output logic
clk16_next <= (others => '0') when clk16_reg = (dvsr - 1) 
else clk16_reg + 1;
syn_pulse <= '1' when clk16_reg = 0 else '0';    
end arch_rtl_uart_rec_control_path;
--rtl_rtl_uart_rec.vhd top module of VHDL program
--rtl_ uart_rec._data_path.vhd and rtl_ uart_rec. control_path.vhd are added as components in this top module

use ieee.std_logic_arith.all;
use ieee.std_logic_unsigned.all;

port ( clk, reset, rec_bit : in std_logic;
          ready                   : out std_logic; 
          pout                      : out std_logic_vector (7 downto 0) );
end rtl_uart_rec;
architecture arch_rtl_uart_rec of rtl_uart_rec is
component rtl_uart_rec_data_path
port ( clk, reset, rec_bit : in std_logic;
           ready                  : out std_logic; 
           pout                    : out std_logic_vector (7 downto 0) );
end component;
component rtl_uart_rec_control_path
port (clk, reset: in std_logic);      
end component;

                                                             ready => ready, pout => pout);
c1 : rtl_uart_rec_control_path port map (clk => clk, reset => reset);
end arch_rtl_uart_rec;
14.15  Summary of Important Concepts
1. VHDL is an acronym for VHSlC (Very High Speed Inte grated Circuits) Hardware Description Language.
2. VHDL is used to model a digital system at multiple levels of abstraction.
3. VHDL supports four levels of abstraction for digital system design: Transistor level, gate level, register-  
 transfer level (RTL), processor level.
4. In transistor level abstraction, basic building blocks are basic electronic components like transistors,  
 resistors, capacitors, etc.
5. In gate level abstraction, basic building blocks are logic gates, flip-flops, multiplexers, etc. 
6. In register-transfer level (RTL) abstraction, the basic building blocks are modules developed using  
 registers, adders, multiplexers, etc. 
7. The RTL abstraction can be called as module-level abstraction. 
8. In processor level abstraction, basic building blocks are processor s, memory modules, bus interfaces, etc.      
9. The basic elements of the VHDL language are literals, comments, identifiers, data objects and operators.
10. Explicit data values that are assigned to objects or used within expressions are called literals.
11. Physical literals are special types of literals used to represent physical quantities such as time, voltage,  
  current, distance, etc. 
12. A comment starts with a minimum of two dashes ( -- ) followed by the text to explain the concepts. 
13. The VHDL IEEE standard package defines a number of  standard data types which are known as predefined  
 data types. 
14. Integer data type is integer decimal number in the range – (2 31 – 1) to + (231 – 1).
15. Enumeration type is associating user defined set of values called enumeration literals to an object. 
16. A composite data type represents a collection of signals or objects. 
17. Composite types can be further classified into array types and record types. 
18. An array type represents a collection of signals or objects belong to a same data type. 
19. A record type represents a collection of signals or objects belong to same or different data types.
20. Data stored as a file in the host environment (the system that simulate and synthesize the code) is called  
 file data type.
21. A constant object is assigned a fixed value and cannot be changed in other part of the code. 
22. A file with a list of input and/or output data can be declared as an object. 
23. The predefined operators in the VHDL language are classified into five categories: logical operators,  
 relational operators, adding operators, multiplying operators, miscellaneous operators.
24. The concurrent statements are used in dataflow architecture. 
25. Signal assignment statements that appear outside of a process are called concurrent signal assignment  
 statements and they are used to assign a value to an object. 

--- Page 1224 ---
Chapter 14 - VHDL 14.133
26. Assertion statements that appear outside of a process are called concurrent assertion statements and they 
 are used to report the error conditions.
27. Configuration is the process of binding a component with an entity and architecture. 
28. A package declaration is used to store a set of common declarations like components, types, procedures,  
 and functions. 
29. A package body is always associated with a package declaration. 
30. A dataflow model specifies the functionality of a design entity or model without specifying the structure  
 of the design.
31. The behavior of the entity is defined using a set of sequentially executed statements.
32. A process statement is the main mechanism used to model the behavior of an entity. 
33. The association-list associates signals in the entity called actuals, with the ports of a component, called  
 locals.
34. A package provides a convenient method to store and share declarations that are common to many design  
 units. 
35. A Package is a VHDL file, contains data types, constants, functions, procedures, etc, that can be shared  
 across many VHDL designs.  
36. A library is a collection of packages that are compiled and stored in a directory in the host environment  
 (or personal computer) in which the VHDL software tool is installed. 
37. The two most commonly used libraries are IEEE and WORK. 
38. A test bench is also a VHDL program that is used to verify the correctness of the VHDL program of the  
 hardware model.  
14.16  Short-Answer Questions
Q14.1 What are components in VHDL?
 Components are reusable VHDL modules compiled as separate entity and can be used in any other structural  
 model of digital systems.
 Instead of coding a complex design in single VHDL Code, it can be divided into sub-modules as components  
 and combine them using port map technique in a main module.
Q14.2 List the operators in VHDL.
 The predefined operators in the VHDL language are classified into the following five categories. 
●  Logical operators   
●  Relational operators 
●  Adding operators   
●  Multiplying operators 
●  Miscellaneous operators 
Q14.3 Define data objects in VHDL.
 Data object or simply object is an identifier that holds a specific data type, which is declared while creating 
 the object. A data object is created by declaring the class, identifier/name, data type and optional initial value.

Q14.16 State the purpose of test bench.
 A test bench is also a VHDL program that is used to verify the correctness of the VHDL program of the  
 hardware model. A test bench VHDL program has three main purposes: 
 1.  Generation of necessary inputs and clock for simulation.
 2.  Apply this inputs and clock to the entity under test and to monitor the output
 3.  Comparing the output of VHDL program model with expected output.

Verilog
15.1  Introduction to Verilog
Hardware Description Languages (HDLs) are modelling language specially developed to describe 
digital hardware structures and to study the behavior of logic circuits. It can be used to implement logic 
circuits, truth tables, Boolean functions and state tables/diagrams as computer programs for simulation 
and verification.
Verilog is a standardized Hardware Description Language (HDL). The name Verilog is the 
combination of two words “verification” and “logic”. 
Verilog was first developed as a proprietary HDL by Gateway automation system in the period 
1983 to 1990 and later acquired by Cadence design system in 1990. In order to popularize the Verilog, 
the Cadence system, transfer the Verilog to a public domain under the name Open Verilog International 
(OVI). Verilog was later submitted to IEEE for standardization and became IEEE Standard 1364-1995. 
Since 1995, IEEE keeps on updating the Verilog and latest update released in December-2023.
The basic structure of Verilog language is a module. Every Verilog program file will have a module 
which starts with keyword module and end with keyword endmodule. The entire Verilog code or program is 
enclosed by the keywords module and endmodule and every line of the code is terminated by a semicolon (;).
 Verilog language supports designing a module using several coding styles. Depending on the needs 
of a design, internals of each module can be defined at different levels of abstractions. Irrespective of the 
internal abstraction level, the module would behave exactly in the similar way to the external environment. 
The various levels of abstraction are common to VHDL and Verilog and hence refer Chapter 14, 
Section 14.1 for various levels of abstraction.
15.2  Elements of Verilog Language
The coding style of Verilog mostly resembles C and C++ language. Verilog is case sensitive language 
and hence lower case and upper case characters are distinguishable. The blank spaces are ignored but blank 
spaces are not allowed in identifiers, keywords and numbers.
The basic elements of Verilog language are,
●  Identifiers  ●  Keywords
●  Comments  ●  Logic values
●  Numbers  ●  Operators
●  Data types
CHAPTER 15

15.2.1  Identifiers
Identifiers are name of objects that are used in Verilog programs . Identifiers are formed using 
English letters/alphabets, decimal numbers and underscore. Special characters except dollar sign ($) are 
not allowed in identifiers. Reserved words of Verilog language cannot be used as identifiers. The list of 
reserved words is listed in Table 15.1. 
Identifiers are case sensitive and hence uppercase and lower case letters are not equivalent. Identifiers 
that start with a dollar sign refer to built-in system functions.
The identifiers have to satisfy the following rules.
●  Identifiers can have only English letters, decimal numbers, dollar and underscore. 
●  First character of an identifier must be an alphabet or an underscore. 
●  Last character of an identifier cannot be an underscore.
●  Identifiers cannot have two underscore in succession.

15.2.3  Comments
Comments are texts that are added as explanations, wherever necessary. Comments can be single 
line comment or multiline comments. A single line comment starts with a minimum of two slashes (//) 
followed by the text to explain the concepts. Multiline begin with /* and terminate with */. The comments 
are provided for explaining the various concepts of Verilog program and hence, comments are ignored 
while compiling the code.

The bitwise logical operators will perform bit by bit logical operation of two n-bit data and generates 
an n-bit result. The reduction operators will perform logical operation on n-bit data and generates 1-bit 
result either true or false. The bitwise and reduction operations are used in assignment statements. The 
logical operators are used in conditional statements to operate on two variables and determine the true or 
false condition.
The arithmetic operators are used to perform binary arithmetic. The concatenation operator is used 
to combine or join two binary data. The conditional operator is used to check true or false condition of a 
variable and execute a statement for true condition or execute an alternative statement for false condition. 
The format of condition statement with condition operator is,
A ? statement_B : statement_C ;
If A is true then statemet_B is executed and if A is false then statement_C is executed. This condition 
statement is another form of if-else statement.

In Verilog every signal, constant, variable and function must be assigned a data type. The data type

data types. The data types of Verilog can be classified into two groups: Net type and Variable type.

Scalars and Vectors
The data types can be a single bit or group of bits. A single bit data type is called scalar and group 
of bits are called vectors. A vector is n-bit wide binary. All data types net, variables and constants can be 
declared as vectors. 
Syntax of vector
data_type [msb : lsb] vector_name;
Example of vector
reg [3 : 0] P_state;        // P_state is a 4-bit vector of data type reg.
wire [7 : 0] sum;          // sum is an 8-bit vector of data type wire.
Individual bit of a vector can be accessed by its bit index. For example, if a variable named count is 
declared as 4-bit vector then each bit of count can be accessed as count[3], count[2], count[1] and count[0].
Array
An array is a set of variables of the same type. In Verilog, arrays allow grouping of multiple variables 
of the same type under a single name and each variable accessible by an index. Arrays are useful for storing 
collections of related data and individual data is accessed by an array index. The elements of array can be 
1-bit or n-bit wide. 
Syntax of array
reg                   identifier [start : end];
reg [msb : lsb]  identifier [start : end];
integer             identifier [start : end];
Example of array
integer [3 : 0] count [0 : 7];        // array of 8 variables named count of size 4-bits.
reg [7 : 0] port_id [0 : 7];            // array of 8 variables named port_id of size 8-bits.  
Individual elements of an array can be accessed by its array index. For example, if a variable named 
port_id is declared as an array of 8 variables then each element of the array port_id can be accessed as 
port_id [7], port_id [6], port_id [5]……… port_id [0].
15.4.1  Net Data Types
Net type signals represent physical connections between the hardware components in a digital circuit. 
The simplest of net data type is wire. The signals in an input/output port list of a module in Verilog code 
is by default wire and it can be changed by declaring other net data type. The net data types can be either 
single bit data or n-bit vector data. The net data types in Verilog are listed in Table 15.6.

--- Page 1238 ---

15.4.2  Variable Data Types
Variables are used for computation, manipulation and temporary storage of data during program 
execution. A variable’s value can be changed only within procedural code of a module and it cannot be 
changed outside the module. Therefore, input and inout ports cannot be variables. But the output port can 
be either net data type or variable data type. The various variable data types are reg, integer, real, string, 
time, realtime and parameter.  
Data type reg, integer and real
The reg data type is the basic and most fundamental data type to hold or store 1-bit or n-bit binary 
in different formats. The variables declared as reg data type can be used to exchange data during program 
execution and output data to output port. 
The integer data type is used to hold or store decimal values as signed or unsigned 32 bit integer.
The real data type is used to hold or store decimal values with integer and fraction part separated 
by decimal point. The real data type is also used to hold or store decimal values in floating point format.
Example of reg, integer and real data types
reg  sum;                // sum is 1-bit reg variable
reg [3 : 0] sum;      // sum is 4-bit reg variable
integer count;        // count is 32-bit integer variable
real power;  // power is a real variable
String
The reg variables are used to store strings in Verilog. The reg variable should be declared with enough 
size to hold the string. Each character in a string represents an ASCII value and requires 1 byte or 8-bit.

Time and Realtime 
The time and realtime are special data types used for representing time-related values in simulations. 
They are useful for modeling delays, timing checks, and other time-sensitive operations. A time variable 
is unsigned 64 bits and can be used to store simulation time quantities for debugging purposes. A realtime 
variable simply stores time as a floating point quantity.
Example of time, realtime
time delay_time;                        // declare a variable delay_time with integer time values.
time delay_time = 20ns;         // time variable initialized with a value 20 nano-seconds.
realtime start_time, end_time;  // two time variables are declared to record the start
                                                   // and end time of simulation in real number format

A parameter data object defines an integer constant. The parameter declaration includes one or 
more identifier with a constant value assigned to each identifier and the identifier can be used in place of 
the constant throughout the module.
Syntax of parameter 
parameter identifier = value;     // declaring single parameter
parameter identifier = value;  identifier =  value;
             …………………………………..
             identifier = value;     // declaring multiple parameters
Example of parameter
parameter address_size = 16;    // declaring an 16-bit address size.
parameter bus_size = 32;           // declaring a 32-bit width bus size.

15.5.1  User Defined Primitive (UDP)
Truth tables can be implemented as user defined primitives in Verilog program. 
The user defined primitive starts with the keyword primitive and ends with the keyword endprimitive 
and do not have a module. Therefore, the primitive has to be inserted before the module in a program in 
which the truth table has to be instantiated. 
The keyword primitive is followed by a name and port list and declaration of output and inputs. Then 
the truth table is created in the same format followed in this book and enclosed by the keyword table and 
endtable. One UDP can have only one output and hence, when there are multiple outputs separate UDP 
has to be created for each output.

//User defined primitive for the truth table of the above Boolean function
primitive UDP_F1 (F1, A, B, C);

       // A B C : F1  --Header for truth table

15.6  Verilog Statements and Loops
Verilog statements can be classified as follows,
●  Continuous assignment statement
●  Procedural statements
○  Continuous assignment, Blocking and nonblocking statements. 
●  Conditional Statements
○  If-else and case statements
●  Loop Statements
○  While, for, forever and repeat statements
15.6.1  Continuous Assignment Statement
 Continuous assignment statements can be used to develop code for combinational circuit in terms 
of the flow of data and operations on the circuit. A continuous assignment statement evaluates the value 
of the expression on its right hand side and assigns it to the variable on left hand side. The continuous 
assignment statements is prefixed with keyword assign.

--- Page 1242 ---
Chapter 15 - Verilog 15.11
Syntax of continuous assignment statement
assign net_name = expression;
assign net_name [bit_index] = expression; 
assign net_name [msb : lsb] = expression;
Verilog Program 15.2
//Example of program with continuous assignment statement
//Refer Chapter 5, Section 5.9.2 for design of full adder
module full_adder (a, b, cin, sum, cout);
input wire  a, b, cin;
output wire  sum, cout;
assign sum = a ^ b ^ cin;
assign cout = (a & b) | (b & cin) | (cin & a);
end module
15.6.2  Procedural Assignment Statement
Procedural assignment occur within procedures such as always, initial, task and functions and are 
used to attach values to variables. They are used to evaluate an expression and assign the value obtained 
by evaluation of the expression to a variable. 
There are two types of procedural assignment statements: Blocking and Nonblocking assignment 
statements. The blocking statements are evaluated s equentially and values assigned sequentially. The 
nonblocking statements are evaluated concurrently and assigned after evaluation of all the expressions.
Syntax of procedural statement
variable_name = expression;    // blocking assignment
variable_name <= expression;  // nonblocking assignment
Example of blocking procedural statement
------------------------------------------------------
------------------------------------------------------
always @ (posedge clk) begin
A  =  B;    
C  =  A;      
end
------------------------------------------------------
------------------------------------------------------
Note: In this example, first value of B is assigned to A and then value of A is assigned 
to C. Hence, C will have the value of B.
Example of nonblocking procedural statement
------------------------------------------------------
always @ (posedge clk) begin
A  <=  B;     
C  <=  A;    
end
------------------------------------------------------
Note: In this example, the value of B is assigned to A and the value of A is assigned to 
C concurrently. Hence, C will have the old value of A.

--- Page 1243 ---

15.6.3  If and If-else Statement
The if statement is used to execute one or more statements when a condition specified in the if 
statement is true. When one or more statements are to be executed for false condition then else statement 
can be used after if statement. When more than one statement are to be executed after if condition or else 
condition then the statements has to be enclosed by keywords begin and end.
The if-else statement will have one if (condition) statement, one or more else if (condition) statement 
and one optional else statement. At any one time only one condition will be true and hence the statements 
followed by the true condition are executed. If no condition is true then the statements followed by else 
will be executed and if there is no else statement then no statement will be executed.
Syntax of  if and if-else statement

           statement;

statement2;

statement1;
statement2;
            …………………………
end
Syntax-4

begin
statement11;
statement12;
…………………………
end
else
begin
statement21;
statement22;
                  …………………………
end

15.6.4  Case Statement
A case statement will check the value of an expression or object that can take multiple values. At 
any one time only one value will be true and one (or a set of) sequential statement after the true case is 
executed. The values of the expression or object are denoted as choice_1 to choice_n and an optional 
default choice. If none of the case is true then the default choice is executed. This statement begins with 
the keyword is case and terminate with keyword end case. 
 The case statement has two other variants casex and casez.  The casex treats x and z logic values 
as x and casez treats z as x while checking the value of expression or object specified in the statement.
Syntax of case statement
case (expression)
choice_1: procedural_statements;
choice_2: procedural_statements;
………………………………….
………………………………….
choice_n: procedural_statements;
default : procedural_statement
endcase
Note: The syntax for casex and casez statements is same as case statement except 
that case is replaced by casex or casez.
Syntax of casex statement
casex (expression)
choice_1: procedural_statements;
choice_2: procedural_statements;
………………………………….
………………………………….
choice_n: procedural_statements;
default : procedural_statement
endcase
Syntax of casez statement
casez (expression)
choice_1: procedural_statements;
choice_2: procedural_statements;
………………………………….
………………………………….
choice_n: procedural_statements;
default : procedural_statement
endcase

module encoder_4_2 (d_in, d_out);
