15.6.5  While Loop
The while loop will test a condition and executes the statements enclosed by while loop as long as 
the condition is true. When the condition is false the program execution will come out of the while loop.
Syntax of while loop
while (logical-expression)
begin
procedural_statements;
end
Example of while loop
while (count < 10)                     // increment count value as long as
begin                                 // count is less than 10
count = count + 1;
end         
15.6.6  For Loop
The for loop will have a loop index to keep track of the number of times the statements enclosed 
by for loop has to be executed. The loop index will have an initial value, final value and increment value.
The loop index is initialized with initial value and incremented each time after execution of the 
statements enclosed by for loop. The execution of statements enclosed by for loop continues till the loop 
index reaches final value. 
Syntax of for loop
for (index = initial_value;  final_value_of_index;  index = index + increment value;)
              procedural_statement;
end

--- Page 1247 ---
15.16                                              Digital Logic Circuits
Example of for loop
for (j = 0 ; j < 16; j = j + 2)    // loop index j is initialized with a value 0 and incremented
       a <= a + 1;                       // by 2 after each execution of the statement enclosed by 
      end                                        // for loop. The execution continues until j is less than 16
15.6.7  Forever and Repeat Loop
The forever loop is used to execute the statements enclosed by forever loop continuously until the 
program execution is stopped. The forever loop is used to generate clock signals. The repeat loop is used 
to execute the statements enclosed by repeat loop a finite number of times specified in the statement. The 
forever and repeat loop will execute the statements without checking any condition.
Syntax of forever loop
forever
begin
procedural_statements;
end
Example of forever loop
initial 
begin
clock = 0;                     // clock signal is initialized to 0 (low)
forever
#5 clock = ~clock;  // clock signal is continuously complemented in a        
end                                   // time of 5 nano-sec so that clock signal will be   
                              // high and low alternatively for 5 nano-sec and 
                              // time period of clock will be 10 nano-sec and 
                              // frequency of clock is 1/10 nano-sec = 10 MHz 
Syntax of repeat loop
repeat (integer_constant)
begin 
procedural_statements;
end 
Example of repeat loop
if (rotate = = 1) begin
repeat(8)                             // if rotate = 1, execute the statements enclosed by
begin                                 // repeat loop 8 times
tmp = data[15];
data = data << 1 + tmp;
 end
end
15.7  Function in Verilog
The function in Verilog is like a subroutine in a programming language. The repeated computation 
of a variable value using a group of statements are coded separately as a function and used any number 
times in a main program.   

--- Page 1248 ---
Chapter 15 - Verilog 15.17
Functions in Verilog are used to code a block of procedural statements that computes a value based on 
the inputs and return a single value (bit, integer, vector, etc.). In Verilog functions, timing control statements 
and continuous assignment statements are not allowed. Functions are typically used for combinatorial logic 
that involves repeated computations.
Syntax of function declaration
function   result_type/size   function_name;
input declarations;
local variable declarations;
parameter declarations;
procedural_statements;
end function
Verilog Program 15.5
//Example of program with function
//Program for full adder using half adder
//Refer Chapter 5, Section 5.9.2, for design of full adder using half adder
module FA_with_function_HA
( input wire a, b, ci,
  output reg s, co);
  reg s1, c1, c2;
  always @ (a, b, ci)
  begin 
s1 = ha_s (a, b);
c1 = ha_co (a, b);
s = ha_s (s1, ci);
c2 = ha_co(s1, ci);
co = c1 | c2; 
        end
        function ha_s;
        input wire a, b;
            ha_s = a ^ b;
        endfunction
        function ha_co;
        input wire a, b;
            ha_co = a & b;
        endfunction
endmodule
15.8  Task in Verilog
The task is a subroutine equivalent to a module that is written inside the main module and can be 
called in a Verilog main module code any number of times. Task is a complete Verilog code similar to a 
module and enclosed with keyword task and endtask instead of module and endmodule. 

--- Page 1249 ---
15.18                                              Digital Logic Circuits
Whenever a component of a digital system are repeatedly used in the system, then the code of that 
component is developed separately as a task and used any number times in a main program. Tasks are 
used for modeling components of both combinational and sequential logic that are used in the system a 
number of times.
Syntax of task declaration
task task_name;
Input declarations;
Inout declarations;
Output declarations;
Variable declarations;
Parameter declarations;
Procedural_statements;
end task
Verilog Program 15.6
//Example of program with task
//Program for full adder using half adder
//Refer Chapter 5, Section 5.9.2, for design of full adder using half adder
module FA_with_task_HA
( input wire a, b, ci,
  output reg s, co);
  reg s1, c1, c2;
  always @ (a, b, ci)
  begin 
ha (a, b, s1, c1);
ha (s1, ci, s, c2);
co = c1 | c2; 
        end
        task ha;
        input wire a, b;
        output reg ha_s, ha_so;
        begin
ha_s = a^ b;
ha_co = a & b;
end 
endtask 
endmodule
15.9  Timescale and Timing Control
The Verilog has a timescale compiler directive.
Syntax of timescale directive
`timescale     time_unit/time_precision
The default time scale in Vivado HDL simulation tool is `timescale 1 ns/1 ps.
The default time scale is followed in all Verilog programs in this book.

--- Page 1250 ---
Chapter 15 - Verilog 15.19
The timing control refers to various methods used to control the timing of the behavior of signals 
and events in a digital system. The Verilog language provides the following three methods of timing control 
during execution of procedural statements. 
●  delay control
●  event control 
●  wait statement
15.9.1  Delay Control (#)
A delay control expression specifies the time duration to be delayed for execution of the statement. 
Syntax for delay control:     
#<time>   <statement>;
Example of delay control:
#10   a = a + 2;  // a = a + 2 will be executed after a delay time of 10 time units
                          // default time unit is nano-second
15.9.2  Event Control
An event control is used to control the execution of a procedural statement at the occurrence of the 
named event.
Syntax for event control:       
@ (event_name);
Examples of event control:
@r begin  a = b & c; end        //a = b & c is executed only if there is a change in r
@(posedge clock) a = b & c;   //a = b & c is executed only at positive edge of clock
@(negedge clock) a = b & c;   //a = b & c is executed only at negative edge of clock 
15.9.3  Wait Statement
The wait statement allows a procedural statement or a block of statements to be delayed until a 
condition become true.
Syntax for wait statement:       
wait    <statement> ;
Example of wait statement:
wait (r == 3) begin a = b & c; end     //a = b & c is executed only when r = 3
15.10  Verilog Program Structure
A Verilog program starts with a keyword module and ends with a keyword endmodule. The module 
will include the following elements.
● Declarations     
● Procedural blocks    
□  Initial and always blocks    
■ Procedural statements

--- Page 1251 ---
15.20                                              Digital Logic Circuits
15.10.1  Module
The module is the main unit of the Verilog program and one program can have only one module. 
The entire Verilog code or program is enclosed by the keywords module and endmodule and every line 
of the code is terminated by a semicolon (;).
The module represents a component of a digital system or the entire digital system. For large digital 
systems, Verilog supports modular programming in which the system with large number of components 
are coded such that each component is coded as a separate module and compiled and then all the modules 
of components are instantiated in a main module.
A name is attached to every module in order to identity the digital component or system represented 
by the module. Every module requires a port list (or list of inputs and outputs) that act as the interface 
between program and the external environment. Each port has a mode or direction and they are  input, 
output or inout. 
Syntax for module:
module <module name> <port list>;
<input and output declaration of port list>
<module blocks and statements>
endmodule
Example of module:
module full_adder (a, b, ci, s, co);
input wire a, b, ci;
output wire s, co;
<module blocks and statements>
endmodule
The module includes one or more always and initial block. The statements of both these blocks are 
enclosed by the keywords begin and end. Each initial block is executed once and always block is executed 
again and again until the program execution is stopped.
15.10.2  Declarations
The declarations refer to input and output declarat ions and their data type declarations. The 
declarations are also made for intermediate variables, constants, functions and task.
Syntax of input and output declarations
input wire   identifier,  identifier, …,  identifier;                   //declaring 1-bit inputs and outputs
output wire identifier, identifier, …,  identifier;
output reg   identifier, identifier, …,  identifier;
inout wire   identifier,  identifier, …,  identifier;
input wire   [msb:lsb]   identifier, identifier, …,  identifier;  //declaring vector inputs and outputs
output wire [msb:lsb]   identifier, identifier, …,  identifier;
output reg   [msb:lsb]   identifier, identifier, …,  identifier;
inout wire   [msb:lsb]   identifier, identifier, …,  identifier;

--- Page 1252 ---
Chapter 15 - Verilog 15.21
15.10.3  Initial Block
The initial blocks are primarily used to initialize variables and ports with specific values. An initial 
block executes only once, at the beginning of simulation. A module can have any number of initial blocks. 
When initial block has multiple statements, they are enclosed by the keywords begin and end. 
Syntax of initial block with single statement
initial
procedural_assignment_statement;
Syntax of initial block with multiple statements
initial 
begin
procedural_assignment_statement;
.....................................................
procedural_assignment_statement;
end
Example of initial block 
module stimulus ( );
reg a, b, m;
initial
m = 1’b0;    // variable m is initialized with value 0.
initial
begin
a = 1’b1;     // variable a is initialized with value 1.
b = 1’b0;     // variable b is initialized with value 0.
end
end module
15.10.4  Always Block
The always blocks are used to enclose the executable statements of the Verilog code. The always 
block is executed repeatedly throughout the simulation. A module can have any number of always blocks. 
When always block has multiple statements, they are enclosed by the keywords begin and end.
Event Control in Always Block
Since always block is executed continuously, an event control is specified to control the execution 
of always block. Mostly event controls are changes in clock, reset and inputs. Most popular events are 
positive edge (posedge) of clock signal or negative edge (negedge) of clock signal.
Syntax for always block:
always @ (event1, event2, …….) begin
<procedural statements> 
end
Example of always block: 
always @ (posedge clock) begin
< procedural statements> 
end

--- Page 1253 ---
15.22                                              Digital Logic Circuits
15.11  Types of Program Modeling in Verilog
Verilog supports the following three basic models for design of a digital system.
●  Dataflow model
●  Behavior model
●  Structural model
The input, output and signal declarations are common for all the above three basic types of Verilog 
program models of digital systems. 
15.11.1  Dataflow Model
The dataflow model describes how data flows through the design. In data flow model, the relationship 
between input and output signals is expressed using Boolean equations. 
In dataflow model, the continuous assignment (assign statement) is used to assign values to outputs 
and these assignment statements are executed concurrently.
Dataflow models are useful for design of combinational logic circuits, where the output depends 
only on the current values of the inputs and not on any previous values.
15.11.2  Behavior Model
The behavior model of digital system employs a set of sequentially or concurrently executed 
statements. The statements like if-else, case, for, while, etc., are used to describe the behavior of the system. 
The statements of behavior model also enclosed by an initial block which is executed once or enclosed by 
an always block which is executed repeatedly.
15.11.3  Structural Model
In structural model, a digital system is designed with the set of components connected by signals. 
Components are separate Verilog modules and compiled separately and can be used in any other structural 
model of digital systems.
Instead of coding a complex design in single Verilog module, it can be divided into a number of 
separate modules as components and combine them using port map technique in a main module. The 
component declaration and component instantiation statements are the primary structures used to describe 
the design in main module.
 In structural model, the primitive gates can be directly used without a code as separate module and 
its instantiation.
Verilog Program 15.7
//Verilog program to demonstrate dataflow, behavioral and structural model
//Program for half adder
//Refer Chapter 5, Section 5.9.1, for design of half adder

--- Page 1254 ---
Chapter 15 - Verilog 15.23

module dfm_half_adder (a, b, s, co);
input wire a, b;
output wire s, co;
assign s = a ^ b;
assign co = a & b;
endmodule
Verilog Program for Behavioral Model of Half Adder
module bm_half_adder (a, b, s, co);
input wire a, b; 
output reg s, co;
always @(a or b)
begin
s   = a ^ b;
co = a & b;
end
endmodule

15.12  Test Bench
A test bench is also a Verilog program that is used to verify the correctness of the Verilog program 
of the hardware model. A test bench Verilog program has three main purposes: 
● Generating inputs and clock signal for simulation of the hardware model.
● Apply this inputs and clock to the module under test and to monitor the output
● Comparison of the output of Verilog program model with expected output. 
The application of inputs and clock to the module under test is accomplished automatically by 
instantiating the module in the test bench model and then specifying the appropriate interface signals.
In test bench, inputs are declared as reg and the signals connected to output are declared as wire. 
The initial block is used specify or apply the inputs to generate the outputs.
In test bench the system command $finish is used to terminate the clock and test inputs.

Verilog Program for Dataflow Model of Boolean Function
module dfm_boolean_func
( input a, b, c, d,
  output f);
  wire m1, m2, m3;
   wire f1, f2, f3, f4;
  assign m1 = ~a;                assign m2 = ~b;         assign m3 = ~d;
  assign f1 = a & m2;          assign f2 = b & d;
  assign f3 = m1 & b & c;    assign f4 = m2 & m3;
  assign f = f1 | f2 | f3 | f4;  
endmodule

Program Logic for Behavioral Model of Square of 3-bit Binary 
Using Fig. 6, the Verilog codes for behavioral model of combinational circuit is developed.
Verilog Program for Behavioral Model of Square of 3-bit Binary
module bm_square_3bit
( input a, b, c,
        output b0, b1, b2, b3, b4, b5 );
  reg b0, b1, b2, b3, b4, b5;
  reg m1, m2;
always @ (a or b or c) begin
m1 = (~a) & b;
m2 = a & (~b);
b0 = c;
b1 = 1'b0;
b2 = b & (~c);
b3 = (m1 & c) | (m2 & c);
b4 = (a & c) | m2;
b5 = a & b;
end
endmodule

Verilog Program 15.10
Write Verilog code for dataflow, behavioral and structural models of a 2-to-4 decoder. 
Program Logic for Dataflow and Behavioral Model
 The Boolean equations for 2-to-4 decoder are,
Y0 = I1' . I0'    ;   Y1 = I1' . I0   ;   Y2 = I1 . I0'    ;    Y3 = I1 . I0 
 Where, I1 and I0 are 1-bit input data and Y0, Y1, Y2 and Y3 are 1-bit output data. The Verilog codes for 
dataflow and behavioral model of 2-to-4 decoder are developed using the above equations. (Refer Chapter 5, 
Section 5.4.1 for design of 2-to-4 decoder).
Verilog Program for Dataflow Model of 2-to-4 Decoder
module dfm_decoder_2_4
( input i1, i0, 
  output y0, y1, y2, y3 );
  wire m1, m2;     
  wire y0, y1, y2, y3;
  assign  m1 = ~i1;     assign m2 = ~i0;
  assign y0 = m1 & m2;
  assign y1 = m1 & i0; 
  assign y2 = i1 & m2;
  assign y3 = i1 & i0;      
endmodule
Verilog Program for Behavioral Model of 2-to-4 Decoder using “case” Statement
module bm_decoder_2_4  
( input [1:0] i,
        output [3:0] y );
        reg[3:0] y;
        always @ (i) begin
        case (i)
2'b00 : y = 4'b0001;
2'b01 : y = 4'b0010;
2'b10 : y = 4'b0100;
2'b11 : y = 4'b1000;
// default : y = 4'b0000;
endcase
end
endmodule
Verilog Program for Behavioral Model of 2-to-4 Decoder using “if elsif” Statement
module bm_decoder_2_4
( input [1:0] i,
  output [3:0] y);
        reg [3:0] y;
  always @ (i)
  begin

Chapter 15 - Verilog 15.29
if (i == 2'b00)           y = 4'b0001;
else if (i == 2'b01)   y = 4'b0010;
else if (i == 2'b10)   y = 4'b0100;
else                          y = 4'b1000;
end
endmodule
Program Logic for Structural Model
The Verilog code for structural model of 2-to-4 decoder is 
developed using the logic circuit shown in Fig. 1. The AND and 
NOT  gates in the logic circuit of Fig. 1 are modeled using primitive 
AND and NOT gates in verilog.
Program for Structural Model of 2-to-4 Decoder
module sm_decoder_2_4
( input [1:0] i,
        output [3:0] y );
        wire m0, m1;
        not G1 (m1, i[1]);
        not G2 (m0, i[0]);
        and G3 (y[0], m1, m0);
        and G4 (y[1], m1, i[0]);
        and G5 (y[2], i[1], m0);
        and G6 (y[3], i[1], i[0]);
endmodule

Verilog Program 15.12
Write a Verilog code for dataflow and structural models of a 4-to-2 encoder.
Program Logic for Dataflow Model
The Boolean equations for 4-to-2 encoder are,
Y1 = I2 + I3   ;   Y0 = I1 + I3
Where, I0, I1, I2 and I3 are 1-bit input data, Y0 and Y1 are 1-bit output data. The Verilog code for

Boolean equations for priority encoder with I3 having highest priority and I0 having lowest priority are,
Y1 = I2 + I3      
Y0 = I1.I2' + I3    
v = I0 + I1 + I2 + I3
Where, I0, I1, I2 and I3 are 1-bit input data and Y0, Y1 and v are 1-bit output data. The Verilog code for

( input i0, i1, i2, i3,
        output y0, y1, v );

  assign m1 = ~i2;
        assign y1 = i2 | i3;
        assign y0 = ( i1 & m1 ) | i3 ;
        assign v  = i0 | i1 | i2 | i3;
endmodule

b) Verilog program for structural model of 4-bit parallel adder using function.
module par_add_4bit_function
( input wire [3:0] A,
input wire [3:0] B,
input wire ci,
output reg [3:0] s,
output reg co );
reg m0, m1, m2;  
always @ (A, B, ci)
begin
s[0] = fa_s (A[0], B[0], ci);
m0  = fa_co (A[0], B[0], ci);
s[1] = fa_s (A[1], B[1], m0);
m1  = fa_co (A[1], B[1], m0);
s[2] = fa_s (A[2], B[2], m1);
m2  = fa_co (A[2], B[2], m1);
s[3] = fa_s (A[3], B[3], m2);
co   = fa_co (A[3], B[3], m2);
end
function fa_s;
input wire a, b, ci;
fa_s = a ^ b ^ ci;
endfunction
function fa_co;
input wire a, b, ci;
fa_co = (a & b) | (b & ci) | (ci & a);
endfunction
endmodule

Verilog Program 15.19
Write a Verilog code for dataflow model of a 4-bit CLA (Carry look ahead adder).
Program Logic for Dataflow Model
si = pi ⊕ ci           
ci+1 = gi + pi ci
pi = ai ⊕ bi        
gi = ai bi 
Where, pi is carry propagate from i th stage and g i is carry generate of i th stage. The Verilog code for 
dataflow model of 4-bit CLA is developed using the above equations. (Refer Chapter 5, Section 5.9.4 for design 
of 4-bit CLA).
Verilog Program for Dataflow Model of 4-bit CLA
module dfm_CL_Adder_4bit(a, b, c0, s, c4);
input [3:0] a;
input [3:0] b;
input c0;
output c4;
output [3:0] s;
wire m1, m2, m3, m4, m5, m6, m7;
wire p0, p1, p2, p3;
wire g0, g1, g2, g3;
assign p0 = a[0] ^ b[0],   p1 = a[1] ^ b[1],  p2 = a[2] ^ b[2],  p3 = a[3] ^ b[3];
assign g0 = a[0] & b[0],  g1 = a[1] & b[1],  g2 = a[2] & b[2],  g3 = a[3] & b[3];
assign m1 = g0 | (p0 & c0);
assign m2 = g1 | (p1 & g0) | (p1 & p0 & c0);
assign m3 = g2 | (p2 & g1) | (p2 & p1 & g0) | (p2 & p1 & p0 & c0);
assign s[0] = p0 ^ c0,   s[1] = p1 ^ m1,   s[2] = p2 ^ m2,   s[3] = p3 ^ m3;
assign m4 = (p3 & g2),  m5 = (p3 & p2 & g1),  m6 = (p3 & p2 & p1 & g0);
assign m7 = (p3 & p2 & p1 & p0 & c0);
assign c4 = g3 | m4 | m5 | m6 | m7 ;  
endmodule

Program Logic for Dataflow Model 
Let a and b are 1-bit binary numbers.
The Boolean equations for 1-bit magnitude comparator are,
if a = b,  then (a ⊕ b)'  = 1
if a > b,  then a b'  = 1
if a < b,  then a' b = 1
The Verilog codes for dataflow model of 1-bit magnitude comaparator are developed using the Boolean 
equations. (Refer Chapter 5, Section 5.12 for design of 1-bit magnitude comparator).

( input a, b,
  output wire a_eq_b, a_gt_b, a_lt_b );

  assign a_eq_b = ~(a ^ b);
  assign a_gt_b = a & b_bar;
  assign a_lt_b = a_bar & b;

Verilog Program 15.23
Write a Verilog code for dataflow model of a 3-bit comparator.
Program Logic for Dataflow Model 
Let a and b are 3-bit binary numbers.
The Boolean equations for 3-bit magnitude comparator are,
if a = b,  then (a0 ⊕ b0)' . (a1 ⊕ b1)' . (a2 ⊕ b2)' = 1
if a > b,  then (a2 . b2) + ((a2 ⊕ b2)' . a1 . b1) + ((a2 ⊕ b2)' . (a1 ⊕ b1)' . a0 . b0) = 1        
if a < b,  then (a2 . b2) + ((a2 ⊕ b2)' . a1 . b1) + ((a2 ⊕ b2)' . (a1 ⊕ b1)' . a0 . b0) = 1
The Verilog codes for dataflow model of 3-bit magnitude comparator are developed using the Boolean 
equations. (Refer Chapter 5, Section 5.12.2 for design of 3-bit magnitude comparator).
Verilog Program for Dataflow Model of 3-bit Comparator
module dfm_comparator_3_bit
( input a0, a1, a2, b0, b1, b2,
output wire a_eq_b, a_gt_b, a_lt_b);
wire a0_bar, a1_bar, a2_bar;
wire b0_bar, b1_bar, b2_bar;
wire m0, m1, m2, m3, m4, m5, m6, m7, m8;
assign m0 = ~(a0 ^ b0),  m1 = ~(a1 ^ b1),  m2 = ~(a2 ^ b2);
assign m3 = a2 & b2_bar;
assign m4 = m2 & a1 & b1_bar; 
assign m5 = m2 & m1 & a0 & b0_bar;
assign m6 = a2_bar & b2;
assign m7 = m2 & a1_bar & b1; 
assign m8 = m2 & m1 & a0_bar & b0;
assign a0_bar = ~a0, a1_bar = ~a1, a2_bar = ~a2;
assign b0_bar = ~b0, b1_bar = ~b1, b2_bar = ~b2;
assign a_eq_b = m0 & m1 & m2;
assign a_gt_b = m3 | m4 | m5;
assign a_lt_b = m6 | m7 | m8;
endmodule

  ( input wire a1, a0,
    input wire b1, b0,     
    output reg p0, p1, p2, p3 );
    wire m0, m1, m2, m3;
    reg m4;
    and G1 (m0, a0, b0);
    and G2 (m1, a1, b1);
    and G3 (m2, a1, b0);
    and G4 (m3, a1, b1);
    always @ (m1, m2, p1, p2, p3)
    begin 
p0 = m0;
ha (m1, m2, p1, m4);
ha (m4, m3, p2, p3);
    end
task ha;
input wire a, b;
output reg s, co;
begin
s    = a ^ b;
co = a & b;
end
endtask
endmodule

Verilog Program 15.25
Write a Verilog code for structural model of parity bit generator to generate even and odd 
parity bit for an 8-bit data.
Program Logic for Structural Model
The Verilog code for structural model of parity bit generator for an 8-bit data is developed using the 
logic circuit shown in Fig. 1. The XOR and NOT gates in the logic circuit of Fig. 1 are modeled using primitive 
XOR and NOT gates in verilog. (Refer Chapter 5, Section 5.15.4 for design of parity bit generator).
Verilog Program for Structural Model of Parity Bit Generator
module sm_parity_bit_generate
( input wire [7:0] d,
output wire p_even,
output wire p_odd );
wire m1, m2, m3, m4, m5, m6;
xor G1 (m1, d[0], d[1]);
xor G2 (m2, m1, d[2]);
xor G3 (m3, m2, d[3]);
xor G4 (m4, m3, d[4]);
xor G5 (m5, m4, d[5]);
xor G6 (m6, m5, d[6]);  
xor G7 (p_even, m6, d[7]);   
not G8 (p_odd, p_even);
endmodule

q = 0;   qbar = 1;

end

Verilog Program 15.30
Write Verilog code for dataflow model of a binary to gray code converter. 
Program Logic for Dataflow Model
The following procedure will be useful for bit-by-bit conversion of n-bit binary to n-bit gray code.
Step 1:  The most significant bit of binary and gray code are same. Hence retain the most significant 
bit of binary as most significant bit of gray code.
Step 2:  Starting from most significant bit of binary, add two consecutive bits of binary and record the 
sum as bit of gray code and discard the carry in every addition.
The Verilog code for dataflow model of binary to gray code converter is developed using the above 
procedure. (Refer Chapter 5, Section 5.3 for design of binary to gray code).
Verilog Program for Dataflow Model of Binary to Gray Code
module dfm_bin_gray_code_con
( input    b3, b2, b1, b0,
  output g3, g2, g1, g0 );
  and (g3, b3, b3);
  xor  (g2, b3, b2);
  xor  (g1, b2, b1);
  xor  (g0, b1, b0);
endmodule
Test Bench
module tb_dfm_bin_gray_code_con( );
//Inputs
reg b3;     reg b2;     reg b1;     reg b0;
//Outputs
wire g3;   wire g2;   wire g1;   wire g0;
//Instantiate the unit under test 
dfm_bin_gray_code_con uut
(.b3(b3),  .b2(b2),  .b1(b1),  .b0(b0),  .g3(g3),  .g2(g2),  .g1(g1),  .g0(g0)); 
//Stimulus inputs
initial begin 
          b3 = 1'b0;    b2 = 1'b1;    b1 = 1'b0;     b0 = 1'b1;       
#10    b3 = 1'b0;    b2 = 1'b1;    b1 = 1'b1;     b0 = 1'b1;
#10    b3 = 1'b1;    b2 = 1'b0;    b1 = 1'b0;     b0 = 1'b1;
#10    b3 = 1'b1;    b2 = 1'b0;    b1 = 1'b1;     b0 = 1'b0;
#10 $finish;
end     
endmodule

Write Verilog code for behavioral model of a 2-to-4 decoder. 
Program Logic for Behavioral Model
The Boolean equations for 2-to-4 decoder are,
Y0 = I1' .I0'
Y1 = I1' .I0
Y2 = I1.I0'
Y3 = I1.I0 
 Where, I1 and I0 are 1-bit input data, Y0, Y1, Y2 and Y3 are 1-bit output data. The Verilog code for 
behavioral model of 2-to-4 decoder is developed using the above equations. (Refer Chapter 5, Section 5.4.1

Verilog Program for Behavioral Model of 2-to-4 Decoder
module bm_decoder2_4
( input   i1, i0,
  output y0, y1, y2, y3 );
reg y0, y1, y2, y3;
always @(i1 or i0)
begin
y0 <= (!i1) && (!i0);
y1 <= (!i1) && i0;
y2 <= i1    && (!i0);
y3 <= i1    && i0;
end

Verilog Program 15.33
Write Verilog code for dataflow model of a 4*1 multiplexer. 
Program Logic for Dataflow Model 
The Boolean equations for 4*1 multiplexer are,
Y = S0' .S1' .I0 + S0' .S1.I1 + S0.S1'. I2 + S0.S1.I3 
Where, S0 and S1 are 1-bit selection input, Y is 1-bit output data. The Verilog code for dataflow model 
of 4*1 multiplexer is developed using the above equations. (Refer Chapter 5, Section 5.7 for design of 4*1 
multiplexer).
Verilog Program for Dataflow Model of 4*1 Multiplexer
module dfm_mux_4_1
( input     i0, i1, i2, i3,
  input     s0, s1, 
  output  y );
wire ns0;   wire ns1;
wire m1;   wire m2;   wire m3;   wire m4;
not (ns0, s0);
not (ns1, s1);      
and (m1, ns0, ns1, i0);
and (m2, ns0, s1, i1);
and (m3, s0, ns1, i2);
and (m4, s0, s1, i3);
or    (y, m1, m2, m3, m4);     
endmodule

Verilog Program 15.36
Write Verilog code for behavioral model of a full adder. 
Program Logic for Behavioral Model
 The Boolean equations for full adder are,
s = a ⊕ b ⊕ ci
 co = (a b) + (b ci) + (ci a)
 Where, a, b and c i are 1-bit input data, sum (s) and carry (co) are 1-bit output data. The Verilog code for 
behavioral model of full adder is developed using the above equations. (Refer Chapter 5, Section 5.9.2 for 
design of full adder).
Verilog Program for Behavioral Model of Full Adder
module bm_full_adder
( input    a, b, ci,
        output s, co );
reg s, co;
always @ (a or b or ci)
begin
s   = (a ^ b) ^ ci;
co = (a & b) | (b & ci) | (ci & a);   
end
endmodule

Verilog Program 15.39
Write Verilog code for behavioral model of the Moore FSM given below. 
Program Logic for Behavioral Model
The given Moore FSM has four states. Here, case statement is used to select a current state and the next 
state is decided based on output and input in each case. (Refer Chapter 7, Section 7.2.1 for design of Moore_fsm).
Verilog Program for Behavioral Model of Moore_FSM
module bm_moore_fsm
( input clk,
  input x,
  output y );
reg y;   
reg [1:0] P_state, N_state;
parameter s0 = 2'b00,  s1 = 2'b01,  s2 = 2'b10, s3 = 2'b11; 
initial begin
P_state <= s0;   y <= 1'b0;
end
always @ (posedge clk) begin
P_state <= N_state;
end  
always @ (posedge clk) begin     
case (P_state)
s0: N_state = x ? s1 : s2;   
s1: N_state = x ? s2 : s0; 
s2: N_state = x ? s3 : s3; 
s3: N_state = x ? s0 : s1;
endcase  
case (P_state)
s0: y = 1'b0;  
s1: y = 1'b0;
s2: y = 1'b0; 
s3: y = 1'b1;

                          x = 1    x= 0    x = 1   x = 0
                                                   y         y
         S0                   S1        S2         0          0
         S1                   S2        S0         0          0 
         S2                   S3        S3         0          0
         S3                   S0        S1         1          1

Verilog Program for Behavioral Model of 4-bit up/down Counter
module bm_updown_4bit
( input clk, a,
        output reg [3:0] dout );
initial begin
dout = 4'b0000;
end
always @(posedge clk) begin
if ((a==1) & (clk ==1))      
begin        
dout = dout + 4'b0001;
end
else if ((a==0) & (clk ==1))
begin       
dout = dout - 4'b0001;
end        
else dout = dout;
end
endmodule

module bm_bcd_counter
( input clk,
        output reg [3:0] dout );
initial begin
dout = 4'b0000; 
end 
always @(posedge clk) begin
if ((clk ==1) & (dout == 4'b1001)) 
dout <= 4'b0000;   
else if (clk ==1) 
dout = dout + 4'b0001; 
else dout = dout;
end

Verilog Program 15.44
Write a Verilog code for behavioral model of 8-bit SISO right shift register.
Program Logic for Behavioral Model 
In the Verilog code, an 8-bit buffer is declared to store the 8-bit data. The LSB (Least Significant Bit) of 
8-bit buffer is output as serial output data. The shift operation is performed by concatenation of input data 
bit as MSB (Most Significant Bit) and upper 7-bit of buffer.  (Refer Chapter 8, Section 8.6.1 for right shift SISO 
register.
Verilog Program for Behavioral Model of 8-bit SISO Right Shift Register
module bm_RS_reg
         ( input clk, 
           input reset, 
           input ser_in,
           output reg ser_out,
           output reg [7:0] rs_reg );
initial begin
rs_reg = 8'b11110000;
end

  input ser_in,
  output reg ser_out,
  output reg [7:0] LS_reg );

LS_reg = 8'b11110000;

end

15.15  Summary of Important Concepts
1. The name Verilog is the combination of two words “verification” and “logic”. 
2. The basic structure of Verilog language is a module.
3. The coding style of Verilog mostly resembles C and C++ language. 
4. Verilog is case sensitive language and hence lower case and upper case characters are distinguishable. 
5. A single line comment starts with a minimum of two slashes (//) followed by the text to explain the  
 concepts. Multiline comment begin with /* and terminate with */.
6. Identifiers are formed using English letters/alphabets, decimal numbers and underscore.
7. Special characters except dollar sign ($) are not allowed in identifiers. Reserved words of Verilog language  
 cannot be used as identifiers.
8. Verilog supports four logic values: 0, 1, x, z.
9. The data types of Verilog can be classified into two groups: Net type and Variable type.
55.000 ns
Fig. e: Input: sel = 2 = 10; ser_data_out = 1; 1111 0010(F2 ) leftshift_reg: 1111 1001(F9 ); ser_data_in = 0 .H H
Left shift
45.000 ns
Fig. d: Input: sel = 2 = 01; ser_data_out = 0; 1111 1001(F9 ) leftshift_reg: 0111 1100(7C ); ser_data_in = 1 .H H
Left shift
66.000 ns
Fig. f: Input: Parallel_in = , Sel = 3 = 11; Output: Shift register = AA . HAAH
Fig. 1: Inputs-output waveform of universal shift register .

--- Page 1322 ---
Chapter 15 - Verilog 15.91
10. Net type signals represent physical connections between the hardware components in a digital circuit.
11. Variables are used for computation, manipulation and temporary storage of data during program execution.
12. A parameter data object defines a constant and only integer constants can be attached to a parameter.
13. Verilog primitives are predefined basic building blocks in Verilog HDL. 
14. The 12 Verilog primitive gates are and, nand, or, nor, xor, xnor, not, buf, bufif1, bufif0, notif1, notif0.
15. Truth tables can be implemented as user defined primitives in Verilog program. 
16. Verilog behavioral statements are declared inside an always or initial block.
17. The procedural assignment statements are used to evaluate an expression and assign the value obtained  
 by evaluation of the expression to a variable. 
18. The two types of procedural assignment statements in Verilog are blocking and nonblocking assignment  
 statements.
19. The blocking statements are evaluated sequentially and values assigned sequentially.
20. The nonblocking statements are evaluated concurren tly and assigned after evaluation of all the expressions.
21.  The conditional statements in Verilog are if-else and case statements
22.   The loop statements in Verilog are while, for, forever and repeat statements.
23.   The function in Verilog is like a subroutine in a programming language.
24.   Timing control statements and continuous assignment statements are not allowed in functions.
25.  Task is a complete Verilog code similar to a module and enclosed with keyword task and endtask.
26.  The default time scale in Vivado HDL simulation tool is `timescale 1 ns/1 ps.
27.  A delay control expression specifies the time duration to be delayed for execution of the statement.
28.  An event control is used to control the execution of a procedural statement at the occurrence of the named 
 event.
29.  The wait statement allows a procedural statement or a block of statements to be delayed until a condition 
 become true.
30.  The module is the main unit of the Verilog program and one program can have only one module. 
31.  The entire Verilog code or program is enclosed by the keywords module and endmodule.
32.  Three possible mode or direction a port in Verilog and input, output or inout.
33.  The initial blocks are primarily used to initialize variables and ports with specific values.
34.  The always blocks are used to enclose the executable statements of the Verilog code.
35.  The three types of programming model in Verilog are dataflow, behavioral and structural models.
36.  The dataflow model is direct implementation of Boolean equations of a system.
37.  The behavioral model is implementation of a digital system using procedural statements.
38.  In structural model, a digital system is designed with the set of components connected by signals. 
39.  A test bench is also a Verilog program that is used to verify the correctness of the Verilog program of the  
 hardware model. 
40.  In test bench the system command $finish is used to terminate the clock and test inputs.

15.16  Short-Answer Questions
Q15.1 List the language elements of Verilog.
 The basic elements of Verilog language are, 
●  Identifiers   ●  Keywords 
●  Comments  ●  Logic values
●  Numbers  ●  Operators 
●  Data types
Q15.2 What are the operators group in Verilog?
 The predefined operators in the Verilog HDL language are classified into the following seven groups. 
●  Bitwise/Reduction operators   
●  Logical operators 
●  Arithmetic operators   
●  Relational operators 
●  Shift operators
●  Equality operators
●  Other operators
Q15.3 Write a Verilog program for AND gate.
 module dfm_and_gate (m, n, p);
        input wire  m, n;
        output wire p;
                       assign p  = m & n;
                endmodule

 module dfm_or_gate (m, n, p);

        output wire p;
                       assign p  = m | n;
                endmodule

 module dfm_not_gate (m, p);

Q15.10 How numbers are represented in Verilog?
 In Verilog, the binary, octal, decimal and hexadecimal numbers are represented by the following format.
Number format:  n'  Bv
where,   n = Number of binary digits used to represent the number
              B = Base of number
              v = Value of the number
 The letters b, o, d and h are used to represent the base of binary, octal, decimal and hexadecimal respectively. 
Q15.11 Give one example of binary, octal, decimal and hexadecimal representation in Verilog.
 Binary : 8'b'11101101 - 8-bit binary number 11101101    
 Octal  : 12'o2467 - 4 digit octal number 2467 represented by 12 bit binary  
 Decimal : 6'd32 - 2 digit decimal number 32 represented by 6 bit binary
 Hexadecimal : 16'h3B8C - 4 digit hexa number 3B8C represented by 16 bit binary 
Q15.12 Explain the conditional operator in Verilog.
  The conditional operator is used to check true or false condition of a variable and execute a statement for 
 true condition or execute an alternative statement  for false condition. The format of condition statement with  
 condition operator is,
A ? statement_B : statement_C ;
 If A is true then statemet_B is executed and if A is false then statement_C is executed.
Q15.13  What are Verilog primitives?. List the Verilog primitive logic gates.
 Verilog primitives are predefined basic building blocks in Verilog HDL that can be used to model or design 
 the structure of large digital circuits. Verilog includes 12 basic logic gates as predefined primitives and they  
 are,
and, nand, or, nor, xor, xnor, not, buf, bufif1, bufif0, notif1, notif0

--- Page 1325 ---
15.94                                              Digital Logic Circuits
Q15.14  Write a short note on user defined primitives.
 Truth tables can be implemented as user defined primitives in Verilog program. 
 The user defined primitive starts with the keyword primitive and ends with the keyword endprimitive and 
 do not have a module. Therefore, the primitive has to be inserted before the module in a program in which  
 the truth table has to be instantiated. 
Q15.15  What are function and task in Verilog?
 The function in Verilog is like a subroutine in a programming language. The repeated computation of a 
 variable value using a group of statements are coded separately as a function and used any number times in  
 a main program.  
 The task is a subroutine equivalent to a module that is written inside the main module and can be called in 
 a Verilog main module code any number of times. Task is a complete Verilog code similar to a module and  
 enclosed with keyword task and endtask.
Q15.16  Write a short note on initial and always blocks in Verilog. 
 The initial blocks are primarily used to initialize variables and ports with specific values. An initial block 
 executes only once, at the beginning of simulation. 
 The always blocks are used to enclose the executable statements of the Verilog code. The always block is  
 executed repeatedly throughout the simulation. 
 A module can have any number of initial and always blocks. When initial and always block has multiple  
 statements, they are enclosed by the keywords begin and end.

Appendix A.15
APPENDIX 5: Boolean Theorems 
Theorem 1:             x + x = x
                                  x . x  = x
Theorem 2:             x + 1 = 1
                                  x . 0  = 0
Theorem 3:             (x' )' = x
(Involution)
Theorem 4:              x + (y + z) = (x + y) + z
(Associative)           x . (y . z) = (x . y) . z
Theorem 5:             (x + y)'  =  x'. y'
(DeMorgan's Law      (x . y)'  = x' + y'
  or DeMorgan's
      Theorem)
Theorem 6:              x + (x . y) = x
(Absorption)              x . (x + y) = x
                                  (y is absorbed)
